The Western Australia (WA) government is funding three WA businesses to support five projects that progress development and manufacture of a range of battery technologies and components for residential, commercial, industrial, and defence applications.

The Round 1 allocation from the WA government’s $50 million (USD 35.8 million) Local Battery Manufacturing Program will enable the three successful applicants to develop and test prototypes, purchase advanced equipment and expand production capacity.

Applications include residential energy storage batteries, large community batteries, inverters, and locally manufactured battery components.

WA Minister for Energy and Decarbonisation and Manufacturing Amber-Jade Sanderson said the projects will support local battery manufacturing.

“We’re helping build resilient supply chains, creating highly skilled jobs, and supporting Australia’s transition to a cleaner energy future,” Sanderson said.

The funding recipients include Magellan Powert, which designs and manufactures industrial-grade AC and DC uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems, energy storage units, batteries and electric vehicle (EV) infrastructure.

Adarsh Investments is a WA-owned and operated manufacturer, fabricator and importer of component parts, and ProtoLab Manufacturing produces electronics solutions.

Funding streams under the WA Local Battery Manufacturing Program includes a production-ready stream, which provides up to $100,000 in matched funding to businesses for projects in three categories of pre-production activities.

The production scale-up stream provides up to $5 million in matched funding to existing battery manufacturers for projects that scale-up their operations, including through purchase of capital equipment, workforce training, costs associated with upgrading existing or new premises, and engaging business or manufacturing expertise.

text:
Another month, another disappointment for Ford as combined sales plummeted 10.3% in August to 170,681 units. That’s a decline of nearly 20,000 vehicles and this can largely be chalked up to the elimination of the Escape.

Electric vehicle sales plunged 79.4% and this was partly due to the axing of the F-150 Lightning. Dealers only sold 148 of them last month, which was down 95.4% from a year ago.

More: Ford Showed Dealers Its Cheapest New Car Yet, A Boxy $25,000 SUV

The aging Mustang Mach-E didn’t do much better as sales tumbled 72.5% to a disappointing 1,989. However, it’s important to note last year’s sales were elevated as there was a mad dash to buy vehicles before the clean vehicle tax credit expired on September 30.

Putting EVs aside, overall Ford sales fell 10.3% to 163,175. The top seller was unsurprisingly the F-Series, which found 67,504 takers. That was a slight 1.2% decline from a year ago and this only equates to 814 units.

In a distant second place was the Explorer, which was down 4% to 19,801. It was followed by the affordable Maverick as 13,680 Americans scooped one up last month.

While the sales chart wasn’t terribly interesting in August, the Mustang was up 12.7% to 3,647 units. Furthermore, the Bronco Sport climbed 8.3% while the Bronco fell 8.8%.

It’s also worth noting the recently redesigned Expedition is having a tough go as August sales were down 11% and it’s off 11.6% year-to-date. Part of this can likely be blamed on high gas prices, which makes it a shame we never got the hybrid variant that was originally promised in the 2023 UAW contract.

Ford August 2026 Sales

Mixed Result At Lincoln

Things were also bad at Lincoln as sales dropped 10.4% to 7,506 units. This can be blamed on the discontinuation of the Corsair as sales fell from 2,526 to just 266.

However, Lincoln recently introduced the 2027 Corsair, which comes with a facelift and a Chinese passport. While it looks great and features a new hybrid powertrain, pricing has shot up $7,310 to begin at $46,495 before a $2,295 destination fee.

Speaking of China, the Nautilus had a good month as sales were up 28.9% to 3,627 units. The American-made Aviator also took to the air as sales climbed 22.4%, but dealers only sold 1,732 vehicles.

Unlike the Expedition, the Navigator ended up in the black as dealers moved 1,881 of them for a 15.8% increase.

text:
How ISAIC and TUKATECH are Building a Blueprint for Workforce Development, Demand Manufacturing, and Domestic Production.

The apparel industry is navigating one of the most significant periods of change in its history. Rising labor costs, increasing material costs, workforce shortages, shorter product lifecycles, and growing sustainability expectations are forcing manufacturers to rethink long-established business models.

For years, these challenges have been discussed at conferences, through pilot programs, and in social media forums. Far fewer organizations have successfully integrated the necessary components into a practical operating model.

With the expansion of its Detroit headquarters, ISAIC has moved beyond proving an idea. It has established a working ecosystem that combines workforce development, digital product creation, entrepreneurship, advanced manufacturing, and commercial production within a single environment.

Jennifer Guarino, President, CEO, and Co-Founder of ISAIC, believes the organization's evolution marks an important milestone.

"We are no longer a proof of concept. We are a working center that brings integrated solutions to industry while making advanced manufacturing technologies accessible to our community."

Addressing Industry-Wide Challenges

Every apparel manufacturer faces the same fundamental pressures: controlling costs, improving speed, increasing flexibility, and responding to changing consumer demand.

According to Ram Sareen, Chairman - Founder of TUKATECH, these challenges cannot be solved simply by shifting production to lower-cost regions. Long-term competitiveness requires manufacturers to improve productivity, reduce material waste, and make greater use of digital technologies throughout the product lifecycle.

"The cost of labor and the cost of material will continue to increase. The question is, how do you control it? Technology allows manufacturers to reduce waste, improve productivity, and make manufacturing competitive where products are actually consumed."

Rather than viewing automation as a replacement for people, Sareen sees technology as an enabler, helping manufacturers produce more efficiently while strengthening regional manufacturing capabilities.

Building on a Proven Foundation

ISAIC's expansion is significant because it builds upon measurable accomplishments rather than future aspirations.

Over the past several years, the organization has established itself as a nationally recognized resource for apparel manufacturing, workforce development, and product innovation. Its integrated operating model combines technical education, commercial manufacturing, product development, entrepreneurship, and technology adoption in a single facility.

That approach has already been validated through collaborations with leading organizations, including Carhartt, supporting domestic manufacturing initiatives, workforce development, and product innovation. At the same time, ISAIC has provided entrepreneurs, emerging brands, and manufacturers with access to professional development and manufacturing capabilities that would otherwise require substantial capital investment.

The expansion into its new headquarters strengthens a model that is already operating successfully while significantly increasing its capacity to serve the industry.

Expanding a Complete Digital Manufacturing Ecosystem

ISAIC's expansion is about far more than adding new equipment. It is creating one of North America's most comprehensive environments for apparel product development, workforce training, and demand-driven manufacturing.

The expanded facility brings together every major stage of the product lifecycle within a single integrated workflow. Designers can develop products digitally, validate fit in a virtual environment, engineer patterns, optimize material utilization, produce prototypes, manufacture production-ready components, and move seamlessly into commercial production—all within the same facility.

The new environment combines advanced digital product development with modern manufacturing technologies, including CAD and pattern engineering workstations, marker making, 3D fit evaluation and virtual sampling, automated fabric spreading, high-ply cutting, single-ply laser cutting, production-length cutting tables, plotting systems, and integrated sewing production capabilities. Dedicated education laboratories equipped with the same professional software used by industry ensure that students and workforce participants learn using current production technologies rather than simplified classroom tools.

For manufacturers, entrepreneurs, and brands, the result is access to a complete digital-to-production ecosystem that supports everything from initial product concepts and rapid prototyping to production planning, workforce development, and commercial manufacturing.

As Guarino explains, "We can now demonstrate these technologies in real time while delivering integrated manufacturing and training solutions from one location."

For Sareen, the significance extends beyond the equipment itself.

"The real value isn't any individual machine or software application. It's the integration of the entire workflow—from product development through manufacturing—allowing companies to access the capabilities they need while preparing for future growth."

Rather than investing in isolated technologies, ISAIC is expanding an operating environment where innovation, education, and production reinforce one another every day.

Connecting Design to Manufacturing

One of the industry's longstanding challenges has been the disconnect between product development and production.

Design, pattern engineering, manufacturing planning, cutting, and production have traditionally operated as separate disciplines, often involving multiple organizations, disconnected workflows, and repeated handoffs.

ISAIC's integrated environment helps eliminate those barriers by bringing together the technologies, expertise, and production capabilities required throughout the development process.

As Sareen explains:

"Our industry has historically been fragmented. ISAIC brings those capabilities together, allowing companies to access the services they need without having to build an entire infrastructure themselves."

Instead of managing disconnected processes, designers and manufacturers can move seamlessly from concept to production through an integrated digital workflow.

Learning in a Production Environment

Perhaps ISAIC's most distinctive characteristic is that education takes place alongside commercial manufacturing.

Rather than separating classroom learning from industrial practice, students, entrepreneurs, designers, and manufacturers work within an environment where products are actively being developed and produced using the same technologies and workflows found throughout the industry.

This creates a learning experience that extends well beyond operating software or equipment. Participants gain an understanding of the complete manufacturing process—from product development through production—while experiencing the realities of quality, workflow, collaboration, and commercial execution.

Guarino believes that people and technology must advance together.

"You can advance technology, but if people don't have the skills to use it, the industry won't move forward. Likewise, you can train people, but without access to modern technology, they won't be prepared for the future."

Sareen sees ISAIC as a modern version of apprenticeship.

"People learn best when they experience the complete process—from design through manufacturing. That creates better professionals and stronger businesses."

ISAIC is not simply teaching the future of manufacturing. It is manufacturing while preparing the future workforce.

Lowering the Barriers to Innovation

Many entrepreneurs and emerging manufacturers possess innovative ideas but lack access to the technology, expertise, or infrastructure required to bring products to market.

ISAIC addresses that challenge by providing access to professional development and manufacturing resources without requiring businesses to make significant upfront investments.

Sareen compares the concept to a familiar service model.

"It's like Kinko's. If you only need a few copies, you don't need to buy a copier. Entrepreneurs can access exactly the technology they need, when they need it, and grow their businesses at the right pace."

This philosophy has guided TUKATECH's global TUKAcenter network for more than two decades, supporting thousands of entrepreneurs and manufacturers as they progressed from initial concepts to successful commercial businesses.

Sustainability Through Better Manufacturing

For manufacturers, sustainability must ultimately align with operational performance.

Reducing physical sampling through digital product development, improving fabric utilization, minimizing material waste, and producing closer to actual demand all contribute to both environmental responsibility and improved profitability.

As Sareen summarizes:

"The first question isn't how we become sustainable. The first question is, how do we sustain the business?"

Technology enables those improvements not by changing individual processes, but by connecting them into an integrated workflow that improves both business performance and environmental outcomes.

A Blueprint for the Industry

Perhaps the greatest significance of ISAIC's expansion is not the installation of new technology.

It is the validation of an operating model.

A model where workforce development, entrepreneurship, digital product creation, education, and advanced manufacturing reinforce one another rather than operating independently.

Guarino believes that model helps organizations move forward with confidence.

"Transformation can feel risky. By bringing people, technology, and manufacturing together, we're helping organizations understand what's possible and giving them the confidence to transform."

For Sareen, the long-term vision is equally straightforward.

"Make what you need, when you need, for who you need."

Detroit may be where this model continues to evolve, but its implications extend well beyond one city. By integrating people, technology, education, and manufacturing into a single ecosystem, ISAIC has established a blueprint that communities, educators, manufacturers, and economic development organizations can adapt as they strengthen the future of domestic apparel manufacturing.

The future of apparel manufacturing is no longer a concept waiting to be proven.

text:
The Trump administration is making moves critics said could slow down the transition to greener transportation and increase emissions. They warned the changes would mean more health issues and higher costs for Oregonians.

As the administration moves forward with lowering federal fuel economy standards, Congress is set to vote to block states from limiting tailpipe pollution.

Rachel Sakata, transportation strategies section manager for the Oregon Department of Environmental Quality, said transportation is the state's largest source of greenhouse gases, responsible for 35% of emissions.

"With the higher emissions that we're going to continue to see, you're going to have more people who may be suffering from adverse health effects such as asthma, respiratory and cardiac diseases, which can lead to more hospital visits and reduced work time," Sakata outlined.

Oregon has joined other states in suing the administration over plans to drop light-duty vehicle fuel economy targets from about 50 to 35 miles per gallon. The White House argued lowering the standards will make cars cheaper for average Americans, estimating purchase costs to drop by nearly $1,000.

While Sakata acknowledged there is a higher up front cost for buying electric cars, the savings from buying less gas and from lower maintenance costs add up. Sakata added with batteries getting cheaper and what would have been increased production by auto manufacturers, EV costs were expected to go down.

"In Oregon, we've seen at least 12% of new vehicle sales were EVs, and so by limiting the types of EVs that are out there, it just makes it harder for people to find the EVs that they really want and are enjoying and are investing in," Sakata explained.

Last year, Republicans in Washington ended federal tax credits for EVs years before they were to expire. Sakata said the Oregon Clean Vehicle Rebate Program can still help reduce the upfront cost of buying or leasing an electric vehicle.

Last year, Republicans in Washington ended federal tax credits for EVs years before they were to expire. Sakata said the Oregon Clean Vehicle Rebate Program can still help reduce the upfront cost of buying or leasing an electric vehicle.

text:
To compare two very different approaches to EV value, a New Jersey family took both on the same 500-mile round trip between New Jersey and Vermont.

The matchup paired Rivian's new R2 against a Chevy Equinox EV 2RS priced roughly $15,000 lower.

Here's what to know

A video from EVenture Family (@Eventurefamily) followed a Rivian R2 Catalina Cove Launch Edition and a Chevy Equinox EV 2RS over almost the same highway loop. Both started fully charged, and each vehicle ran on 21-inch wheels.

Rather than making it a flat-out race, the couple used the drive to look at the issues families tend to care about on longer EV trips: highway energy use, charging stops, navigation and planning, and overall comfort.

Despite the large price gap, the creator said he expected both SUVs to end up "probably right around 3 miles per kilowatt-hour."

EPA ratings make the range comparison look straightforward, but the drive suggested the answer is messier in practice. The all-wheel-drive Equinox EV is rated at 285 miles, while the R2 carries a 330-mile EPA estimate, though the creator said of the Rivian, "nobody's getting that."

Charging specs also didn't tell the whole story on this route. The Equinox can top out at about 150 kilowatts, and the R2 is capable of higher rates, but the available stations did not include the hardware Rivian needs to reach its best numbers, so both SUVs mostly ended up using Tesla Superchargers.

More background

When the Equinox arrived at a Tesla Supercharger in Bennington, Vermont, it still had about 25% battery left, which was better than predicted.

A charger error appeared after about five minutes at one stall, so the driver moved to another unit, and the session then continued normally until charging began tapering near 70%.

One commenter wrote, "Efficiency without compromise is my gold standard to assess real advancement in this space."

What can be done?

How long an EV trip really takes depends on more than the window sticker, including speed, weather, wheel choice, charger access, and whether the route lets the vehicle use its fastest charging capability.

The test also underscored how competitive cheaper EVs have become. The Rivian offers a newer design and a more premium cabin, but the Equinox still looked like a credible road-trip choice because of its strong efficiency and lower purchase price.

One commenter put it this way: "Really conflicted. Don't need another crossover/small suv thing in my stable, but the R2 clearly is the better vehicle ... is it $30k better? ... ehhhh ... EQ is absolutely 100% a great value and a good car, but it's looking like it will be getting replaced shortly because I make bad decisions."

Where can I learn more?

The Vermont run showed how quickly EV value turns into a real-world question of price, charging access, and everyday efficiency — not just EPA range. The coverage here digs into those same tradeoffs, from Rivian's push to win over more buyers to the cost and range questions that can sway a family toward a premium model or a cheaper one.

• As prices keep shifting, misunderstood myths about EVs still shape family buying decisions.

• Over a decade of ownership, shocking cost differences of maintaining EVs kept showing up.

• For many households, surprising savings from owning an EV can outweigh sticker shock.

Each one adds a little more context to the question hanging over this road-trip test: how much extra capability is really worth paying for. That calculation gets tougher as lower-cost EVs keep getting better.

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Congressman Brett Guthrie (KY-02), Chairman of the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, delivered the following opening statement at today’s markup of 10 bills.

Chairman Guthrie’s opening statement as prepared for delivery:

“Good morning, and thank you all for attending today’s markup. We are taking up several bills that highlight the Committee’s effort to support energy innovation, cut burdensome red tape, and lower costs for hardworking American families.

“We know that success for the nuclear industry—from the fuels, manufacturers, and reactors to the operators and workers—will be essential for long term American technological leadership globally and for reliable and abundant energy here at home.

“We must strive to return to a pace of nuclear expansion that surpasses other nations. And we must do so in a way that strengthens public confidence in American technology.

“This morning we are considering six nuclear related bills that build on the bipartisan reforms we started two years ago with the ADVANCE Act, which improved nuclear permitting, brought the benefits of nuclear energy to Americans faster, and maintained our commitment to safety.

“The bills before us today clarify pay authority, improve transparency, and eliminate unnecessary Atomic Energy Act requirements to ensure licensing runs more smoothly.

“The continued bipartisan work on nuclear policy reflects well on this Committee’s ability to advance critical energy policies, and we’ll see that bipartisan spirit reflected in several of the amendments to the bills before us today. And all of these bills deserve strong bipartisan support.

“We are also examining legislation that would provide needed updates to the Clean Air Act. Outdated provisions in the law have created counterintuitive and burdensome policies that increase costs and negatively impact quality of life across this country. These are commonsense solutions.

“The bills before us will cover a range of issues, including ensuring that the federal government retains the authority to regulate interstate commerce on our nation’s railways, preventing one state from being able to dictate policy for the rest of the nation; and reauthorizing a successful grant program to help bus operators replace old equipment with new technology.

“We will also consider a bill to support the recovery of critical minerals from domestic sources by modernizing and streamlining EPA regulations of lithium-ion batteries, providing greater clarity and certainty for our domestic battery recycling industry.

“I want to thank all of the Members who have worked so hard to help bring these important bills before the Committee today.

“Thank you, and I yield to the Ranking Member for his opening statement.”

title: How a Georgia Power Workforce Program Bet on Atlanta's Westside
description:
Someone asked why the workforce training that Georgia Power already ran through community college partnerships couldn’t be brought directly to the community.
“We couldn’t care less about the program,” Watters says.
That question captures a huge lesson learned from the program: job awareness is as much a barrier as job readiness.
What Georgia Power Gets Out of It Watters is candid about the business case.
An HR specialist now working at Georgia Tech is a natural future candidate for an HR role at Georgia Power.
text:
Every Monday evening for ten weeks, Jason Watters drove two and a half hours from Birmingham, Alabama, to Atlanta, ran a two-hour career training session at Vicars Community Center, then turned around and drove home. He did it rain or shine, week after week, because he wanted the participants to see his commitment.

“They saw that Mr. Jason is coming two and a half hours away every Monday,” says Watters, Workforce Development Manager at Southern Company. “We owe it to ourselves to show up.”

That consistency and the philosophy behind it are the heart of what Watters calls one of the better workforce initiatives he has been part of. The pre-employment training program, launched as part of the broader Westside Resilience Corridor effort, brought together Georgia Power, Southern Company, Groundswell, the City of Atlanta, and Vicars Community Center to offer residents of Atlanta’s historically underserved westside a pathway into energy sector careers. What it delivered was something larger than any of those partners initially anticipated.

Beginning With the End in Mind

The program grew out of conversations that were originally much more modest in scope. Georgia Power’s Community Resilience Group had been meeting with corridor partners to discuss how infrastructure investment alone could not deliver equitable outcomes for westside neighborhoods. Someone asked why the workforce training that Georgia Power already ran through community college partnerships couldn’t be brought directly to the community.

“Our answer was, well, why not,” Watters recalls.

Within two or three email exchanges, a planning process was underway. The goal, as Watters put it, was to begin with the end in mind: identify jobs that mattered — both to Georgia Power and to the broader energy industry — and work backwards to identify the skills people would need to compete for them. The target population was residents who were underserved, underrepresented, or underemployed.

The curriculum that emerged covered electrical and energy system fundamentals, construction readiness and tool proficiency, solar and distributed energy basics, and soft skills, which Watters considers most essential. Every week, regardless of which technical module was on the agenda, the program wove in coaching on communication, workplace readiness, resume writing, elevator pitches, and interview prep.

“That last one was probably the most important,” he says. The cohort turned out to be far more diverse than anyone had planned for: participants ranged in age from 21 to considerably older, and included college graduates, people working toward their GED, mothers returning to the workforce after years away, and people new to the city altogether.

“Regardless of what their interests were, we wanted to develop something where everybody left better to compete for whatever roles they have an interest in,” Watters says.

Removing Barriers Before They Become Reasons to Leave

The program recruited from a wide network: the Urban League of Greater Atlanta, Black Men Lab, a radio partnership with WAOK, and the four West Side corridor churches, whose pastors advertised the opportunity directly to their congregations. Over two weeks, the outreach generated more than 90 applicants. All were invited to an orientation at Vicars Community Center. The event was standing-room only.

The cohort was screened down to 22 individuals. Over ten weeks, 20 completed the program — and the two who left did so for reasons unrelated to the program itself, one of whom had to relocate to care for a family member.

Watters attributes that retention rate largely to the wraparound support built into the program’s design. Participants received hot meals at each session and food boxes to take home. Transportation was covered through rideshare funding. Childcare was available. Stipends were distributed periodically. None of this was framed as charity — the program was intentional about not calling out individuals who needed support, instead communicating at the outset that resources were available for anyone who needed them.

“Those three components, more so than the curriculum and just the engagement we have with students, really served us well,” Watters says.

The support extended well beyond the classroom. Watters describes one participant — recently released from a correctional facility and living in transitional housing — who maintained perfect attendance throughout the program. When he secured full-time employment, transitional housing immediately moved him out, leaving him without stable housing just as he was getting back on his feet. The team scrambled to coordinate temporary living arrangements.

“We couldn’t care less about the program,” Watters says. “We wanted to make sure that this gentleman was good, because he worked so hard to get himself back on his feet.” He is now working as an equipment operator for the City of Atlanta.

Placement, Not Placement Rate

The program’s first job placement came after week one — before the curriculum had even fully begun. A participant expressed interest in supply chain; Watters’s team connected him with employers in the southwest Atlanta area. By that Thursday he had an interview. By Friday he had a job. He kept coming to the sessions anyway, rolling in each week with three friends who were also in the cohort.

That early success sparked what Watters calls the “praise report”: a standing segment at the start of each Monday session in which participants shared job offers, interviews, assessments passed, or continuing education milestones.

“It made people want to have something to celebrate,” he says. “It really motivated everybody.”

About a month after graduation, 16 of the 20 graduates were either employed or enrolled in formal continuing education programs in fields spanning supply chain, human resources, customer service, skilled trades, construction, energy efficiency, and even audio engineering. An engineering graduate who had no idea what to do with his degree is now working as an energy assessor for a utility services firm headquartered two blocks from where he grew up.

“How do you aspire to a job that you didn’t know existed?” Watters asks.

That question captures a huge lesson learned from the program: job awareness is as much a barrier as job readiness.

“Sometimes we take for granted that people are aware of the opportunities that we have, because they’re on a website,” Watters says. A posting on a careers page does not reach the same people that a pastor does, or that a neighbor in a utility truck does.

The program addressed this gap through an “employer spotlight” segment built into each weekly session — a 20-minute window for a hiring manager or small business CEO to talk about their work directly with participants. The effect was practical: a participant might leave that session knowing not just that a job existed, but also that someone at the company could vouch for them.

What Georgia Power Gets Out of It

Watters is candid about the business case. The program was not charity, and framing it as such would undersell what it actually accomplished. The graduates, even if they are not Georgia Power employees, are working in fields directly transferable to the company’s workforce needs — HR, supply chain, construction, energy efficiency, skilled trades. They are also, by working and earning, more likely to be stable utility customers. And they are, in Watters’s framing, boots on the ground: people who go home every evening in the logo shirt of wherever they work, as organic advocates for what a career in this industry can look like.

“The quickest way to economic development is economic empowerment,” he says. “The more people that you have working, the more likelihood you have of being able to pay your Georgia Power bill on time — but not only that, we want strong communities.”

There is also a longer-term talent pipeline logic. An HR specialist now working at Georgia Tech is a natural future candidate for an HR role at Georgia Power. A construction worker placing underground infrastructure is building skills directly applicable to utility work. None of these are guaranteed outcomes, but they are probable ones — and they cost far less to develop than recruiting from scratch.

What Watters pushes back against is the framing of workforce development as a box to check. Georgia Power has been present in Atlanta neighborhoods through K-through-12 career exposure days, community college sponsorships, summer internship programs, and community resilience education — work that predates and outlasts this particular cohort.

“You have to do the work, and you have to be consistent with doing the work,” he says. “You can never really unmeet someone.” Watters reports still hearing regularly from graduates, even receiving a text on Father’s Day or a call to share news of a new apartment.

What Comes Next

Both Watters and West Hunter Baptist Church’s Rev. Cedrick Von Jackson have expressed interest in a second cohort as soon as logistics allow. In the interim, Watters is hoping to organize a hiring fair at Vicars Community Center — not a job fair, he is careful to say, but a hiring fair, with actual employer partners ready to make connections with the roughly 70 applicants who expressed interest but were not selected for the first cohort.

“We now have a product that those employer partners recognize and can trust,” he says.

For a second full training cohort, Watters says he would design things somewhat differently: recruiting more specifically to particular trades or job families, then building the curriculum around those targets rather than trying to serve everyone at once.

“We ended up doing what you never do for a pilot,” he says. “We didn’t make it easy for ourselves. We had a diverse group of people with many different interests, yet we found a way for everybody to get something.”

That improvisational generosity — the willingness to bring in an extra child for an evening, to record a session for someone who couldn’t make it, to stay until everyone had a safe way home — is what Watters describes as the program’s real operating principle. The curriculum was a framework. The relationships were the work.

“Relationships don’t expire,” he told participants every week. “Once you meet someone, you can never really unmeet them.”

name: Texas Environment
title: Texas A&M System could cut dozens of core courses, including race, gender and climate classes
description:
Last month, the University of Houston cut about 40% of its courses from the core, from 241 courses to 144.
Separate from A&M's review of core curriculum under SB37, the system has also reviewed courses to make sure they comply with an A&M system policy banning the teaching of race and gender "ideology."
Other A&M system institutions recorded similar recommended cuts, to varying degrees.
Tarleton State University could also cut geology classes like "Intro to Environmental Science," and "Natural Disasters" from its science requirement.
If approved, the revised cores will be effective for new A&M students starting in fall 2027.
text:
The Texas A&M University System Board of Regents will consider cutting dozens of courses from the core curriculum across 11 universities on Thursday, in response to a state law requiring all general education classes to be "foundational."

Among the proposed deletions are various courses about women and gender; climate and the environment; as well as Black and Latino history, literature and culture.

Texas colleges have historically decided what courses count toward the core curriculum for all their undergraduates, but state lawmakers have asserted more oversight of that process. Senate Bill 37, passed in 2025, required public colleges and universities to review almost 13,000 general education courses, emphasizing that they should prepare students for life and work. Some institutions, like the University of Houston, have already pared down what general courses count toward a college diploma.

READ MORE: How a battle over workforce, 'indoctrination' is reshaping the Texas core curriculum

A&M's suggested cuts would reduce the core by 30%, from 260 courses to 182, interim provost Jerry Strawser said in a Wednesday email to faculty and staff. A committee of 20 faculty members, administrators, community leaders and industry representatives helped make the recommendations.

"The courses recommended for removal may be relevant within specific areas of study; however, they did not meet the committee's threshold for remaining part of the core curriculum," Strawser wrote.

Texas requires all undergraduates to take 42 credit hours across specific subjects and learning objectives, which are set by the state.

SB37 doesn't explicitly ban any topics from the core. However, courses about diverse populations have been a frequent casualty of the reviews. Some conservative lawmakers and administrators have framed those courses as too niche for a core that is supposed to indicate what every student should know.

The law largely left it up to universities to define what meets the new state standards of "foundational" and "fundamental." Some administrators have also framed the cuts as an effort to reduce the size of a bloated course catalog. Last month, the University of Houston cut about 40% of its courses from the core, from 241 courses to 144.

The A&M flagship will delete more courses than the other A&M system institutions, possibly because it had a larger core to begin with, according to a list included in the board's meeting agenda. The flagship also enrolls more students: Out of the system's 133,000 undergraduates in fall 2024 - the most recent year for which data was available - Texas A&M enrolled more than 57,000 of them.

Separate from A&M's review of core curriculum under SB37, the system has also reviewed courses to make sure they comply with an A&M system policy banning the teaching of race and gender "ideology." There are some exemptions for classes outside the core or at the graduate level.

It's unclear how many courses moved out of the core due to the race and gender review, but the SB37 review will cull the core even further.

TEXAS A&M: Board names insider Susan Ballabina as flagship president

At the flagship, the latest potential cuts include core courses cross-listed in women's and gender studies - a program that is already being phased out. Those include "Gender and Health," "Feminist Science, Tech, and Medicine," and "LGBTQ Literatures."

Others involve global cultures or demographics: "Intro to Latinx Literary Studies," "Dance in World Cultures," a sociology course called "Intro to Race and Ethnicity" and an African American studies course called "Popular Musics in the African Diaspora."

Some involve the environment or social justice, like an atmospheric science course called "Climate Change," a performing arts course called "Aesthetics of Activism," and a human health course called "Introduction to Health Disparity and Diversity."

A&M will also consider removing some courses that count toward the state's core history requirement,

including

"Southwest Borderlands," "Blacks in the U.S. 1607-1877" and "Blacks in the U.S. since 1877." A course about Native American history would remain an option for students.

The university didn't appear to take a blanket approach, as not all courses touching on topics of race or ethnicity were slated for removal. Some also involved topics unrelated to "culture wars," like "Finite Mathematics," and "Geography of Texas."

All students are required to take one course to satisfy a language, philosophy and culture requirement, and the English department took a particular hit in the proposal. If approved, it would lose

"21st Century Literature and Culture," "Arthurian Literature," "Sci-fi Present and Past," and "Bible as Literature," among others currently in the core.

Other A&M system institutions recorded similar recommended cuts, to varying degrees.

Prairie View A&M University, a historically Black university that opened 150 years ago on a former slave plantation, could slash some courses from its core, like "Sociology of Minorities," "Blacks and the American Political System," "Social Problems," and "Mexican-American Culture." Several race-related courses would remain, however.

Texas A&M University-Victoria's proposed cuts included "Women in the U.S.," "Mexican-American History," "Immigration in the U.S." and "African American History."

Tarleton State University could also cut geology classes like "Intro to Environmental Science," and "Natural Disasters" from its science requirement.

If approved, the revised cores will be effective for new A&M students starting in fall 2027. Students can still take the courses as electives, a designation that could potentially lead to fewer people taking the classes.

title: Part 3: Which announcements are becoming reality in the US PV manufacturing boom?
description:
Stage 1 – Announced and Planning: Cell capacity totals 10.8GW and module capacity 8.6GW.
Polysilicon leads with 8.8GW, alongside 12GW of cell capacity and 5 GW of module capacity.
Stage 3 – Finishing Up (build well underway): Cell capacity leads at 25.66GW, module capacity follows at 17.16GW.
Across every stage of the tracker (Announced, Planning, Construction and Operational), wafer capacity is the smallest number on the page, and by a wide margin.
The 55.90GW of cell capacity currently under construction represents real progress, but scale alone does not determine market access.
text:
Pipeline status: four stages, four realities

The reason headline gigawatt figures are a poor guide to the state of the market is that “announced” encompasses an enormous range of project maturity levels. PV Tech Research’s tracker breaks the pipeline into four stages, and the distribution across them tells a more precise story than any single aggregate number.

Stage 1 – Announced and Planning: Cell capacity totals 10.8GW and module capacity 8.6GW. These are the least certain figures in the pipeline. Projects at this stage are most exposed to cancellation, delay, or changes in scale or technology.

Stage 2 – Construction: The picture shifts upstream. Polysilicon leads with 8.8GW, alongside 12GW of cell capacity and 5 GW of module capacity. This is a meaningful signal in its own right. The polysilicon investment that looked comparatively thin against the scale of the gap in the second article is, in fact, further along in its execution than the headline capacity number alone would suggest.

Stage 3 – Finishing Up (build well underway): Cell capacity leads at 25.66GW, module capacity follows at 17.16GW. This is the most encouraging tier of the tracker, since it represents the capacity closest to becoming a shippable product. The focus on cells and modules, however, also highlights the persistent problem of insufficient wafer capacity to support this pipeline in the US.

Stage 4 – Operational: 36GW of polysilicon capacity producing 15.5GW, 5GW of wafer capacity producing 3.2GW, and cell and module capacity and production as detailed across the first two articles in this series. This is the only tier where the numbers are not projections.

Why project-level tracking beats headline counting

The case for tracking individual projects rather than adding announced gigawatts is straightforward once the four-stage breakdown is laid out: not all announcements are equally verifiable, and treating a 50%-complete project the same as an operational line overstates the real capacity available at any given moment. Knowing the stage a project has actually reached is what turns a raw announcement total into a usable market signal, because it separates capacity that is genuinely close to shipping from capacity that still depends on financing, permitting, or policy conditions holding steady.

That distinction is also what makes the wafer gap the clearest finding in this dataset. Across every stage of the tracker (Announced, Planning, Construction and Operational), wafer capacity is the smallest number on the page, and by a wide margin. The great majority of US manufacturers currently building capacity are concentrated in cells and modules, with only a minority committing capital to wafering. That leaves the question raised in the second article unresolved: without meaningfully more wafer capacity under construction, a domestically produced polysilicon ingot still has nowhere to go but overseas, where it is sliced into a wafer and shipped back into the country before it can become a US-made cell. Of everything the tracker shows, this is the gap most likely to still be open in 2030 unless investment patterns shift.

From capacity to compliance

Understanding where capacity sits across the four stages is essential, but it does not answer the more urgent question facing manufacturers, developers and investors: which of these facilities will produce cells that meet the overlapping requirements of Anti-Dumping and Countervailing Duty (AD/CVD) rules, Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) restrictions and potential Section 232 tariffs on solar imports?

The 55.90GW of cell capacity currently under construction represents real progress, but scale alone does not determine market access. A domestically located facility does not automatically produce compliant output if its cells rely on Chinese polysilicon or on wafers processed by entities subject to FEOC restrictions. And if Section 232 tariffs are imposed, the compliance balance shifts again: cells that currently qualify under AD/CVD rules may still face tariffs if their upstream inputs, wafers, polysilicon, or both, originate in countries subject to Section 232 measures.

This is where the wafer gap becomes a multi-layered compliance issue. If US-made cells depend on offshore wafers, their compliance status depends not only on the origin of those wafers and the polysilicon inside them, but also on whether that origin exposes them to tariffs that could erase their cost competitiveness. The more fragmented the domestic supply chain remains, the more exposure manufacturers and developers carry across multiple regulatory fronts.

Applying the framework to the pipeline

The next article in this series applies the four-tier cell procurement framework we have developed at PV Tech Research to the capacity tracked here, mapping announced and operational projects against AD/CVD, FEOC and Section 232 compliance requirements. It identifies which portions of the 55.90GW cell pipeline are likely to qualify as Tier 1 (fully compliant across all three regimes), which face compliance uncertainty, and which are structurally unlikely to meet the requirements that govern federal procurement and IRA incentive eligibility.

title: One fewer barrier for farmers who want to cover fields with solar panels - LA Times
description:
It makes it easier for farmers to convert their fields to solar panels.
California has set a goal of reaching 100% clean electricity by 2045, and building more solar projects on farmland would help.
Converting fields to solar arrays has become an attractive option for farmers who are grappling with restrictions limiting the groundwater they can pump from wells.
The water limits get stricter each year until 2040 in many areas, and farmers face fines if they exceed them.
“But some transformation is appropriate given the water shortage that we have and the clean energy issues that we have.”
text:
A bill that exemplifies the lack of water for farming in California just passed the state Legislature. It makes it easier for farmers to convert their fields to solar panels.

Decades ago, state lawmakers were concerned about too many farms being turned into new subdivisions. So in 1965, the state started giving tax breaks to growers who agreed to keep their land in farming. But now farmers who want to switch to solar are finding the strict rules are like expensive locks on their property, with high fees to get out of the agreements.

The bill adopted Monday night targets areas where growers are now limited in how much groundwater they can pump and are being forced to leave some of their land dry and unplanted.

These landowners, largely in the Central Valley and the Central Coast, would no longer have to pay fees for the conversions.

The legislation, Assembly Bill 1156, “gives farmers and local communities in our most water-constrained regions another option for land that can no longer be productively farmed: use it to generate clean energy,” its author, Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-Oakland), said.

The bill, which the Senate approved in a 21-14 vote at the end of the legislative session, now awaits Gov. Gavin Newsom’s signature.

California has set a goal of reaching 100% clean electricity by 2045, and building more solar projects on farmland would help.

Converting fields to solar arrays has become an attractive option for farmers who are grappling with restrictions limiting the groundwater they can pump from wells.

California’s Sustainable Groundwater Management Act was adopted in 2014 to address chronic overpumping that has led to falling aquifer levels and caused dry wells and sinking ground. The water limits get stricter each year until 2040 in many areas, and farmers face fines if they exceed them.

Researchers at the Public Policy Institute of California estimate that as much as 900,000 acres of farmland in the San Joaquin Valley may need to be left dry by 2040, largely because of the pumping limits. At the same time, global warming is worsening droughts throughout the West, putting even more strain on scarce water.

“As climate change forces difficult transitions across California’s agricultural communities, we should be looking for practical ways to help them adapt while moving us closer to our clean energy goals,” Wicks said.

The California Farm Bureau and other agricultural groups oppose the bill. In a letter before the Senate vote, they said that the latest version discards a carefully designed plan that would have included more protections for agricultural land and instead takes a blanket approach “that can convert the state’s best farmland to industrial use.”

Assemblymember Steve Bennett (D-Ventura), who voted for the bill, said it promotes solar energy while enabling farm owners with inadequate water to find another use for their land.

“I’m not overly concerned that there’s going to be this massive transformation of agriculture,” he said. “But some transformation is appropriate given the water shortage that we have and the clean energy issues that we have.”

name: EPA
title: EPA Proposes 2027 Construction General Permit For Public Comment - Environmental Law
authors: Andrew C.  Silton, Andrew C. Silton, Erika H. Spanton, Julia F. Li
description:
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) recently published its proposed 2027 National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) Construction General Permit (CGP) for public comment.
Longer term, the proposal may influence state construction stormwater permits as states renew their own general permits.
Most construction stormwater discharges are regulated under general permits, which authorize them on a categorical basis.
Although the federal CGP’s coverage is limited, states often look to the federal permit when developing or renewing their own construction stormwater permits.
Public Comment and Next Steps EPA is soliciting public comments on the proposed 2027 CGP and its accompanying fact sheet through September 17, 2026.
text:
Article Insights

Key Takeaways

What Happened? The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) recently published its proposed 2027 National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) Construction General Permit (CGP) for public comment. The proposal would replace the current 2022 CGP, which will expire in February 2027, and includes targeted changes addressing (1) the Supreme Court’s decision in City and County of San Francisco v. EPA, (2) submission of Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plans (SWPPPs) when seeking coverage, (3) sediment basin stabilization measures, and (4) purported streamlining of certain permit requirements.

Who Is Impacted? When it goes into effect in 2027, the permit will affect construction site operators that obtain CGP coverage in areas where EPA administers the NPDES program, including Massachusetts, New Hampshire, New Mexico, and the District of Columbia. Longer term, the proposal may influence state construction stormwater permits as states renew their own general permits.

Next Steps? Developers, builders, contractors, companies that commission substantial construction projects, and trade associations should consider submitting public comments by the (recently extended) September 17, 2026 deadline. Find EPA’s proposed 2027 CGP and accompanying fact sheet here.

Background

The Clean Water Act (CWA) generally requires NPDES permit coverage for stormwater discharges associated with construction activities that disturb one or more acres of land, as well as smaller construction activities that are part of a common plan of development or sale that will ultimately disturb one or more acres. Most construction stormwater discharges are regulated under general permits, which authorize them on a categorical basis.

EPA’s CGP applies where EPA, rather than an authorized state, serves as the NPDES permitting authority. Although the federal CGP’s coverage is limited, states often look to the federal permit when developing or renewing their own construction stormwater permits. Simply put, the final permit will impact updates to construction general permits issued in states where EPA is not the permitting authority.

Significant Proposed Changes

1. EPA proposes to revise water quality-based requirements in an attempt to implement San Francisco. The draft permit proposes an approach to implement City and County of San Francisco v. EPA, 604 U.S. 334 (2025), in which a B&D team led by Principal Drew Silton secured a major CWA victory on behalf of San Francisco. In San Francisco, the Supreme Court held that the CWA does not authorize EPA to impose “end-result” permit requirements in NPDES permits that make permitholders responsible for the overall quality of receiving waterbodies. In this proposed CGP, EPA acknowledged that its 2022 CGP “includes language that could be considered the type of end-result provision addressed in the San Francisco decision.”

EPA thus proposes to remove a narrative condition in the 2022 CGP requiring discharges to be “controlled as necessary to meet applicable water quality standards.” Instead, EPA has proposed more specific conditions tied to characteristics of the discharge itself. For example, EPA’s proposed changes intend to clarify that discharge conditions in Part 3.1 would be “limited to pollutants associated with construction activity” by changing “floating solids” to “floating, settled, or suspended solids.” Observing these conditions in the discharge could trigger corrective action. EPA previously added similar conditions in its 2025 CGP modification for newly eligible projects in Lands of Exclusive Federal Jurisdiction; the 2027 proposal would extend those conditions to all CGP permittees.

2. Operators to submit SWPPP information with the Notice of Intent. EPA proposes a consequential administrative change to the permit: an operator submitting a Notice of Intent (NOI) to obtain coverage would need to provide either its full SWPPP, a webpage where the SWPPP remains available throughout CGP coverage, or the SWPPP site map together with the signed SWPPP certification. EPA says a submitted SWPPP would serve as a reference and would not provide a definitive basis for compliance determinations because SWPPPs change during construction.

Although several states require submission of a SWPPP with the NOI, EPA has not to date required this of operators. This proposal could give EPA immediate access to information that operators generally provide only upon request or during an inspection. Before submitting SWPPP materials, including site maps or certifications, operators may want to establish procedures to identify information that is appropriately protected from disclosure and to determine which of EPA’s submission options best fits their projects.

3. New requirements affecting sediment basins and site stabilization. For operators that use sediment basins, EPA proposes to require stabilization before stormwater is first directed to the basin. At a minimum, operators would need to stabilize the embankment and side slopes following construction. EPA developed this proposal after finding certain sediment releases associated with use of newly excavated basins before sufficient stabilization.

4. Permit streamlining measures. The proposed permit would clarify that perimeter controls are necessary only in areas that could receive stormwater from disturbed areas, simplify stabilization deadlines for sites in arid, semi-arid, and drought-stricken areas, and provide additional flexibility when unforeseeable snow or frozen ground makes compliance with ordinary stabilization deadlines impracticable.

5. Reduced dewatering monitoring and reporting burdens. The existing CGP requires daily turbidity monitoring when dewatering discharges reach certain sensitive waters and quarterly reporting of weekly averages. EPA specifically requests comment on whether longer-term, continuous dewatering operations should qualify for less frequent monitoring. One option would allow weekly monitoring after more than three days of continuous discharge if the average turbidity during the first three days does not exceed the applicable benchmark. EPA also seeks input on reducing duplicative quarterly reporting where multiple operators coordinate monitoring at the same site and on reporting obligations when no dewatering discharge occurs during a quarter.

EPA seeks input on all provisions in the proposed CGP, but expressly requests input on the SWPPP submission requirement, the new water quality-based conditions implementing San Francisco, turbidity reporting for sites with multiple operators, and potential monitoring flexibility for longer-term dewatering.

Public Comment and Next Steps

EPA is soliciting public comments on the proposed 2027 CGP and its accompanying fact sheet through September 17, 2026. Operators, trade associations, and other entities that are currently or potentially affected may consider submitting public comments. Existing 2022 CGP permittees should monitor the status of EPA’s final permit and consider transition steps.

At the time of this writing, EPA is not planning to hold a public hearing, but interested parties may request one pursuant to 40 C.F.R. § 124.12.

2027 Range Rover Electric

Land Rover’s most radical flagship has officially arrived. Say hello to the first-ever, internal combustion-less Range Rover Electric. text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, the House Committee on Small Business Subcommittee on Rural Development, Energy, and Supply Chains is holding a hearing titled “Fueling the Golden Age: Future Resource Needs and Small Business Opportunity.”

Subcommittee Chairman Jake Ellzey’s opening statement as prepared for delivery:

Welcome to today’s hearing, “Fueling The Golden Age: Future Resource Needs and Small Business Opportunity.”

Thank you to our witnesses for traveling here today and for sharing your expertise with the Subcommittee.

As Industy and the American people are increasingly moving to usiness-friendly states, American energy and water markets are being tested like never before. In my home state of Texas, the population has grown by almost 10 million residents over the last 20 years.

Expanded domestic manufacturing, grid buildout, and emerging technology are driving the highest demand on these resources in decades. In states like Texas with a rapidly growing population, we also need to ensure we have the water resources for new homes. While we welcome this growth, it brings with it a duty for this Committee, Congress, and state legislatures to ensure that its costs do not fall unfairly on Main Street.

Small businesses depend on reliable and affordable electricity and water. Aging infrastructure and rising demand means higher rates, slower upgrades, and less certainty. Especially as manufacturing jobs return to the United States and new technologies increase demand for reliable resources, small business owners cannot be left behind.

Today, we will hear about the efforts underway at the state level to respond to growing resource needs and how the federal government can best partner with government agencies, corporations, and rural electric cooperatives to plan for long-term sustainable growth.

While some states are investing directly in new energy and water supplies, others are adopting rate structures that require large users to pay for the upgrades they trigger, ensuring that American households and small-business ratepayers don’t bear the upgrade costs. The variety of solutions presented today provide models for how communities across the nation can prepare for future growth.

With this unprecedented surge in demand comes an opportunity to support our small businesses in meeting this challenge head-on. Small businesses are an essential part of our energy and water industries. Local contractors, suppliers, rural electric cooperatives, and equipment manufacturers are central to building the generation, transmission, and water infrastructure needed to support economic expansion and the return of industry to American soil.

The ability for small businesses to bid on projects, scale workforces, and secure certifications will determine whether local communities enjoy the benefits of new development or see the work move elsewhere.

I look forward to hearing from today’s witnesses about the state of America’s existing electric and water infrastructure and how states are preparing to respond to growing resource demand, and how Congress can support small business needs through this rapid growth.

And with that, I now recognize the Ranking Member, Representative Morrison, for her opening remarks.

text:
NEW YORK--U.S. new-vehicle sales slipped in July as buyers continued to face elevated prices, with GlobalData reporting light-vehicle sales declined 1.2% from a year earlier to 1.38 million units.

The annualized U.S. selling rate eased to 16.6 million vehicles from 16.7 million in June. GlobalData noted July marked the first year-over-year decline in three months, although the comparison was made more difficult by relatively strong sales in July 2025, when buyers were accelerating battery-electric vehicle purchases ahead of the expiration of federal tax credits at the end of September 2025.

Affordability remains a key issue for U.S. consumers. GlobalData said average transaction prices reached $45,969 in July, an increase of $1,129, or 2.5%, from a year earlier. Automakers were also spending more to move vehicles, with average incentives rising 5.7% year over year to $3,375.

The U.S. weakness came as the broader global market remained relatively soft. GlobalData said the worldwide light-vehicle selling rate improved slightly from June to more than 90 million units annually, but year-to-date sales totaled 50 million vehicles, nearly 4% below the first seven months of 2025. Results varied sharply by market, with China sales falling 22.9% year over year while India posted a record month with sales surging 33.8%.

name: Indiana Environment
title: This environment is antagonistic to local business - Smile Politely — Champaign-Urbana's ...
description:
This type of corporate bullying is openly hostile to small, locally owned businesses.
Most small businesses do not have the financial means to fight a Fortune 50 company.
But if we’re being honest with each other, it’s not just massive corporations stymieing the establishment and growth of local businesses.
It’s also other local businesses, albeit bigger ones.
We have to put our money where our mouths are and shop and support small, locally owned businesses.
text:
Last week, The News-Gazette reported on a real estate covenant gumming things up for a potential locally owned and operated pharmacy in Urbana. As you may recall, both the Walgreens and CVS on Philo Road in Urbana closed. A new, locally owned, small pharmacy wants to open in the Sunnycrest Center, but a restrictive covenant signed by Walgreens and other Sunnycrest businesses means that no pharmacy may open in the designated area until 2042. Even though Walgreens and CVS are closed it doesn’t seem to matter to Walgreens, which “has declined to remove these restrictions.” Seems petty at best, insidious at worst.

This type of corporate bullying is openly hostile to small, locally owned businesses. Most small businesses do not have the financial means to fight a Fortune 50 company. In 2025, Walgreens ranked 26 on the Fortune 500 list, with an estimated profit of nearly $150 billion. We’ve written about corporate greed, but this seems to take the cake for the most absurd and gratuitous example of that power being wielded against Champaign-Urbana.

But if we’re being honest with each other, it’s not just massive corporations stymieing the establishment and growth of local businesses. It’s also other local businesses, albeit bigger ones. We’ve seen how some local companies have grown to be large enough to buy up other smaller local entities—last week the owners of Pekara Bakery and Bistro, Central Illinois Bakehouse, Martinelli’s, Prairie Fruits Farm & Creamery, Salt Fork Food Works and Espresso Royale cafes also purchased The Literary. It’s not inherently a bad thing; we love to see local folks invest in the community and create fantastic places for eating, drinking, and entertainment. Sometimes, though, there is a confluence of not enough competition and systemic and infrastructural circumstances that create a mostly hostile environment for experimentation and building something long lasting.

Recently, we have seen a Downtown Champaign staple, Watson’s Shack & Rail, announce that it will close its doors. While the food truck and vendor stall at The Yard will remain open, the sit-down, table service, and full bar experience of the restaurant will be gone. We’re not privy to all of the exact reasons for this decision, but in the announcement they cited “the current downtown landscape, economic hardships and ever-changing hospitality trends.” You don’t have to be a real estate or hospitality expert to read between the lines that it is no longer financially viable to continue to operate that space. Lease prices are extremely high, staffing has become an issue for restaurants everywhere, and this economy doesn’t exactly encourage extra spending on leisure and dining. Everything is more expensive for everyone, full stop.

The ever-rising cost of commercial rents across Champaign and Urbana means that some people literally cannot afford to open a business. In looking at some listings online, you can see that many retail spaces are upwards of $10 per square foot. Coupled with a triple net lease where the tenant pays insurance, maintenance, and taxes (never mind utilities), it’s simply cost prohibitive, unless you can take out a massive loan. In Midtown Champaign, for instance, some leases are $14 per square foot. Multiply that by 1500+ square feet and you’re looking at at least $21,000 a year for rent. The space soon-to-be-formerly occupied by C-U Flower House on South Neil Street is $27 per square foot with a modified gross lease. To be clear: We are not suggesting that the landlords of the spaces are maliciously trying to gouge their tenants. What we are saying is that it’s really hard to foot those bills while trying to establish a new business. It means that someone successfully selling their goods at the farmers market might not be able to leverage enough to take the loan that secures them the ideal location, or earn enough profit to pay employees well, afford the lease, and put money into research, development, and keeping things fresh.

And note that we haven’t even talked about historic opposition to new bus routes, the ways in which liquor licenses are awarded, the slim profit margins for restaurants, meeting the demands of codes, regulations, and inspections, and workers deserving to earn enough for them to pay their (also increasingly high) rents and mortgages.

Let us return to the problem of the pharmacy in Urbana. The Philo Road corridor in Urbana is in need of assistance. It demands more economic development. It requires places for the community to meet their needs. Salt & Light, the anchor business in the Sunnycrest Center, is doing a lot of programming to help meet those needs, including offering meeting space, hosting the Carle Mobile Clinic, and creating a third space for people to use wi-fi and build relationships. But they cannot do it alone. Perhaps what we’ve all grown to understand in this particular political moment is that no one single entity—non profits, government, higher education, the corporate sector—can fill the gaps left by a lack of cooperation among all entities. As community members, we have to advocate for our elected officials to modify the system to help constituents. We have to push back on what could be described as corporate greed. We have to put our money where our mouths are and shop and support small, locally owned businesses. As for that small pharmacy that is so needed in Urbana? Contact your elected reps. Make a fuss. Send letters to Walgreens. If we all do our tiny parts, perhaps we can push against bureaucratic nonsense to inspire real change that makes things a little better for all of us.

The Editorial Board is Jessica Hammie, Louise Knight-Gibson, Julie McClure, and Mara Thacker.

text:
Wieland, headquartered in Ulm, Germany, says it is significantly increasing the share of renewable energy used at its German production sites.

Through its partnership with Vattenfall, a leading European energy company, Wieland has inaugurated the Nauen Solar Park near Berlin. The facility will generate approximately 47 gigawatt-hours of renewable electricity annually.

Developed, built and operated by Vattenfall, Wieland will purchase the entire electricity output from the solar park under a long-term power purchase agreement (PPA) for the next 10 years. This volume corresponds to approximately 15 percent of the electricity Wieland procures each year for its German operations, the company says.

Key to decarbonizing production

Wieland says it aims to achieve net-zero emissions across its entire value chain by 2045. To accomplish this, the company is pursuing a comprehensive decarbonization strategy built on increasing the use of recycled materials, electrifying production processes and expanding the use of renewable energy.

The Nauen Solar Park particularly supports the third pillar by increasing the share of renewable energy in Wieland’s electricity supply and reducing indirect emissions associated with purchased electricity, the company says. The site has an installed capacity of 46 megawatts peak. The facility comprises approximately 80,000 solar modules across roughly 40 hectares and will generate around 47 gigawatt hours of renewable electricity annually.

"Reducing our CO₂ emissions is one of the most important long-term priorities for our company,” says Wieland Group CEO Erwin Mayr. “That is why we continue to invest in recycling, the electrification of our operations and the expansion of renewable energy. The Nauen Solar Park is another important building block on our path to net-zero emissions by 2045. It demonstrates how sustainability and industrial value creation can successfully go hand in hand."

Renewable energy strengthens supply security, competitiveness

The partnership with Vattenfall is part of a broader set of initiatives through which Wieland continues to increase the share of renewable energy in its electricity supply while strengthening the foundation for competitive manufacturing, according to the company.

In addition to long-term power purchase agreements, Wieland is investing in its own renewable electricity generation to secure long-term energy supplies for its sites, further reduce emissions and strengthen sustainability as a key competitive advantage.

To expand its renewable energy portfolio, Wieland pursues a technology-neutral approach that includes hydropower generation at its Voehringen production site in Germany, rooftop photovoltaic systems installed around the world and the company-owned Erbach Solar Park near Ulm, one of the largest solar parks in southern Germany. Wieland also is evaluating investments in its own wind power installations.

"There is no single solution for decarbonizing energy-intensive manufacturing processes,” says Andreas Torka, senior vice president sustainability & technology for the Wieland Group. “Success depends on a combination of measures. Long-term power purchase agreements such as the one we have signed with Vattenfall are an important tool for reducing our indirect emissions from purchased electricity, expanding the share of renewable energy in our energy mix and strengthening the long-term competitiveness of our operations."

A GOP precinct chair, a Democratic candidate for Texas House and Prosper Mayor David Bristol all had the same message: say no to data centers.

Prosper’s planning and zoning commission sided with them, voting unanimously Tuesday night against rezoning land for the $580 million Project Tomahawk near the town's western border, where it meets Aubrey and Celina. Commissioners said they received about 400 emails opposing the project.

Commissioner Glen Blanscet said he denied it because of unanswered questions about its energy usage. He said data centers, though controversial, will be crucial to ensuring the United States remains technologically competitive.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Even so, they don’t belong in Prosper, he said.

“I think data centers are the current bogeyman of our country … I’m not sure they necessarily deserve to be the bogeyman,” Blanscet said. “But … there are right places for it and wrong places.”

Related:Project Tomahawk: What to know about proposed $500M Prosper data center

As demand for artificial intelligence grows, the construction of data centers has accelerated. Opponents have voiced concerns over proposed facilities causing a strain on water and electricity resources while supporters emphasize tax revenue data center projects can generate for cities.

A survey conducted by a regional planning body in North Texas recently found that many local governments in Texas don't have the infrastructure to support the expected growth of data centers. Cities such as Fort Worth and Denton have taken steps toward enacting moratoriums on data center projects.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The data center in Prosper, a suburb about 35 miles north of downtown Dallas, had been proposed east of FM 1385 and south of Parvin Road in Denton County. The developer, Dallas-based White Rose Partners, said the data center would have occupied less than 20% of a 37-acre site.

The facility was expected to use around 301 gallons of water a day, which is about 40% of the maximum water used by the average single-family home, according to Prosper’s engineering standards.

Related:More than half of Texas data centers broke law by not responding to water use inquiry

The developer said they couldn’t estimate how much power the data center would consume because they hadn’t identified a tenant and the facility’s power usage would depend on the tenant’s needs.

John Varin, senior director of development and acquisitions for White Rose Partners, said the project could have generated up to 50 jobs on-site and $2.5 million in annual tax revenue for Prosper once fully operational.

Article continues below this ad

Resident Aileen Blachowski said her neighbors at the master-planned community Windsong Ranch were concerned the developer would not give them information on who the potential tenant would be. Blachowski, a Denton County GOP precinct chair, also asked the town to conduct its own study on how the data center would contribute to noise in the area.

“This is not about [not in my backyard]. This is not about understanding the importance of data centers,” Blachowski said. “It's about understanding what's the truth.”

Related:'Make no mistake: Keller will be heard.' City considers legal action over proposed Westlake data center

Aubrey resident Monica Barlow, who lives near the proposed project site, said the voices of neighbors mattered.

“Noise, traffic, light pollution, utility strain, environmental concerns and changes to neighborhood character affect people based on proximity, not city lines,” Barlow said.

Before the planning and zoning commission heard public input on the data center, Bristol urged the body to deny the project until the town develops ordinances and design standards related to data centers.

“Whatever you approve here becomes a precedent for the next application,” Bristol said. “Prosper will have to negotiate each of them one at a time, with nothing on the books to negotiate from.”
