text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, Congressman Jake Ellzey (R-TX), Chairman of the Small Business Subcommittee on Rural Development, Energy, and Supply Chains, held a hearing titled “Fueling the Golden Age: Future Resource Needs and Small Business Opportunity” to examine the energy, water, and workforce needs necessary to support America's next generation of manufacturing, technology, and industrial growth.

“We must build the infrastructure needed to keep growing, alongside water and energy demands, without leaving families, farmers, and small businesses to pay the bill. If we get this right, we can protect ratepayers, strengthen our communities, and create lasting opportunities for the local contractors, manufacturers, and skilled workers who will help build America’s future,” said Chairman Ellzey. “Small businesses are ready to help meet this moment. Congress should make sure they have the trained workers, certifications, and opportunity to compete for these projects, so the economic benefits stay in the communities where the work is being done.”

---

Watch the full hearing here.

Below are some key excerpts from today’s hearing:

Chairman Ellzey: “Representative Harris, how can the federal government best partner with States to ensure our water and electric infrastructure is capable of sustaining long term growth?” State Rep. Harris: “Thank you for the question, Mr. Chairman. What we are seeing in Texas is that the best approach for us, as a state, has been for the federal government to grant our state agencies primacy in regulatory matters, like the Railroad Commission of Texas and the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality, as they relate to water issues. As we transition into that nuclear renaissance that I was talking about in my testimony, that’s one of the primary areas of focus. How can we make the permitting process more efficient? We know that as soon as these reactors are demonstrated as safe, then it’s just a matter of site selection. Could the federal government then grant primacy on, at least, site selection to the state of Texas to expedite the process of building and locating those nuclear reactors where they’re needed throughout the state?”

Chairman Williams: “Infrastructure projects are often announced before a community has enough trained workers to execute them. So, to you, Mr. Harris, what workforce needs do you see in your district, particularly for electricians, line workers, welders, pipefitters, water operators, industrial-controls technicians, and on, and on?” State Rep. Harris: “Great question, Mr. Chairman. Water operators are one of the most significant needs that we see in the rural areas. We’ve got multiple; one county can have several different water systems operating. All mostly non-profit. And for those guys to find water operators is almost impossible. So, we’ve been working with the Texas Education Agency and our career and technical colleges to develop pathways for kids out of high school to get certifications in water system operation. Electrical work is another, especially as we see the proliferation of data centers and all these new technologies being built; we don’t have enough electricians and skilled labor like that. We, as the legislature, have been working for years with our education agencies to try to develop a fast track for taking kids directly out of high school, with certification, directly into the workforce as skilled labor.” Chairman Williams: “Well, plumbers, welders, carpenters, etc., save our economy.” State Rep. Harris: “That’s right.”

Rep. Finstad: “For rural manufacturing communities in states like Minnesota, what would it take to make those sites competitive locations for new energy and manufacturing investments? Mr. Ellis: “Thank you, Congressman. I think it’s an important question. My colleagues at AFPI have highlighted that the cheapest megawatt of power is usually the one we already have. Similarly, the best workforce we can use to revitalize former industrial sites is the workforce that's already there. I think we can invest in workforce development. I think we can site new large projects on brownfield industrial sites. That way, we can skip some of the remediation process. We can provide liability protection for pollution or other remediation elements that might already be there. I think that those sites can really be a place where we can springboard into the next generation of manufacturing.”

text:
In a few short weeks we'll get our first real look at the Bentley Torcal, the first all-electric ultra-luxury car from Bentley.

And with it, Bentley will quietly advance its place in the world of super-luxury cars.

With the official release of the Torcal, named for the ancient rock formations of El Torcal, Andalusia, and fitting for the way torque shapes the Bentley experience, Bentley will build its most powerful car ever, generating 850 hp and 738 pound-feet of torque.

But as with any Bentley, power is only the start of the luxury experience, though its core to the Bentley ethos. A quiet but powerful drive experience is complemented by interiors that set the stage for a personalized experience, finished with details that clients will specify and craftsmanship that lends a hand-made appeal to a car clearly born in the digital age.

Torcal Will Evolve Bentley's Design Language

While details are still scant, there are a few clear ideas in the information that Bentley has released so far. First, we'll see more crystal—both hand-made crystal inside the car and replications of crystal on the multimedia system. We may see new crystal headlight details and tail lights, too, since these applications have been a Bentley signature since 2019.

And the addition of hand-blown, faceted crystal is sublime; it amplifies the light that passes through it adding depth, color and a spiritual sense. The concept of crystal makes its way onto the multimedia system, too, using color-changing graphics to communicate the Torcal's cabin modes, which presumably pair with drive modes, to convey an overall sensory experience in the cabin.

The teaser videos and photos that Bentley has shared indicate an SUV-style body with flatter surfaces than we see in the Bentayga; the tail lights and Bentley badge also look evolved. Inside, teaser images also show new door panels and softer materials than we've seen in the past.

The big question is whether or not the Torcal will feature evolved headlights and tail lights, but the answer to that will have to wait until September 23rd.

A Cabin Experience Designed To Evolve The Bentley Experience

Bentley calls the in-cabin experience of the Torcal a "curation engine driven by sensory neuroscience." The idea is to add more than fine finishes and bespoke design by complementing it with air that adjusts to your mood and drive settings, sound that reflects this and lighting that highlights, or downplays, the mood. Using sensors, engineered sound, advanced lighting and climate modulators, drivers of the Bentley Torcal can create the ultimate environment in the cabin.

Buyers can also, of course, create their ultimate Bentley, opting for bespoke details and Mulliner finishes.

Electric Driving Is True To Bentley's Roots

Electrification has been part of the Bentley ethos for decades; the company was among the first carmakers to top its assembly plant with solar panels and work toward a carbon-free footprint. Sustainability and sensitivity to the environment remains an important initiative for the company.

Incorporating that electric idea into its vehicles proved popular among Bentley buyers. The company introduced the hybrid Continental and Flying Spur to much success; the Continental GT Speed, at 771 hp, is, until the Torcal makes its debut, the fastest Bentley on the road. It achieves that power via a plug-in hybrid and V8 powertrain that delivers 61 more hp than the now phased-out 12-cylinder engine that previously held the power record, which it also outsells.

The Bentley Torcal shares its unique electric platform with the Porsche Cayenne, a more powerful and more sharply intentioned EV. It's estimated that the Torcal will have a driving range of just over 300 miles and a charge time of less than 20 minutes using a DC fast charge station. Or, owners will be able to charge it at home overnight with a level 2 charge system.

Will The Market Welcome An Electric Bentley?

The big question for Bentley though, is will the Torcal prove popular with buyers? If the Rolls-Royce Spectre is any indication, it should. The Spectre is Rolls-Royce's second-best-selling vehicle, reflecting both the innovation and luxury of the electric coupe, as well as the luxury buyer's penchant for owning the car they want without worry about range anxiety.

And the reception of the all-electric Genesis GV90, the brand's first foray into the ultra-luxury category, has been overwhelmingly positive, showing that powertrain is not a detriment to a model's intrigue.

The growing popularity of EVs, thanks to the global spike in oil prices and increasing availability of public charging, adds to the lure and the luxury of the Bentley Torcal. But charging at home in privacy, driving in stealth mode and having Bentley's fabled torque underfoot is an unbeatable lure.

text:
The new facility was first announced in 2024, when Midsummer revealed plans to build a 200MW line to produce its copper indium gallium selenide (CIGS) cells in the Flen area of Sweden. The project attracted a €32 million (US$37 million) grant from the European Commission to finance the new line.

But in a statement yesterday, Midsummer said it would decline the EU grant and halt its plans for the facility.

It said the project’s financing had been adversely affected when Midsummer was denied financial support from the Swedish Energy Agency’s ‘Industriklivet’ programme, the country’s flagship initiative to cut industrial emissions.

“We are happy to establish a new factory in Sweden in the future when the commercial and financial conditions allow it, but it will not happen within the framework of the specific project we have been awarded time-limited EU support for. A major reason is that we have strategically decided to choose other financing models for new factories than self-financing,” said Midsummer’s CEO Eric Jaremalm.

Midsummer said it was now exploring “significantly less capital-intensive opportunities” for establishing manufacturing facilities abroad, in collaboration with established global and “very large industrial players”.

The company said this so-called “asset-light model was based on collaboration with large industrial partners.

“Instead of owning and operating all the factories itself, the company supplies machinery, raw materials and know-how to enable local production of solar cells on different continents. This provides significant early income in the form of machine orders and also ongoing income after the factory is operational,” the company’s statement said.

This approach is reflected in Midsummer’s recent activities, which have included several significant turnkey orders from overseas customers for its CIGS production equipment.

Midsummer highlighted one of these deals to illustrate its change of tack—a contract last year to deliver machinery with operational responsibility to a solar cell factory in Colombia, with an annual production capacity of at least 100MW. Midsummer said that so far it had received machinery orders worth approximately SEK380 million (US$39.3 million) for this purpose. It said it would also continue to expand production in its own factory in Bari, Italy, which, fully operational, produces 50MW annually.

“Even with the EU grant, self-financing a completely new factory of this size in Flen would have cost us several hundred million SEK, and we do not find it responsible to take such large loans or ask our shareholders for such amounts when we have found other ways to finance our expansion, which in addition to being financially more advantageous are also geographically closer to the fastest growing markets today,” added Jaremalm.

Today, G20 member ministers concluded a two-day Innovation Ministerial in Chapel Hill, North Carolina. The Ministerial was hosted by the Department of Commerce and the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP).

At the conclusion of the Ministerial, G20 Ministers released a consensus statement recognizing that “emerging technologies have the potential to unlock prosperity, enhance productivity, and expand opportunity for all our peoples.”

The Innovation Ministerial Statement articulates shared principles across six pillars: pro-innovation policy frameworks; technology for opportunity and prosperity; skilled technical workforce development; intellectual property policies for artificial intelligence; AI for standards and standards for AI; and industrial innovation and investment in supply chains. Ministers also reached consensus on the Carolina Principles for Emerging Technologies, which call on countries to invest in foundational research, strengthen commercialization pathways, and enable trusted technology adoption and deployment.

The full G20 Innovation Ministerial Statement can be accessed here.

“Achieving consensus in the G20 is no small feat, but the topic of innovation as a driver of growth brought us together for a historic moment of unity,” said Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick. “The statement released by the G20 members ministers today gives entrepreneurs the confidence to invest in their ideas, promotes domestic manufacturing, and ensures intellectual property frameworks foster and protect innovation.”

“In Chapel Hill, G20 countries realized an optimistic vision for the future of emerging technologies, recognizing that flexible policy frameworks crafted to promote innovation will drive economic growth and prosperity. That is the spirit of the Carolina Principles, and that is how we will expand opportunity for Americans and people around the world,” said OSTP Director Michael Kratsios.

At the Innovation Ministerial, OSTP Director Kratsios hosted fireside chats with Elon Musk, CEO of Tesla and SpaceX; David Sacks, Co-Chair of the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology; Bob Mumgaard, CEO of Commonwealth Fusion Systems; Demis Hassabis, Co-Founder and Chair of Google DeepMind; Mark Zuckerberg, Chairman and CEO of Meta; and Michael Crow, President of Arizona State University.

Secretary Lutnick hosted fireside chats with Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of NVIDIA; Tom Brown, Co-Founder of Anthropic; Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI; and Alex Karp, CEO of Palantir.

Other deliverables of the Ministerial included the AI Prosperity Objectives and the AI Prosperity Compact which will further technical workforce development across G20 nations and expand opportunities for private sector partnership.

Representatives from the following nations and unions were present at the two-day Ministerial: the African Union, the Argentine Republic, the Commonwealth of Australia, the Federative Republic of Brazil, Canada, the People’s Republic of China, the European Union, the French Republic, the Federal Republic of Germany, the Republic of India, the Republic of Indonesia, the Italian Republic, Japan, the United Mexican States, the Republic of Poland, the Russian Federation, the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, the Republic of Korea, the Republic of Türkiye, and the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.

text:
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has granted 1.76 billion Renewable Identification Number (RIN) exemptions to small refiners for the 2025 compliance year, raising concerns among farmers and biofuel producers about the potential impact on demand for renewable fuel.

RINs are compliance credits and the “currency” of the RFS program. A RIN is generated when renewable fuel is produced, which can be bought and sold separately from the fuel. Learn more about RINs.

The EPA issued 29 full and partial Small Refinery Exemptions (SREs), allowing refineries to avoid some or all of their obligations under the Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS). In total, 1.76 billion RINS are being exempted.

Learn more about how the RFS requirements work

The EPA will propose reallocating 100% of the difference between the projected and actual 2025 exempted volumes into the Renewable Volume Obligations (RVOs) for 2026 and 2027. EPA says it plans to propose the reallocation before the end of October.

“While we are disappointed that the EPA granted 1.76 billion RIN exemptions, we appreciate the agency’s commitment to fully reallocate those volumes and protect demand that farmers and biofuel producers rely on,” said Maroa, Illinois farmer and IL Corn Growers Association President, Mark Bunselmeyer. “Illinois corn farmers need certainty and strong domestic markets for their crop, and ethanol is an important part of that equation.”

IL Corn will continue to closely follow EPA’s reallocation process and push for policies that protect and expand opportunities for ethanol.

Bengaluru (Karnataka) [India], September 2 (ANI): Union Minister for Heavy Industries and Steel H D Kumaraswamy on Wednesday called upon India's automobile and auto component industry to move beyond resilience and position the country as a global hub for advanced and green mobility technologies.

Addressing the 66th Annual Session of the Automotive Component Manufacturers Association of India (ACMA) in New Delhi, themed 'Beyond Resilience', the Union Minister said the next phase of India's automotive growth must be driven by scale, deeper localisation, accelerated innovation and technological leadership.

'The next phase must be about leadership - building scale, deepening localisation, accelerating innovation and establishing India as a globally competitive hub for advanced and green mobility technologies,' Kumaraswamy said.

The Minister said the automotive and auto component industry is central to India's manufacturing ambitions, supporting millions of livelihoods, anchoring a vast MSME ecosystem and generating a multiplier effect across sectors including steel, electronics, engineering, chemicals, logistics and services.

Highlighting the impact of government interventions, Kumaraswamy said the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme for Automobile and Auto Components is delivering encouraging results.

As of June 30, approved applicants under the scheme had reported investments of Rs 45,477 crore and generated more than 67,000 employment opportunities*, he said.

He said the objective of policy support was not merely to increase production, but to build genuine domestic capabilities, strengthen value addition and establish India as a competitive base for advanced automotive technologies.

The Minister also highlighted the progress made under the government's green mobility initiatives.

The enhanced PM E-DRIVE outlay now stands at Rs 11,900 crore, with the scheme intended to support 45.79 lakh electric two-wheelers. More than 25.66 lakh electric two-wheelers, 2.75 lakh three-wheelers and 53 electric trucks have already been supported, according to the figures shared by the Minister.

He further highlighted the allocation of Rs 4,391 crore for 14,028 electric buses, with 13,800 buses already allocated, as well as Rs 2,000 crore earmarked for public charging infrastructure.

The PM e-Bus Sewa-Payment Security Mechanism, with an outlay of Rs 3,435 crore, is aimed at supporting the deployment of more than 38,000 electric buses.

Battery manufacturing is another key pillar of the transition. The PLI Scheme for Advanced Chemistry Cell Battery Storage, with an outlay of Rs 18,100 crore, aims to establish domestic battery capacity.

The government is also strengthening domestic capabilities in sintered rare-earth permanent magnets, an important input for electric motors and advanced mobility applications, to reduce strategic import dependence and strengthen supply-chain security.

He said the real measure of success must include how much technology is designed in India, how much value is added domestically, how many MSMEs participate in emerging supply chains and how effectively Indian products compete in global markets.

Calling for greater investment in cleaner and emerging technologies, the Minister urged the industry to move beyond manufacturing for the domestic market and develop products and technologies for global markets.

'India should not merely participate in the global mobility transition; India should help lead it,' he said.

The Minister's call comes as India's auto component industry continues to post strong growth.

According to ACMA data, the sector recorded a turnover of Rs 7.60 lakh crore in FY 2025-26, registering 12.7% growth over the previous fiscal. Supplies to OEMs rose 16.3% to Rs 6.63 lakh crore, while exports increased to USD 24 billion.

The industry's strong performance underlines its growing role in India's manufacturing ecosystem and its increasing integration with global value chains.

Speaking at the session, industry leaders also emphasised the need for deeper localisation, stronger Tier-2 and Tier-3 supplier capabilities and greater focus on technology and quality. Maruti Suzuki India MD and CEO Hisashi Takeuchi stressed that global supply-chain restructuring presents an opportunity for India to emerge as a trusted manufacturing hub.

Kumaraswamy said the Ministry of Heavy Industries will continue to work closely with ACMA, SIAM and other industry stakeholders to improve scheme implementation, address operational challenges and create an enabling environment for investment and innovation.

He called upon the industry to invest more boldly in electric powertrains, batteries, power electronics, lightweight materials, vehicle software, sensors and other emerging technologies while strengthening domestic value chains.

text:
The Coalition held a press conference on the banks of the Delaware River where George Washington and his army crossed to New Jersey to win independence from royal oppression and exploitation.

Freedom from the oppressive and devastating impacts of fracking was expressed in the banner they held: “Delaware River, Frack Free Forever!”

The DRBC held their business meeting inside the Visitors Center at noon. Some people went into the DRBC meeting after the press conference to participate in their public comment session.

The Coalition said fracking interests have been trying to overturn the ban on fracking for more than a year through federal legislation, lobbying, and a lawsuit in New York.

In July, Pennsylvania Congressman Scott Perry (R-PA 10th Congressional District) introduced an Amendment to the Water Resources Development Act (WRDA, H.R. 9497) aimed at overturning the ban on fracking in the Delaware River Watershed.

Public pushback and action by legislators who support the ban led to the amendment dying in Committee.

Congressman Perry also has introduced legislation to take away the power of DRBC and the other Commissions to ban fracking—the “Drill Now Act”.

Community support for the campaign to defend the frack ban was expressed by people from the region who attended the press conference.

“Catskill Mountainkeeper is proud to stand with our allies and support the Delaware River Basin Commission in keeping the Delaware River frack free forever!” said Catskill Mountainkeeper’s Program Manager, Taylor Jaffe. “Our communities rely on this watershed as a source of clean drinking water, a destination for recreation and relaxation, and for its ecological and economic benefits. Protecting our shared waters from the harms and pollutants of fracking will always be essential to supporting healthy, vibrant towns and communities.”

"China is the world's largest greenhouse gas emitter, but the U.S. may not be far behind according to projections from the International Energy Agency that say spending '…will outstrip that of China for the first time in decades.' We here in the Delaware River Watershed refuse to be part of that fossil gas buildout and we urge all the Watershed states to stop the devastating development of more fossil fuels," said Karen Feridun, Founder of Berks Gas Truth.

“The Delaware River Basin Commissioners have clear reasons to defend and enforce the Commission's ban on fracking. In Pennsylvania and New York in particular, defending the ban is also an opportunity to protect the constitutional environmental rights of the people, as outlined in the PA and NY Green Amendments,” said Shaelyn Parker, Advocate & Educator at Green Amendments For The Generations. “Green Amendments For The Generations stands beside the DRBC as they protect our right to clean, safe, healthy environments from the ruthless attacks by profit-first industry and politicians.”

B. Arrindell, Director of Damascus Citizens for Sustainability (DCS) said, “To DCS, opposing fracking has always been a matter of protecting public health, both in the present as drilling, pipelines etc. pump poisons into the air and water near these activities but also looking into the future since, for example, once an aquifer is contaminated there is no going back and we are witnessing the health and climate impacts of carbon loading our air. The Delaware River Basin Ban is a vital economic and health protection.”

"More than 15 years into the fracking boom, we have overwhelming evidence on the danger fracking poses to our drinking water supplies and environment. This science is what led the DRBC to declare a temporary and then a permanent moratorium on fracking in the watershed more than 5 years ago. Even in the face of Congressional attempts to overturn this decision, the public—and the science—are clear as the waters of the upper Delaware: don't frack our watershed. We urge the DRBC to stay the course and all political leaders across the watershed to support drinking water by upholding the moratorium," said Doug O'Malley, Director of Environment New Jersey.

“We all fought back last month when fracking interests tried to pass federal legislation to overturn the ban on fracking in the Delaware River Watershed. We prevailed and the ban is still in place but efforts to undo that protection are still underway and we are here today to stand with the DRBC to defend the ban, to call for an end to all fracking everywhere and make it clear to all those who attack the ban: We will never tolerate fracking in our watershed, and pledge to ensure our watershed is Frack Free Forever,” said Tracy Carluccio, Deputy Director, Delaware Riverkeeper Network.

"Overturning the ban on fracking in the Delaware River watershed would put at risk the 15 million people who depend on its drinking water, as well as deepening our global climate crisis,” said Matt Smith, NJ State Director for Food & Water Watch. "Our communities should not be sacrificed for the greedy fossil fuel industry and we stand by the DRBC in maintaining a complete ban on fracking."

More Attempts To Overturn The Frack Ban

Pennsylvania Congressman Rob Bresnahan (R-PA 8th District), who pulled together US Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin and fracking proponents at a closed-door meeting in March 2025, criticized the DRBC’s ban on fracking, calling for “unleashing energy dominance.”

He also has introduced the Mid-Atlantic River Basin Commissions Review Act, which is a witch hunt to undermine DRBC and the other Commissions’ authority by discrediting them. The bill has passed the House and now goes to the Senate.

People Fight Back to Resist Fracking

People have pledged to defend the river in an organized resistance to combat these attempts.

Despite these attacks, the public remains vigilant as the frack ban lives on.

Background

The Delaware River Basin Commission is an interstate commission formed in 1961 by a Supreme Court Decree, and Congressional and state legislation, forming a Compact that governs water resource management in the Delaware River Watershed.

The voting Commissioners are the Governors of the 4 watershed states—New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, and Delaware—and the federal government, represented by the Army Corps of Engineers.

The agency is dedicated to a watershed-based approach to planning and management to protect the shared waters of the river and its watershed, which is why it adopted a fracking ban.

DRBC instituted a fracking moratorium in 2010 when drillers first tried to drill in the Watershed.

The agency researched and deliberated for another 11 years culminating in the adoption of a prohibition on high-volume hydraulic fracturing, or “fracking,” throughout the Delaware River Watershed in 2021.

The Delaware River Frack Ban Climate Action Coalition is made up of organizations that have worked to defend the Delaware River from fracking and advocate for action by the DRBC to address the climate crisis and its ongoing/growing damage in the Watershed, many active for at least the past 16 years.

The groups include (alphabetical order): Berks Gas Truth, Catskill Mountainkeeper, Damascus Citizens for Sustainability, Delaware Riverkeeper Network, Environment New Jersey, Food and Water Watch, Green Amendments for the Generations, and League of Women Voters of Delaware.

“Balcony solar is a practical, easy-to-use tool that can help families save money while allowing more people to participate in our clean energy future,” said Sherrill. “This bill cuts unnecessary red tape, expands access to affordable solar power, and proves that affordability and sustainability can go hand in hand.”

Access to electricity generation beyond the PJM grid

The New Jersey bill also does not include a provision that residential customers secure approval from a utility prior to installing a plug-in solar system, a key component of the bill that will help facilitate energy security for homes outside of conventional grid infrastructure.

This is particularly significant in New Jersey, which is part of the PJM grid network in the north-east US. In April, PJM started its first grid application process under a ‘first-ready, first-served’ approach, which differs from the old ‘first-come, first-served’ approach that had led to significant delays in securing grid connection.

However, the new application process, in which applicants must demonstrate that they own the site on which they intend to build electricity generation projects and make “meaningful up-front financial commitments”, has led to a significant capacity of fossil fuel applications. Of the 220GW of capacity applied for in the first round of the new bidding process in April, natural gas projects accounted for 105.8GW, with nuclear accounting for a further 17.9GW. The Amplify Lithium & Battery Technology ETF (BATT ) had a strong August, thanks to impressive performances by its holdings in the consumer discretionary, materials and technology sectors.

BATT gained about 10.38%, due to its holdings in the lithium battery, copper mining and electrical vehicle industries.

Unlike traditional EV-only funds, BATT’s broad exposure across battery storage, materials, and EVs allowed it to capture simultaneous gains from top holdings like BHP Group, Freeport-McMoRan, and Tesla.

Demand is growing for lithium batteries, propelling the stock prices of companies operating in and supporting the industry upwards. Lithium carbonate and spodumene prices moved higher during August, with concerns about potential supply disruptions in China adding to the bullish sentiment. In particular, news that Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Ltd. could shut down its Jianxiawo lithium mine raised concerns that the lithium market could move toward a deficit.

See more: Balance China’s Shifting Lithium Market With the BATT ETF

This was particularly relevant for BATT due to its exposure to companies throughout the battery supply chain. As of August 31, CATL represented about 6.2% of the fund, while lithium producer Albemarle accounted for roughly 1.7% and Pilbara Minerals represented another 1.6%, according to VettaFi data.

The fund offers direct exposure to companies focused on the lithium battery industry. This includes battery storage operations, battery metals, and also electric vehicle providers.

BATT’s top holdings include mining and metals company BHP Group Limited, which saw a 12.05% return; electric car maker and lithium batteries consumer Tesla, with 18.23%; and copper miner Freeport-McMoRan, with 20.93%.

Materials stocks, with a 59.3% weighting, generated a 15.53% return, according to VettaFi data. That return translated into an 8.96 percentage point contribution to BATT’s monthly gain.

Technology was the second-best-performing sector within the fund, with a return of 6.10% on a 14.96% weighting. Battery manufacturing companies in the portfolio — including Ecopro BM Co Ltd., LG Energy Solution Ltd., and Samsung SDI Co Ltd. — saw the biggest earnings for the month.

Coming in third place, consumer discretionary posted a return of 2.25%, on an 18.49% weighting. BATT’S exposure to Tesla provided another boost. The company represented about 6.9% of the portfolio at the end of August, and its shares rose sharply during the month. Tesla stock closed at $367.95 on August 31, compared with $322.08 on August 3., as investors focused on its upcoming product developments and energy-storage business.

BATT is a little different from a traditional electric-vehicle ETF, since it offers exposure to several parts of the battery industry, including battery storage, metals and materials, and EV companies.

That mix helped the fund in August, as the gains weren’t coming from just one area. Higher lithium prices, stronger copper miners and gains in some of the bigger EV and battery names all helped push BATT higher during the month.

The future: charging where the car already is The central prediction for the next decade is a shift away from thinking about EV charging exclusively as a gas-station replacement.
text:
Summary

This episode of the Urban EV Podcast focuses on one of the biggest obstacles to EV adoption in cities: where people charge their vehicles. Host Rob Hoffman interviews Samuel Bordenave, chief commercial officer at Switch, an EV-charging company focused on multifamily housing and commercial parking. Bourne previously worked at Tesla Energy and says his experience there helped shape Switch's emphasis on technology and customer experience. Switch has deployed charging infrastructure in more than 2,000 buildings across more than 300 cities in the U.S. and Canada.

Charging access is an equity issue

A major theme is that EV adoption cannot become widespread if people living in apartments and condominiums cannot charge at home. Bordenave points out that more than one-third of Americans live in multifamily housing, where residents often share parking garages or park on the street. He argues that these residents — who are disproportionately lower income — risk being excluded from EV adoption if charging infrastructure isn't available where they live.

The economics are also changing. Bordenave notes that EVs have historically been more expensive and that early adopters tended to have higher incomes, but used EV availability is increasing and more affordable new EVs are entering the market. He argues that lower-income consumers may actually benefit from EV ownership because the total cost of ownership can be lower than that of a gasoline vehicle.

Ride-share drivers provide an interesting example. Many urban Uber drivers already use EVs but lack charging at home, forcing them to rely on public chargers. That costs more and takes time away from earning money.

Retrofitting older buildings is a major challenge

Installing chargers in existing apartment buildings is considerably more complicated than putting a charger in a single-family garage. Many multifamily and commercial buildings are decades old and weren't designed to accommodate dozens of EVs charging simultaneously.

A conventional approach could require additional electrical capacity, transformers or expensive infrastructure upgrades — potentially costing hundreds of thousands of dollars before the first charger is installed.

Switch's solution is smart load management. Sensors monitor how much electricity a building is using and charging is adjusted around periods of peak demand. Instead of charging every vehicle at maximum power simultaneously, the system can distribute available electrical capacity intelligently. Bordenave says this can allow a building to support 10 or 15 chargers where it might otherwise only support one or two.

Connectivity and software are just as important as the chargers

The discussion makes clear that an EV charger is much more than a piece of hardware. Chargers need internet connectivity for payments, load management, monitoring, troubleshooting and future utility programs.

Underground parking garages create another problem because installing cellular connections or Wi-Fi throughout a garage can become expensive. Switch has developed a proprietary mesh-network approach intended to reduce the amount of communications infrastructure required.

Switch also emphasizes customer support and proactive charger monitoring. The broader lesson is that charging infrastructure must work reliably after installation; otherwise, property owners can wind up with an expensive problem instead of an amenity for residents.

Interoperability remains a frustrating problem

Another major issue is the fragmented nature of the charging industry. Drivers can find themselves needing multiple apps and accounts to use different charging networks.

Switch is working with FLO and other charging providers on OCPI integrations, which allow customers from one network to access chargers belonging to another. Bourne sees this as a necessary step toward a truly seamless charging experience.

The ultimate goal is universal Plug & Charge: a driver simply plugs in, and charging begins without opening an app or dealing with payment authentication. Bourne says Switch is working with charging companies and automakers on pilots and industry efforts to make that possible. The challenge isn't necessarily the underlying technology; agreements between competing companies and the engineering work required to integrate their systems take time.

Lessons from Tesla

Bordenave’s experience at Tesla also figures prominently in the conversation. He says Tesla taught him the importance of making the customer experience central to the product.

He cites the Powerwall as an example: attractive hardware, an intuitive app and an integrated energy-management experience made the technology appealing rather than simply functional. He says Switch has adopted a similar philosophy by continually improving its app, customer support, reservation capabilities and access controls.

Politics and the end of subsidies

The conversation also examines the impact of changing U.S. EV policies. Bordenave expects the reduction or elimination of incentives to create some short-term pain for the industry. Tariffs are increasing charger costs, while the loss of EV tax credits could cause a temporary drop in vehicle demand.

However, he doesn't believe the EV transition is ending. Lower-cost EVs and an expanding used-EV market could eventually compensate for the loss of incentives. He also sees the current environment as a reason for charging companies to become more efficient, including using AI and other technologies to reduce costs and improve customer service.

EVs could become part of the electrical grid

Perhaps the most forward-looking part of the discussion involves bidirectional charging and vehicle-to-grid (V2G) technology.

Instead of EVs simply consuming electricity, bidirectional vehicles can send electricity back into a building or the electrical grid. Vehicles could charge when electricity demand is low, then provide some of that stored energy during periods of peak demand. This could reduce the need for utilities to build additional generation and transmission infrastructure.

Bordenave says Switch has already conducted projects involving bidirectional technology. The company is also preparing its software infrastructure so it can take advantage of V2G as more compatible vehicles and chargers reach the market.

The future: charging where the car already is

The central prediction for the next decade is a shift away from thinking about EV charging exclusively as a gas-station replacement.

Bourne describes this as the “cell phone model” of charging. Rather than driving somewhere specifically to refuel, EV owners should charge wherever the vehicle is already parked: at home, at work, while shopping or in a residential parking garage.

That means cities will need a much more distributed network of chargers rather than relying solely on large public fast-charging stations. Bordenave expects public charging congestion to get worse before it gets better as EV adoption increases, but believes ubiquitous destination, workplace, residential and curbside charging will ultimately reduce pressure on fast-charging hubs.

Bottom line

The transcript's central argument is that the future of EV adoption will depend as much on infrastructure, software and convenience as on the vehicles themselves. Multifamily residents need affordable home charging, older buildings need intelligent load management, charging networks need to cooperate, and utilities need to embrace EVs as potential grid assets.

Part 98 (Subpart RR).
Background On January 15, 2021, the Treasury Department and IRS issued final regulations under Section 45Q.
Section 1.45Q-3(b) provides, in part, that the requirements for secure geologic storage include compliance with Subpart RR: (b) Requirements for secure geological storage.

Safe Harbor Notice 2026-50 extends and expands the safe harbor described in Notice 2026-1.
text:
The U.S. Department of the Treasury and IRS released Notice 2026-1 on December 19, 2025, to provide interim guidance issued in response to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's (EPA) proposed regulations removing certain reporting obligations under Subpart RR of 40 C.F.R. Part 98 (Subpart RR).

On August 14, 2026, the Treasury Department and IRS released Notice 2026-50, which significantly broadens the relief available to taxpayers claiming the Section 45Q credit by 1) extending the safe harbor to qualified carbon oxide used as a tertiary injectant in a qualified enhanced oil or natural gas recovery project, 2) confirming that taxpayers may rely on the safe harbor to determine amounts subject to recapture under Treas. Reg. Section 1.45Q-5(a) and (c), and 3) extending the safe harbor's applicability beyond calendar year 2025.

Taxpayers may rely on the expanded safe harbor for each reporting year in which the EPA fails to launch its electronic Greenhouse Gas Reporting Tool (e-GGRT) by March 31 of the following calendar year, and this relief remains available through December 31 of the calendar year in which the Treasury Department and IRS publish further interim guidance or forthcoming proposed regulations addressing Section 45Q measurement, reporting and verification requirements.

Background

On January 15, 2021, the Treasury Department and IRS issued final regulations under Section 45Q. Treas. Reg. Section 1.45Q-3(b) provides, in part, that the requirements for secure geologic storage include compliance with Subpart RR:

(b) Requirements for secure geological storage. For purposes of the section 45Q credit, qualified carbon oxide is considered disposed of by the taxpayer in secure geological storage such that the qualified carbon oxide does not escape into the atmosphere if the qualified carbon oxide is – (1) Injected into a well that (i) Complies with applicable Underground Injection Control or other regulations, located onshore or offshore under submerged lands within the territorial jurisdiction of States or federal waters, and (ii) Is not used as a tertiary injectant in a qualified enhanced oil or natural gas recovery project, in compliance with applicable requirements under 40 CFR part 98 subpart RR; …

Section 1.45Q-2(h)(5) provides that, in general, carbon oxide that is injected into an oil reservoir that is not a qualified enhanced oil recovery project under Section 43(c)(2) of the Code due to circumstances such as 1) the first injection of a tertiary injectant occurring before 1991 or 2) a petroleum engineer's certification not being timely filed, cannot be treated as qualified carbon oxide, disposed of in secure geologic storage or utilized in a manner described in Section 45Q(f)(5).

Section 1.45Q-2(h)(5) does not apply to an oil reservoir if:

(i) the reservoir has permanently ceased oil production; (ii) the operator has obtained an Underground Injection Control Class VI permit; and (iii) the operator complies with subpart RR.

Section 1.45Q-3(d) allows a taxpayer to self-certify the volume of qualified carbon oxide claimed for the Section 45Q credit for an enhanced oil or natural gas recovery project if that volume was reported to the EPA under Subpart RR. Notice 2026-50 confirms that a taxpayer using an alternative industry measurement standard for such projects may instead prepare its own supporting documentation internally, as long as a qualified independent engineer or geologist certifies that the documentation is accurate and complete.

Facilities that are subject to Subpart RR are required to 1) report basic information on carbon oxide received for injection, 2) develop and implement an EPA-approved site-specific monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV) plan, and 3) report the amount of carbon oxide geologically sequestered using a mass balance approach and annual monitoring activities. Those reports under Subpart RR must be prepared on a calendar year basis (Annual Reports). The EPA generally requires Annual Reports to be submitted through the e-GGRT system. Historically, the EPA launches the e-GGRT system in mid-February for a given reporting year.

On September 16, 2025, the EPA proposed regulations proposing to remove certain program obligations from the greenhouse gas reporting program, including the obligations in Subpart RR, for reporting years after 2024. The EPA has proposed that the amendments, if finalized, would become effective within 60 days of publication in the Federal Register.

On February 27, 2026, the EPA issued a final rule extending the deadline for Annual Reports for reporting year 2025 to October 30, 2026, underscoring the continuing uncertainty that prompted the Treasury Department's decision to extend and expand its interim relief.

Safe Harbor

Notice 2026-50 extends and expands the safe harbor described in Notice 2026-1. The safe harbor now covers secure geological storage occurring on or after January 1, 2025, and remains available through December 31 of the calendar year in which the Treasury Department and IRS publish further interim guidance or forthcoming proposed regulations rather than being limited to calendar year 2025 as under Notice 2026-1. For each relevant reporting year, the safe harbor applies only if the EPA fails to launch the e-GGRT system by March 31 of the following calendar year.

A taxpayer satisfies the Section 45Q Subpart RR, certification and recapture-determination requirements for a given reporting year if 1) its secure geological storage complies with Subpart RR as in effect on December 31, 2025, 2) the taxpayer has an EPA-approved MRV plan for the project, and 3) the taxpayer submits its Annual Report to an independent engineer or geologist for certification in lieu of filing through the e-GGRT system.

This is a significant expansion from Notice 2026-1, which did not cover carbon oxide used as a tertiary injectant in an enhanced oil or natural gas recovery project and did not address recapture determinations.

Reliance Considerations

Taxpayers may rely on Notice 2026-50 to satisfy the Section 45Q Subpart RR, certification and recapture-determination requirements for secure geological storage occurring on or after January 1, 2025, provided 1) the EPA does not launch the e-GGRT system for the relevant reporting year by the following March 31 and 2) the taxpayer completes the required documentation and obtains certification by the time it timely files its return. That said, similar to Notice 2026-1, this interim guidance is pending forthcoming proposed regulations, and the Treasury Department and IRS may modify or narrow the safe harbor once such guidance is issued.

Energy and Commerce Committee Ranking Member Frank Pallone, Jr. (D-NJ) delivered the following opening remarks at a Full Committee markup of six energy bills and four environment bills:

Today the full Committee is marking up 10 bills – six nuclear bills out of our Energy Subcommittee and four bills from our Environment Subcommittee.

Nuclear energy plays a vital role in our nation’s power grid, providing carbon-free power to the grid around the clock. But we must ensure there is public confidence that nuclear power is safe, and that the cops on the beat are keeping it safe. One of the best ways to ensure that is through transparency. I want to once again state that my support for nuclear energy legislation is contingent upon the Nuclear Regulatory Commission and the Department of Energy having sufficient transparency into their safety rules and regulations, so the American public can be sure that our nation’s nuclear industry is safe.

That’s why I want to compliment Energy Subcommittee Ranking Member Castor on her bill, H.R. 9084, the Department of Energy Nuclear Transparency Act. It is an important piece of legislation that will help build confidence in the American nuclear industry as a whole. As the nation continues to invest in expanding nuclear energy, it is critical we have these important transparency guardrails in place.

I thank the Chairman and his staff for their willingness to work with us on these nuclear bills. In July, I expressed concerns about two of the bills before us today: H.R. 9612 and H.R. 9613. On the Nuclear Advisory Committee Reform Act, the amendment in the nature of a substitute strikes a provision from the introduced bill that would have only allowed the independent Advisory Committee on Reactor Safeguards to review and investigate issues if asked by the NRC. Chairman Guthrie’s staff worked diligently with us to find a path forward that worked for everyone. If the amendments for those bills are adopted, I will support all six nuclear bills on today’s markup.

We are also considering several bills from our Environment Subcommittee.

H.R. 9615, the BRACE Act, will help increase the domestic recycling batteries and ensure the critical minerals recovered from those batteries stay here in the United States. This is a critical first step to get the Environmental Protection Agency moving on a regulatory framework for lithium-ion battery recycling that provides certainty for industry and addresses safety concerns, while maintaining critical protections for the environment and public health. This bill is a compromise so neither side got everything they wanted, but I support this reasonable approach. It is also not the end of the conversation on battery recycling, and I look forward to continuing to work across the aisle to address this growing issue.

I am also pleased we are considering a bipartisan reauthorization of the Diesel Emissions Reduction Act. This long-standing program helps replace older, dirty diesel engines across the nation, cleaning up our air and cutting down on fuel costs.

Unfortunately, I will not be able to support the remaining bills out of the Environment Subcommittee. In the wake of Trump’s reckless war of choice in Iran, Americans are facing a fuel affordability crisis, with diesel prices over five dollars a gallon and gas prices up thirty percent compared to last year. American families are struggling to afford groceries and school supplies due to high fuel costs having a devastating ripple effect throughout the economy.

Yet today Committee Republicans want to move two bills that would increase fuel use and health-harming and smog-forming pollution, and undermine states’ ability to improve air quality and protect public health.

H.R. 9317, the BUSES Act, needlessly attacks state policies to allow school buses and motor coaches to idle for fifteen minutes or longer. This would allow toxic diesel exhaust to poison children going to school and increase fueling costs in the process, putting a strain on school budgets.

And H.R. 3194, the LOCOMOTIVES Act, attacks states’ ability to control pollution from older, dirtier locomotives in use today, locking in this harmful pollution for years to come and leaving communities and workers to foot the bill with their health.

I will oppose both of these bills and with that I yield back the balance of my time.

text:
The executive director of the Iowa Renewable Fuels Association has a mixed reaction to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency decision to give 34 small refineries exemptions from mixing reneable fuels with gas.

Monte Shaw describes the announcement as a “bad news-maybe not so bad news” situation. “These are only going to be granted if refineries are suffering economic harm from the renewable fuel standard, and they’re not,” Shaw says. “They’re making record profits (with) the war in Iran. Their profit margins are called crack spit spreads in the petroleum industry. We just think these are completely unjustified on one hand.”

But Shaw also believes the Trump Administration will protect ethanol producers through the proposed reallocation of the waived gallons in the 2026 and 2027 renewable fuel obligations. “Right now, the key thing is the market believes they’re going to do it,” he says. “The demand has stayed strong for renewable fuels. If there starts to be some questions about it, then the market drops, then assumptions become reality, and we pay the price.”

Shaw is cautiously optimistic that the reallocation will happen. “I do feel like, unless something else happens, they’re going to follow through on that,” he says. Shaw and other renewable fuel supporters are pleased about the California Legislature’s approval this week of the E-15 Cleanup Act the removes the final technical barrier to year-round E-15 sales in that state.

Shaw says it will take months and years to implement E-15 sales, but he says the market there has the huge potential for 600 or 700 million gallons of new ethanol demand.

text:
Good afternoon! It’s Wednesday, and my TBR is laughing at how many great new books are releasing this month. (The roundup in the link doesn’t even include everything I’m interested in.) Here’s what you need to know today.

1. ComEd customers pay billions to keep the lights on during storms. Will it be enough?

ComEd customers have footed the bill for billions of dollars spent by the utility in recent years to help ensure that power stays on in Northern Illinois even during the worst weather. Yet the lights still went out in 2.4 million homes during storms this year, my colleague Brett Chase writes.

Keeping the power on during increasingly extreme weather costs a lot. As a result, ComEd says it needs to raise more than $15 billion through rate increases so it can handle rising demand and deal with intense storms that experts say are getting worse because of climate change.

That’s on top of $4.4 billion being spent on a previously approved initiative to strengthen the electric grid — the system of lines, towers, poles and other equipment connecting power plants to homes and businesses. As a regulated utility, ComEd has to apply to the state of Illinois for any rate increases, a move the company has regularly made over the past couple decades.

To see what’s at stake, consider what happened recently in Gary, Indiana, where a storm with the velocity of a Category 2 hurricane tore through the city, knocking out power for two weeks. Many blamed the Northern Indiana Public Service Co. In a lawsuit, Northwest Indiana residents say electric utility NIPSCO didn’t protect its power lines and utility poles from tree damage ahead of the storms. NIPSCO disputes that claim.

“Gary should be a warning to all utilities — in Illinois and across the nation,” said Sarah Moskowitz, executive director of Illinois watchdog group the Citizens Utility Board. “It’s their duty to cost-effectively maintain the system and preserve affordability. If that duty takes a backseat to their profit margin, they risk disaster.” [Chicago Sun-Times]

2. Chicago just had its first West Nile death of the year. Here’s how to protect yourself

The threat of West Nile virus has ranged from moderate to very high this summer. The virus, also detected in the suburbs, can cause mild flu-like symptoms or none at all. However, it can be deadly in older adults and anyone with a weak immune system.

Effective precautions range from well-tested repellents that ward off biters to steps that everyone should take to stop the mosquito population from growing, my colleague Brett Chase reports.

Use sprays or balms that have at least 30% of an ingredient approved by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, such as DEET, picaridin and lemon eucalyptus oil. Experts also recommend dumping all standing water. Bird baths and rain barrels can be treated with a larvicide, which is an insecticide that targets mosquitoes in their early stages. These chemicals can be purchased at hardware or home improvement stores.

Meanwhile, don’t count on citronella, marigold and other plants for protection. A fan may be a better option because mosquitoes are too light to navigate through the wind. (It’s the same reason a breezy beach usually doesn’t have a lot of mosquitoes.) [Chicago Sun-Times]

3. Mayoral candidates decry Chicago’s violence ‘crisis,’ even as summer murders hit a 61-year low

Despite historically low levels of violent crime in Chicago this year, candidates trying to replace Mayor Brandon Johnson are sweeping aside numbers in favor of anecdotes, depicting the city in a “crisis” of gun violence and lawlessness.

As WBEZ’s Chip Mitchell reports, Chicago had 122 murders in June, July and August, according to city and police data posted through yesterday evening. That’s the lowest summer total since 1965. Overall violent crime hit its lowest level last year in more than four decades. City data shows the downward trend has continued this year.

Johnson links the improved numbers to his selection of Larry Snelling as police superintendent, Chicago’s focus on CTA safety and its investments in community violence intervention and youth summer jobs.

But some of his challengers have suggested Johnson doesn’t deserve much credit because the downward murder trend began in 2022, the year before his mayoral tenure began, and because murder numbers have been falling in cities across the country. [WBEZ]

4. A heat-related issue left DuSable Lake Shore Drive bridge over the Chicago River unusable for more than 4 hours

Car traffic stood at a standstill on both sides of the bridge this morning as Office of Emergency Management and Communications authorities told drivers to seek an alternative route.

“During a scheduled bridge lift this morning, the DLSD bridge experienced a heat-related issue preventing it from fully closing,” the Chicago Department of Transportation said in a statement. “Crews are making the necessary adjustments to safely close the bridge and reopen the roadway as quickly as possible.” [Chicago Sun-Times]

In other heat-related news, Chicago Public Schools moved all outdoor activities indoors, including recess, physical education and athletics. [Chicago Sun-Times]

Temperatures are about 10 degrees hotter than the normal average for late August and early September, but late-season heatwaves aren’t that unusual. [Chicago Sun-Times]

5. How did a native Chicago plant disappear forever?

Thismia americana is a tiny, blue-white flower first discovered in Chicago in 1912. By 1916, the plant had vanished, never to be seen in the wild again. Despite the odds, scientists continue to search for it.

In recent decades, organizations around Chicago have taken steps to restore the city’s green spaces, including Indian Ridge Marsh Park, where Thismia americana was discovered. The plant is a symbol that represents the power of Chicago’s unique natural environment and the people who take care of it, WBEZ contributor Andrew Stojkovich writes.

“There is a story of recovery here, and that’s super exciting,” said Trevor Edmonson, restoration ecologist with The Nature Conservancy in Indiana. “If you can do that here, you can pretty much do that anywhere.” [WBEZ]

Here’s what else is happening

The latest COVID-19, flu and RSV vaccines remain safe and highly effective for protecting people against severe complications from the potentially life-threatening respiratory viruses, according to independent analyses from medical groups. [NPR]

Dan Driscoll offered no reason for his departure as U.S. Army secretary but said yesterday was his last full day. [AP]

The mother of a Faceworld gang member was found guilty of retaliating against a witness in her son’s murder case in Chicago. [Chicago Sun-Times]

Aspira will let a judge decide what happens to the money from selling the nonprofit’s taxpayer-funded school. [WBEZ]

Oh, and one more thing …

Ahead of this week’s nearly sold-out Soldier Field performances, WBEZ/Chicago Sun-Times asked three Black Chicagoans to reflect on the legacy of Ye (formerly Kanye West) in the city that helped shape him.

Arionne Nettles said Kanye West’s bravado and confidence was a comfort in a world that pushed respectability on Black millennials like her. But his outspokenness later became a cloudy, indistinguishable mess. [WBEZ]

To Chicago kid Nile Lansana, Kanye once touched the sky. Lansana said the fall has been hard to watch — and harder to forgive. [WBEZ]

Mary L. Datcher believes there’s still room at Chicago’s table for Ye, as the singer represents the city — the good, bad and ugly. [WBEZ]

Tell me something good …

What is your favorite memory from this summer?

Paula writes:

“My favorite memory from this summer was my week-long cycling tour in Idaho. In Spokane, Washington, I got to visit with a college friend whom I haven’t seen in twenty-some years. Then, with a group of my Chicago area bicycle club friends, I rode the scenic bike trails of the Coeur d’Alene and Wallace, Idaho areas.”

Phyllis writes:

“Favorite memory: showing pictures from our Alaska expedition and serving mini ice cream cones that everyone enjoyed!”

Feel free to email me, and your response may be included in the newsletter this week.

text:
I loved “Choose Your Own Adventure” stories when I was a kid. Each book in the series began with a brief set-up and then the whole thing became a maze of decision-making.

In “The Mystery of Chimney Rock,” for example, the end of the introductory section reads: “On your right is a flight of steps leading from the kitchen upstairs. To the left is a swinging door, which you imagine leads to the dining room.”

At the bottom of the page, the author gives you two options: “If you go up the stairs, turn to page 8. If you go through the swinging door into the dining room, turn to page 10.”

And on it goes until you arrive at your happy, tragic, or indeterminate end.

I couldn’t help but think of those books when news dropped this week that a data center has come knocking in Bow, a town of about 8,200 just south of Concord. While it’s very early in the process, and with far more questions than answers about every aspect of the potential project, the town’s residents already have a decision to make: If you answer the door, turn to page 8. If you shout “Go away,” turn to page 10.

There’s no official confirmation of where the center would be located, but the tea leaves couldn’t be clearer: Granite Shore Power got the data center ball rolling with a Federal Energy Regulatory Commission filing, and Granite Shore happens to own Merrimack Station, Bow’s recently closed coal-fired power plant.

The move also tracks with what’s happening in other states. In Pennsylvania, for example, the former coal-fired Homer City Generating Station is under consideration for conversion to natural gas that could create “up to 4.7 GW of power” for data centers, Inside Climate News reports. That’s an enormous amount of power, which dwarfs even the “hyperscale” 350 MW project being kicked around in Bow. And, as Inside Climate News points out, that’s an enormous amount of greenhouse gases, too.

“Nationally, at least 74 gas-fired power plants, nearly all of them new, are planned to fuel the data-center industry, generating 662 million tons of greenhouse gases, equal to the annual emissions of Australia,” reporter John Hurdle writes.

But if New Hampshire’s existing natural gas infrastructure makes converting Merrimack Station a particularly tall order, and adding new strain to the grid is a deal-breaker, maybe Granite Shore will just jump back on the Trump administration’s beloved coal train.

So many questions in the Bow data center story, and that’s just the beginning of the power generation chapter.

Gov. Kelly Ayotte, as pro-business as she is, seems to understand that data centers are a different animal. In a statement to the Bulletin Tuesday in the wake of the Bow news, she said, “I will always advocate for our towns to decide what’s best for them, but with too many unknowns surrounding these facilities, I think it is best for us to institute a moratorium for the time being.”

Some of those unknowns are related to power generation and ratepayer impacts, as well as the potential for increased fossil fuel emissions in a state that also just eliminated annual vehicle emissions testing. But there are others, like the heat and noise they generate, the water they need, the neighborhoods they disrupt, and the precious land they swallow.

The Trump administration doesn’t want to hear the valid concerns of the people, however, and has moved to block communities from even raising them.

There’s a lot for towns to think about when it comes to these structures, including weighing the very real need to bolster the tax base against potential environmental, health, and quality-of-life consequences. There was a time, I’m sure, when Merrimack was thrilled to have Saint-Gobain Performance Plastics on the rolls, but what wouldn’t they give now for the chance at a do-over?

In other ways, though, the debate is bigger than the centers themselves. It’s also about the artificial intelligence that’s driving the construction boom.

Last week, more than 100 companies — OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google among them — signed a letter calling for a “collective action on cyber defense.”

“We have a limited window to strengthen cyber defenses,” the letter begins. “In the coming months, AI-enabled cyber attacks will become far more widespread and sophisticated as models around the world become increasingly capable.”

They could have saved some characters and just written: “The thing we created is already out of control and coming for all of us. Help.”

And if you want to get really nerdy, you can check out a recent incident recap from METR, a nonprofit AI research organization. It’s about the Hugging Face hack by swarms of AI agents earlier this summer — and rarely have I read something so technical that still manages to be terrifying.

But the thing that really troubles me is this: I am one of the least tech-savvy people I know. Most of this stuff is way over my head, and I stumble around wondering whether I’m too worried about AI or not worried enough.

I don’t have a good answer, but I’m not convinced anyone else does, either.

The best we can hope for now, it seems to me, is the pressing of the brakes — maybe a moratorium, or a data center blocked here and there, or a committed consumer and societal rebellion against AI’s sprawling and multiplying tentacles. That is not nothing, and every stand the people take will be meaningful in its own way. And collectively, maybe even powerful.

But I can’t shake the feeling that we’re well past the first decision in a “Choose Your Own Adventure” book and hurtling along this path we’ve chosen. Your guess is as good as mine about how it all ends, and when.

text:
The Trump administration is preparing to unveil significantly lower vehicle fuel economy standards, marking a massive shift in how the federal government approaches automotive manufacturing, Reuters reported. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced this update on Monday, confirming that the current administration plans to move away from the aggressive efficiency mandates set by the previous leadership.

This change is all about shifting the focus back to what the market actually demands. During an appearance in Michigan, Secretary Duffy explained the reasoning behind this pivot. “We are about to announce a common-sense fuel economy standard because we want Detroit to build cars that Americans want to buy — not cars that Democrats want Washington to build,” Duffy said.

While the final details are still not out, automakers are bracing for standards that align closely with a proposal released in December by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. This proposal targets a fleetwide average of 34.5 miles per gallon by 2031. This is a noticeable drop from the 50.4 miles per gallon target established under Joe Biden.

The Trump administration intends to prioritize consumer choice and the preferences of the automotive industry

The previous rules were designed to push the industry toward electric vehicles by requiring strict annual efficiency increases, specifically 8% for 2024 and 2025, 10% for 2026, and 2% annually from 2027 through 2031.

The new approach also includes a retroactive revision to the 2022 fuel economy standards. It allows vehicle manufacturers to gain additional compliance credits for past performance, which makes meeting future requirements much easier. By easing these burdens, the administration hopes to lower the price of new vehicles. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration estimates that this proposal could cut the cost of a new vehicle by $930.

Of course, these changes come with tradeoffs. Analysts note that this shift could lead to an increase in fuel consumption by roughly 100 billion gallons through 2050, which would also raise fuel spending by $185 billion and increase carbon dioxide emissions by about 5%. It is a significant change in direction from the previous focus on reducing greenhouse gas emissions and positioning the United States as a global leader in clean energy technology.

The landscape for the automotive industry has evolved quickly over the last year. In 2025, Congress made several major changes, including the decision to stop collecting penalties for failing to meet fuel economy standards. This policy alone saves automakers hundreds of millions of dollars.

title: Polluting Nylon Plants Clean Up Their Acts - Inside Climate News
description:
Many of our impact case studies cover ongoing stories that Inside Climate News continues to actively cover.
Its emissions of nitrous oxide—a greenhouse gas 300 times worse than carbon dioxide—were equal to the annual climate pollution of 2.1 million automobiles.
Several months later, with help from Inside Climate News interns Lili Pike (now at Bloomberg), and Katrina Northrop (now at The Wall Street Journal), I wrote about 11 similar nylon plants in China.
