text:
ALBANY — A federal judge has struck down New York’s Climate Change Superfund Act, ruling that it is “simply beyond the limits of state law.”

The ruling stems from a federal lawsuit that more than 20 states filed against New York in February 2025 challenging the constitutionality of the Climate Change Superfund Act, which established regulations seeking to collect roughly $75 billion from companies — some controlled by foreign nations — deemed responsible for greenhouse gas emissions due to their refinement and production of fossil fuels.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

U.S. District Court Chief Judge Brenda K. Sannes stopped short of declaring the statute is unconstitutional, but ruled that it is preempted by federal law and cannot be legally enforced.

“In seeking damages 'for the cumulative impact' of conduct that has occurred 'simultaneously across just about every jurisdiction on the planet,' the Climate Act conflicts with 'the overriding … need for a uniform rule of decision’ on matters influencing national energy and environmental policy, and ‘basic interests of federalism,’” Sannes wrote in a 63-page decision.

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, whose state is one of the plaintiffs in the case, had last year called the law “nothing more than an unconstitutional shakedown of vital American energy industries that form the bedrock of our national economic independence.”

The legislation was signed into law at the end of December 2024 by Gov. Kathy Hochul, over the objections of a coalition of business, energy and labor organizations aligned with the Business Council of New York State, which had asked the governor to veto the bill.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

It had been stripped from the state budget in 2024 but passed by the state Senate that May and the Assembly a month later.

“This decision underscores the concerns we have continued to raise surrounding New York’s Climate Change Superfund Act,” said Heather Mulligan, president and CEO of the Business Council of New York State. “While we certainly support efforts to improve our state’s climate and environment, it’s equally important that those policies are both sound and recognize the impact on businesses.”

The federal lawsuit was filed in U.S. District Court in Albany by attorneys generals from Alabama, Arkanas, Georgia, Idaho, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah and Wyoming. Several industry groups, including the West Virginia Coal Association, Alpha Metallurgical Resources, and the Gas and Oil Association of West Virginia, are also parties to the litigation.

The lawsuit was filed against state Attorney General Letitia James, Department of Environmental Conservation interim Commissioner Sean Mahar, who is now a regional director with the agency, and acting Department of Taxation and Finance Commissioner Amanda Hiller. In the ruling this week, Sannes dismissed the case against Hiller but also denied the state’s request for summary judgment on the merits of their arguments.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The U.S. Department of Justice joined the legal battle last September, asking a judge to declare that New York’s Climate Change Superfund Act is unconstitutional, and asserting that the legislation is a “lawless overreach” and that the federal government’s motion for summary judgment in the case should be granted.

A similar lawsuit filed by the administration of President Donald J. Trump has targeted similar legislation in Vermont.

“The state of New York believes it can seize control over the makeup of America’s energy industry,” the 76-page complaint filed by the 20 states had asserted. “In an unprecedented effort, New York has set out to impose tens of billions of dollars of liability on traditional energy producers disfavored by certain New York politicians.”

The superfund act tasked the state Department of Environmental Conservation with establishing regulations to identify “responsible parties” and the procedures for collecting payments from those companies after issuing notices of cost recovery demands. Although the state attorney general’s office and Department of Taxation and Finance would be given authority to enforce the payment demands, it’s unclear how that would work, including if the targets are in Russia or other nations at odds with U.S. interests.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The coalition supported by the Business Council characterized the legislation as “bad public policy” in a letter they sent to Hochul two years ago. The letter noted there were significant questions about the implementation of the regulations, whether they would meet constitutional muster, and the potential for “unintended consequences and increased costs for households and businesses.”

The group said that the legislation also ignored the direct culprit for carbon emissions — consumers — and was discriminatory because it targeted only the largest fossil fuel extraction and processing firms, including those that produce petroleum, natural gas and coal.

State and federal lawmakers who supported the legislation have taken varied positions on fossil fuels. Under former Gov. Andrew M. Cuomo, the state created the “FUEL NY” initiative in response to Superstorm Sandy in 2012, a catastrophic event that created extensive power outages and disruptions to fuel supply systems. That initiative, which remains in place, notes that New York “relies on the continuous availability and resupply of gasoline and diesel fuel to maintain public safety, commerce, and the well-being and economic vitality of its residents, businesses, and governments.”

The FUEL NY plan sought to mitigate disruptions in fuel distribution and establish two fuel reserves, as well as a back-up generator program for gas stations in strategic locations, to make it easier for New Yorkers to resume “daily life” following a severe storm.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“Now, state government is proposing to penalize the very same suppliers of gasoline, natural gas, and other fossil fuel-based products,” the business coalition group wrote. “By targeting and imposing strict liability only on the extraction and refinement of fossil fuels, the bill disregards the fact that most emissions are generated by the actual use of fossil fuels and not by their refinement or extraction. Imposing a fee on this past activity means is not designed to impact business or consumer behavior, suggesting the main goal of the legislation is to receive funding from the fuels sector.”

A memo circulated in the Legislature three years ago by state Sen. Liz Krueger, a Manhattan Democrat, and Assemblyman Jeffrey Dinowtiz, a Bronx Democrat, cited a “peer-reviewed” article that they said ranked a list of violators and helped establish the amount of money they should pay New York. The article analyzed global emissions since 2000 and based the penalties on each company’s annual assessment, and placed “the burden of the damages caused on the manufacturer, not the users, even if the substance was legally produced and emitted at the time the harm was caused.”

That annual assessment list ranged from $222 million for Exxon Mobil to $100 million for Lukoil in Russia and $23 million for Novatek, an oil and gas company that is Russia's second-largest producer of natural gas. There were also more than a dozen U.S. companies on the bill’s list.

The legislation entitled a fossil fuel company to contest any financial assessments “consistent with due process requirements of the U.S. Constitution.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

But the lawsuit filed in federal court against New York asserted the law ran afoul of the Constitution and the federal Clean Air Act, which regulates emissions across state lines.

Krueger, in a statement issued Tuesday morning, criticized Sannes' ruling and noted, “I have always said that there would be many rounds of legal wrangling before the Climate Change Superfund (Act) could begin to provide relief for New Yorkers.”

“It is unfortunate that Judge Sannes failed to recognize the clear distinction between a tort lawsuit, which was at issue in the New York City v Chevron decision, and a state Legislature exercising its constitutional powers to raise revenues and protect its citizen,” Krueger said. “Regardless, this case will now move up to the 2nd Circuit, where a new panel of judges will have the opportunity to acknowledge the difference between this case and Chevron, or, failing that, to revisit the Chevron decision, which has been widely criticized on both the left and the right.”

Krueger was referring to a case in which New York City sued five multinational oil companies under state tort law alleging public and private nuisance and trespass as a result of pollution. That lawsuit, which was dismissed in a unanimous decision by the 2nd Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals, sought billions of dollars to pay for sea-walls and other infrastructure improvements, including a new sewer system, to deal with storm events. The city argued fossil fuel producers were responsible for global warming.

Blair Horner, executive director of New York Public Interest Research Group, had pushed back on the Business Council during the legislative wrangling over the Climate Superfund Act, claiming the organization would rather have “taxpayers and small business owners pick up the entire tab for climate destruction, instead of the wealthy fossil fuel companies who knew they were causing climate change for decades and did nothing to change course.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

In a statement issued late Monday, Horner that “the damages caused by the worsening climate are hammering (New Yorkers') wallets and unless this decision is reversed, they will face higher taxes or reduced public services — or both — to the tune of $75 billion.”

text:
Grant Township trustees and Grand Traverse County commissioners will meet separately this week to explore options for responding to a proposed 375-megawatt solar project spanning Grand Traverse and Wexford counties. The project highlights zoning control tensions after a 2023 Michigan law change allowed solar developers to bypass local boards and go directly to the state for approval – a path developer Ranger Power is now pursuing after running into local resistance.

Ranger Power, under the affiliate name Shipyard Solar LLC, began appearing before local boards this spring to present the project. Primarily located in northern Wexford County – with parts of the infrastructure planned for Grant Township in Grand Traverse County – the project was initially presented as a 300-megawatt facility with solar panels on 1,800 fenced acres. Representatives said the company had “partnered with several local farmers through long-term lease agreements to include land in the project,” acquisition work that started in 2023.

When describing the site selection process, Ranger Power emphasized it only partners with landowners who voluntarily participate and doesn’t use eminent domain. Projects are located near existing transmission infrastructure, avoid wetlands/streams/endangered species, and are based near load centers like Traverse City, representatives said. Ranger Power touted the proposal’s economic benefits, saying it could “generate tens of millions of dollars in personal property tax revenues during its lifespan” and “create hundreds of construction jobs.”

Representatives also noted that the state’s Renewable Ready Communities Award offers communities up to $5,000 per megawatt for the portion of projects they permit. The company said the project uses permanent vegetative ground cover that allows farmlands to regenerate and would “provide supplemental income to local farmers,” diversifying their revenue streams. But at multiple public meetings, dozens of residents including farmers pushed back on the proposal. Several said they supported renewable or solar energy but were firmly against converting valuable farmland for such projects.

Ranger Power said its goal was to work with local communities to design a project that addressed their concerns. But it also pointed out that if it didn’t receive local approval, it could go directly to the state instead. That’s because Public Act 233, which was passed in 2023, gives the state instead of townships the power to approve large-scale renewable energy projects. The controversial law was recently upheld by the Michigan Court of Appeals, but 79 townships and counties across Michigan are challenging it to the Michigan Supreme Court.

Under the law, developers can directly seek Michigan Public Service Commission (MPSC) approval unless a local unit of government has a compatible renewable energy ordinance (CREO) in place that is “no more restrictive” than state requirements. Many communities began creating CREOs after the law change. However, MPSC later issued an order limiting the conditions CREOs could address, which rendered many of them non-compliant.

The order, which says a CREO can only address setbacks, fencing, height, sound, and other express requirements and not anything beyond that, is one of the issues being challenged in the lawsuit. Communities have argued the order is overly limiting and that MPSC has exceeded its authority by narrowing local oversight beyond what was intended by legislators.

Ranger Power initially sought to work through the local approval process by applying for a zoning amendment to the Wexford Joint Planning Commission (WJPC). The WJPC represents nearly a dozen townships across Wexford County. Its zoning ordinance does not allow for utility-scale solar projects in the Ag-Forest Production zoning district where the proposed facility would be located. Ranger Power promised to provide sound and glare studies, a decommissioning plan, and a community benefits agreement as part of a special use permit if the zoning amendment was approved.

However, the WJPC unanimously voted on July 27 to recommend that townships deny the zoning ordinance amendment for being too broad. Shortly after, Ranger Power began notifying local governments that the company plans to apply to MPSC directly. The project is now described as a 375-megawatt instead of 300-megawatt facility. That would make it one of Ranger Power’s largest projects, as the company previously said its developments range in size from 50 to 400 megawatts.

Developers must get written acknowledgement from each affected jurisdiction as to whether a local CREO is in place before they apply to the state. Under the recent Michigan Court of Appeals ruling, affected jurisdictions include not only townships but any counties, villages, or cities where the project is located. Grant Township trustees will meet tonight (Tuesday) at 5:30pm to discuss the acknowledgement request and will consider hiring special legal counsel to guide them through the process. Grand Traverse County commissioners will discuss the request at their 9am meeting Wednesday.

County Administrator Nate Alger says this is a new issue for county officials, so they’re “relying heavily on legal counsel” for advice. That includes a deadline for responding, which the courts have interpreted would be within 30 days of meeting with developers – not just receiving their letter, which Ranger Power sent on August 14. Commissioners will vote Wednesday on having the county’s attorneys work with Alger to respond to Ranger Power and set up a meeting.

The solar project could have ramifications beyond zoning control and land use. Just last week, MPSC approved its first application under Public Act 233 – a 90-megawatt facility in Ingham County also led by Ranger Power. A settlement agreement outlined detailed construction requirements for Ranger Power as well as financial benefits for the townships. Ingham County worked out a separate agreement with the developers for funding benefits. “That’s an option that’s available to us,” says Alger of financial compensation.

In an emailed statement to The Ticker, Ranger Power said: "We remain fully committed to open dialogue and active collaboration with local leaders as we evaluate the next steps for the Shipyard Solar project. While we determine the path forward, our core priority has not changed. We will continue working with community members and stakeholders to ensure a positive, meaningful outcome." name: Louisiana Environment
title: Climate denial is not an option: Louisiana needs the political will to act | The Lens
authors: Jessica Dandridge-Smith, The Water Collaborative of Greater New Orleans, Jessica Dandridge-Smith
description:
New Orleans communities, working with scientists, have done what we could.
But those solutions remain unimplemented because too many of our elected officials are stuck in climate denial or lack the will to confront the escalating climate threats Louisiana residents live with every day.
We cannot deny the climate change that shapes our everyday lives Climate denial is not an option when Louisiana residents are already living with the consequences.
We cannot acknowledge the realities of a changing climate without making the political choices necessary to prepare for it.
The beat may change, but the lyrics are clear: Climate denial is not an option.
text:
Twenty-one years ago, Katrina reshaped my life and the lives of many in New Orleans.

Loss, tragedy, classism, and racism were flung in our faces. To solve this nation’s greatest sins, the country left us with only our willpower and tenacity.

For two decades, I’ve fought to help tackle our cities’ most pressing water challenges.

Water is complex and knows no bounds. It is gentle yet powerful in its rage, and more so, it remembers every act of kindness and every act of malice.

As I grappled with the dichotomies that water holds, I worked tirelessly to educate everyone I encountered. No matter one’s background, every person deserves clean water and to live in a world free from the burden of floods every time a storm cloud forms.

We have always been at odds with our landscape, blaming the swamp and our marshes for what they are, while demanding more of them daily — more seafood, more shipping, more energy extraction — while draining it dry of water, the very thing it needs.

As sea levels rise and storms get stronger, communities have stepped up to the challenge. Local community leaders and residents across New Orleans have figured out how to turn anything into the sweetest lemonade, with or without sugar. And yet, as we wipe the literal and figurative sweat off our brows, the people elected to fight for our communities have chosen, time and time again, to turn their backs on us.

Our state has a history of bravery and ingenuity, from our ancestral heritage of indigenous communities and enslaved Africans. To Acadians, Sicilians, Jews, and, more recently, Vietnamese and Palestinians, each community fled persecution to help build the beauty that makes New Orleans the most irreplaceable city in America. Unfortunately, our elected officials are falling short.

Sadly, if that doesn’t change soon, the most important city in the nation will be lost to ineptitude.

Our grassroots efforts alone are not enough to save the region. To save our beautiful, unique city, we need those who represent us to step up.

New Orleans communities, working with scientists, have done what we could. We created solutions, through water plans that help our land absorb excess water. But those solutions remain unimplemented because too many of our elected officials are stuck in climate denial or lack the will to confront the escalating climate threats Louisiana residents live with every day.

Though people know what needs to be done, elected officials falling short Louisianians do not lack information about the challenges facing our communities. If there is any group of people that can comprehend life’s many complexities, it is us. But somehow, our elected leaders have chosen to do anything but what’s right.

A recent poll by the Mississippi River Delta (MRD) Coalition found that 76% of voters oppose canceling the sediment diversion projects, with 47% strongly opposing it. Yet not long after taking office, the will of the people was ignored and canceled overnight.

A prior poll by the Restore the Mississippi River Delta coalition found that 72% of Louisiana voters feel climate change is already having a serious negative impact on the state. Yet again, too few elected officials have acted with the urgency or scale these challenges demand.

In New Orleans, significant budget deficits led to cuts to the Office of Resilience and Sustainability, even as climate risks continue to grow. As they say, the saxophones are getting louder.

We cannot deny the climate change that shapes our everyday lives Climate denial is not an option when Louisiana residents are already living with the consequences.

We know families are confronting housing and insurance crises that make it harder to stay in their communities. We know our coast is disappearing, our communities are sinking, and increasingly intense rainfall is overwhelming infrastructure built for a different climate.

Residents, scientists, engineers, advocates, and government agencies have spent decades studying these problems, proposing solutions, and working hard to prove that these issues not only matter but also can be solved. We’re no longer discussing feasibility; we’re long past that reality. We know what is needed, but we are missing the political will to act on what we already know.

On July 11, an intense rainstorm flooded streets across Mid-City, Lakeview, City Park, Hollygrove and Uptown, among other areas. Some neighborhoods received more than 3.5 inches of rain in less than an hour, while problems at two drainage pumping stations worsened flooding in parts of Lakeview and Mid-City. The flooding renewed important questions about whether our pumps were working, stations were adequately staffed, and drainage infrastructure was sufficiently maintained. Those systems matter, but they cannot be our only answer to flooding.

Yet too often, the conversation after a flood begins and ends with “Are the pumps on?” It makes for a great headline, but it does little to address the larger problem. Blaming a historically underfunded utility built for a city of 600,000, but funded by 300,000 people today, while the federal government claws back funding for flood mitigation and resilience, will not solve it either.

Pumps and drainage systems are not enough.

Creating a holistic approach, where water is absorbed not left to be pumped New Orleans needs a holistic approach to water. We’ve spent over a century and billions of dollars trying to engineer the city into an ecosystem it simply is not. The most beneficial approach is to work with water — rather than solely trying to pump it away — by investing in nature-based solutions such as native plants, trees, and green spaces that can absorb it where it falls.

In 2013, the Greater New Orleans Urban Water Plan proposed taking the burden off of our already aging pumps by giving water somewhere to go. Implementing these nature-based solutions would capture rainfall where it falls while also improving quality of life, reducing negative public health outcomes, increasing economic development, and cooling neighborhoods, especially in historically redlined communities.

When put to work, these solutions have worked to help stop flooding in key areas. But they are not being used with regularity. The Urban Water Plan is not being implemented by our elected officials.

Time and time again, the people who could lead the way in making our city and state a thriving place to live for children and families have turned their backs on the facts in favor of short-term wins, political favors, and social media views.

There’s proof that these solutions work. The Gentilly Resilience District demonstrates how green spaces can be integrated into our stormwater system. The Sankofa Wetland Park and Nature Trail in the Lower 9th Ward restored approximately 40 acres of wetlands and community space. The Urban Conservancy’s Front Yard Initiative helps residents replace excessive paving with permeable surfaces and native plants, showing the capacity of individual properties to contribute. Groundwork New Orleans, Thrive New Orleans, and Louisiana Green Corps have also connected this work to green workforce development, training local residents for careers to build and maintain the infrastructure our communities need.

Louisiana is already implementing nature-based solutions at a much larger scale through the Louisiana Coastal Protection and Restoration Authority’s Coastal Master Plan. It is still the only Gulf state with an office dedicated to researching, protecting, and restoring our disappearing coast. Sediment diversions protect Louisiana by reconnecting the Mississippi River with surrounding wetlands and working with natural processes. Years of research and collaboration between businesses and communities have been ignored for a short-term win for some fisheries who will eventually succumb to the very thing they hope to avoid.

The city’s biggest investments in green infrastructure were made possible by federal funding All of the City of New Orleans’ largest public green infrastructure investments have depended on federal funding provided following disasters. The Gentilly Resilience District, for example, was made possible through more than $141 million awarded through HUD’s National Disaster Resilience Competition following Hurricane Isaac. Those investments have been transformative.

But we cannot wait for another disaster to fund the infrastructure we need to protect us from the next one, leaving the most vulnerable to shoulder the burden of recovery.

The problem is not a lack of solutions. We have studied, discussed, and reported ourselves into oblivion. The world watches us, while we drown under the weight of cowardice and ignorance.

It is a matter of whether we have the political will to truly invest in our future.

Twenty-one years after Katrina, we know the cost of waiting for catastrophe to expose vulnerabilities we already knew existed. We need dedicated, recurring funding for our entire stormwater system, investment in our water champions and future workforce, and a willingness to work with our natural landscape rather than against it. We have the data, plans, science, and solutions. Communities have been telling us what they need for years.

The clock is ticking, and we’re running out of time.

Those who know me know I say this often: our culture, food, and traditions will mean nothing if they are underwater. We cannot second-line, play a trumpet, or sing a song under the encroaching Gulf of Mexico. Our communities have worked tirelessly to make this place a home worth fighting for. We need elected leaders willing to meet the moment and stand with us.

We cannot pump our way out of every storm, wall our way out of rising seas, or grant-fund our way into a thriving city. We cannot acknowledge the realities of a changing climate without making the political choices necessary to prepare for it. Katrina taught us this lesson, and every storm keeps singing the same song.

The beat may change, but the lyrics are clear: Climate denial is not an option. Neither is political inaction.

Dandridge-Smith is executive director of The Water Collaborative of Greater New Orleans. She has dedicated her life to community advocacy and campaign development for organizations seeking to be socially, economically, and culturally inclusive. Dandridge received her B.A at Xavier University in Political Science and her M.A in International Affairs with a concentration in security in conflict from The New School for Public Engagement in New York City. Since 2005, she has worked for, or in collaboration with dozens of organizations in Greater New Orleans.

text:
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Monday commended Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Administrator Lee Zeldin for targeting his “pet peeve” — an auto feature intended to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

“You know the on-off, the stop-start button on your car? I hate that thing,” Duffy told the crowd at an event in Detroit. “Thank you, Lee Zeldin. He’s gotten rid of it, and the first cars without the start-stop button are rolling off the line.”

In February, the EPA announced it would axe federal incentives for vehicle manufacturers that include the feature in their models. Former President Obama’s administration introduced “off-cycle” credits for vehicles that used the technology in 2012 as a way to reduce greenhouse gases.

The tech automatically stops an engine when the car is not moving and starts again when the driver presses the pedal. It cut nearly 10 million tons of greenhouse gas emissions annually as of 2023, according to Battery Council International.

In a statement announcing the change, Zeldin pushed back against the fuel efficiency regulations.

“Not only do many people find start-stop annoying, but it kills the battery of your car without any significant benefit to the environment,” he said. “The Trump EPA is proudly fixing this stupid feature at Trump speed.”

The elimination of the start-stop button credits was part of the Trump administration’s broader efforts to reverse federal emission rules to reduce costs for manufacturers and consumers.

Earlier this year, the EPA also rescinded a 2009 endangerment finding under the Obama administration that held greenhouse gas emissions from vehicles pose a threat to public health. The finding was used to require automakers to follow certain fuel efficiency standards, such as hitting an average of more than 50 miles per gallon across their fleets.

President Trump slammed these regulations as “ridiculous” during White House remarks in which he announced his administration would cancel the finding. He called the move “the single largest deregulatory action in American history.”

The president also downplayed concerns about the impact of these actions on Americans’ public health when asked by a reporter at a White House event.

“Don’t worry about it, because it has nothing to do with public health,” he said at the time. “This was all a scam, a giant scam.”

Justin Chen, the president of the American Federation of Government Employees Council 238, which represents thousands of EPA staffers, criticized the repeal as a “deep betrayal” of the agency’s mission.

“This rollback is nothing short of disastrous for the health and safety of our communities, and it also slams the brakes on the future EPA workers are helping to build,” Chen said in a statement following the announcement. “The clean energy and advanced vehicle industries are creating good-paying American jobs and positioning us to lead the world.”

He added, “Killing that progress now doesn’t just hurt innovation — it hurts workers, families, and the next generation.”

text:
The U.S. energy storage industry installed a record 20.2 GWh of new capacity in the second quarter of 2026, bringing total installations in the first half of the year to 30.8 GWh, according to the “U.S. Energy Storage Market Outlook Q3 2026 (ESMO)” report released today by the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence.

Utility-scale energy storage capacity has nearly doubled from 88 GWh to 165 GWh in the first 18 months of the Trump administration, as grid operators, utilities and energy buyers turn to storage to strengthen reliability and meet rising electricity demand.

Demand for energy storage is outpacing expectations, prompting a 11.5% increase in the report’s forecast through 2030 to 683 GWh. The upward revision comes as the industry continues to set deployment records, with more than 10% of all energy storage capacity currently installed in the U.S. coming online in Q2 alone.

“This record growth highlights that storage is a powerful reliability tool that strengthens our energy security, meets rising demand and puts downward pressure on electricity bills,” said Tim Pawlenty, president and CEO of SEIA.

More than 74% of the energy storage capacity installed in Q2 was built in states won by President Donald Trump in 2024, led largely by Arizona, Texas and Utah. Arizona led the country with 6.2 GWh of new storage installations in Q2, the strongest quarter for any one state on record. Arizona, which has the nation’s fourth-largest solar market, is increasingly pairing its abundant solar resources with storage to capture more homegrown power, meet rising demand and help keep electricity costs down.

“Energy storage is no longer just a California and Texas story anymore,” said Shan Tomouk, BESS & Energy Lead at Benchmark Minerals. “We’re seeing strong pipeline growth in Arizona, Nevada, Oregon, Colorado and several other states.”

Battery energy storage supplied more electricity to the grid in the first eight months of 2026 than in all of 2025. During periods of extreme heat in states like Texas and California, storage has helped provide power when demand is highest, supporting grid reliability and helping protect consumers from price spikes. Texas and California installed 3.8 GWh and 3.6 GWh of storage, respectively, in Q2.

The United States also set domestic manufacturing records, with the opening of two new battery cell manufacturing facilities by LGES in Ohio and Tennessee, and a new 50-GWh Tesla battery module facility in Texas. Together, these facilities bring U.S. battery cell and module manufacturing capacity to record highs, ensuring that more of the batteries being deployed to strengthen the grid are made in the United States.

Utility-scale projects accounted for the vast majority of Q2 installations, with 17.9 GWh deployed, followed by 1.8 GWh of commercial and industrial storage, and 657 MWh of residential storage.

text:
LG Energy Solution has secured 80,000 metric tons of lithium carbonate in the US, expanding local sourcing of a key raw material for energy storage system (ESS) and electric vehicle (EV) batteries in North America.

LG Energy Solution said on Sept. 1 that it signed a long-term lithium carbonate supply agreement with US-based Smackover Lithium. Smackover Lithium is a joint venture between US lithium developer Standard Lithium and Norwegian state-owned energy company Equinor.

LG Energy Solution will receive a total of 80,000 metric tons of lithium carbonate over 10 years starting in 2029. The volume is enough to produce batteries for about 1.8 million EVs capable of traveling more than 500 kilometers on a single charge.

Smackover Lithium will produce the lithium carbonate at the South West Arkansas Project in Arkansas. The project uses direct lithium extraction (DLE) technology to extract lithium.

Lithium carbonate is a key raw material used in cathode materials for lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries. LG Energy Solution is increasing LFP battery production as the North American ESS market expands, raising its need for locally sourced lithium carbonate.

LG Energy Solution currently operates or is developing eight production facilities in North America. By securing US-produced lithium carbonate, the company plans to strengthen its supply chain from local raw-material sourcing through battery production.

"Securing key minerals produced in an environmentally responsible manner in the strategic North American market has strengthened our supply chain stability," said Lee Kang-yeol, senior vice president and head of the Procurement Center at LG Energy Solution. "We will enhance our product competitiveness based on local production and raw-material sourcing in the US."

name: Louisiana Environment
title: When Climate Forces Us to Move, Who Gets to Decide Where We Go?
description:
They’re considered the first community in the United States to undergo a federally funded climate relocation.
For more than 170 years, the Biloxi-Chitimacha-Choctaw community has lived on Isle de Jean Charles, a narrow island in coastal Louisiana.
Climate relocation and immigration enforcement involve different laws, populations, and governmental authorities.
My thesis concluded that climate relocation must move away from ad hoc, discretionary approaches and toward systems that are codified, participatory, and rights-based.
If we wait until water is at people’s doors to decide what rights they have, it’ll already be too late.
text:
We’re living through a moment when questions about government power over where people can live, work, travel, and belong have become too important to ignore. At a glance, the topic of migration/immigration might seem far removed from climate change. It isn’t; I wouldn’t be writing this if it was.

I recently completed my Master’s thesis on the legal consequences of climate change-induced displacement. I focused on an Indigenous American tribe, the Biloxi-Chitimacha-Choctaw from the Isle de Jean Charles, who live not even two hours south of where I do. They’re considered the first community in the United States to undergo a federally funded climate relocation.

For more than 170 years, the Biloxi-Chitimacha-Choctaw community has lived on Isle de Jean Charles, a narrow island in coastal Louisiana. The island was more than a place to live. It was a refuge. In the 1830s, Indigenous families sailed to the island to settle and escape the Indian Removal Act and the Trail of Tears, as well as the ongoing colonial violence and discrimination.

Then in the 1950s, the island started to disappear.

Sea-level rise, erosion, subsidence, and environmental degradation caused by oil and gas canalization demolished the landscape. Hurricanes like Katrina dumped saltwater on the land, making many livelihoods like farming no longer an option. By the early 2000s, the island had lost more than 98 percent of its landmass. Homes flooded repeatedly. Roads washed away. Wetlands disappeared. Eventually, remaining on the island became harder and harder.

Relocation isn’t moving houses from one place to another. Home is community, and a community needs a place to call home, as well. The place where relationships have been built, lasting through generations. Where your grandparents and great-grandparents have been buried. Where you’ve made memories, grown your livelihoods. Where you’ve watched your children learn family traditions and cultural practices.

As I examined the laws and programs used to facilitate the Isle de Jean Charles relocation, I found a fundamental problem. The United States doesn’t have a comprehensive federal legal framework governing climate-induced relocation.

Instead, communities must navigate a patchwork of disaster programs, grants, and state-level decisions they’re not involved in.

That was particularly consequential because while the Biloxi-Chitimacha-Choctaw are recognized as an Indigenous group at the state level, they lack federal recognition. This resulted in the government determining how the community would relocate, while the Tribal leadership itself lacked authority over the many choices shaping its future.

But the lesson from all this shouldn’t be “don’t relocate.” It becomes “don’t displace people without protecting their rights.” Sometimes relocation will unfortunately become unavoidable. So how do we help communities move without losing their rights and the ability to determine their own future?

My research points toward several answers

The federal government needs clear statutory authority and a dedicated framework for climate-related relocation

Relocation must include enforceable participation requirements

Communities must retain meaningful authority over relocation choices

Relocation policy must recognize that community/cultural survival is part of survival

A successful relocation can’t be measured solely on whether houses were built on safer ground. It must also ask whether families can remain together, livelihoods can survive, and the community itself remains intact.

Climate migration is going to happen. We need to decide what kind. The U.S. is going to see more displacement. That’s not an if it happens, it’s when, and the answer is it’s already started.

So now we’re forced to ask, what happens when it reaches me? I think about this often for different reasons. In New Orleans, hurricanes leave us without clean water and electricity, sometimes for months. Flooding that overtakes our homes and tornadoes that destroy them. But there’s another reason I think about it often.

Immigration.

I was an art teacher when ICE raids started in New Orleans. I watched with my fellow teachers as classes shrank. My own students came to me with their fears of not only losing their homes, but families too. I watch my hometown, Chicago, with bated breath as my dad escorts my stepsiblings to and from school with passports in their pockets because of the color of their skin. I think of my sister in Minneapolis. My mom who worries that someone will see my headscarf and nothing else.

The situations aren’t identical. Some may say I’m still making a stretch with the comparison. Climate relocation and immigration enforcement involve different laws, populations, and governmental authorities. But it raises a common democratic principle: People shouldn’t lose their fundamental rights because the government has the power to move them.

What happened to the Biloxi-Chitimacha-Choctaw shows what happens when legal authority is fragmented, when participation isn’t enforceable, and when vulnerable communities are expected to rely on administrative goodwill. My thesis concluded that climate relocation must move away from ad hoc, discretionary approaches and toward systems that are codified, participatory, and rights-based.

Climate change will eventually make relocation unavoidable for many Americans. If we wait until water is at people’s doors to decide what rights they have, it’ll already be too late.

We have an opportunity right now to build a system in which adaptation doesn’t become another form of dispossession. We can prepare our communities without treating them as problems. We can recognize that home is more than a structure. We can make sure that when climate change makes us move, we have a say in where we go and what we take with us: our rights, culture, and community.

“That’s how we’ll get good growth and jobs in every postcode.”

title: Why Innovative Economic Models Can Rewrite Nuclear Energy's Playbook
description:
While nuclear energy project costs and returns have traditionally determined investment decisions, they often overlook the broader societal benefits nuclear projects have on the region.
These nuclear power projects are not just engineering undertakings; they are investments with far-reaching social, political, geostrategic, and financial consequences.
France vs. Italy—A Case Study in Nuclear Energy Security In 1986, Italy shuttered its nuclear energy program.
Building an Integrated Economic Impact Model for Nuclear Fleets Economic impact modeling is not a new concept.
In conclusion, when we think of nuclear energy as critical infrastructure, we have to go beyond financial models.
text:
While nuclear energy project costs and returns have traditionally determined investment decisions, they often overlook the broader societal benefits nuclear projects have on the region.

All potential megaprojects, including nuclear energy projects, should be strictly assessed across multiple dimensions. However, judging an infrastructure project of the complexity of a nuclear power plant requires an especially detailed analysis of all aspects of the project. These nuclear power projects are not just engineering undertakings; they are investments with far-reaching social, political, geostrategic, and financial consequences.

A facility of two AP1000 reactors would produce more than 2 gigawatts of electricity each hour. From there, the output enters one of the nation’s six major regional transmission systems as high-voltage current. Then it travels across hundreds of miles of transmission lines, stepping down through substations to progressively lower voltages, until reaching local distribution networks where it becomes suitable for residential and commercial use. Ultimately, the steady supply from these reactors provides enough energy to meet the daily needs of about 1.7 million households, powering everything from lights and appliances to heating and digital infrastructure.

The societal, political, economic, and strategic importance of nuclear projects is also well established. According to the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), the nuclear sector is “so vital to the United States that its incapacitation or destruction would have a debilitating effect on security, national economic security, national public health or safety, or any combination thereof.” Nuclear facilities anchor the reliability of many grids as baseload generation, ensuring consistent electricity for hospitals, transportation networks, data centers, and defense installations.

Nuclear power projects require significant capital early in the lifecycle of the asset. With each reactor a multi-billion-dollar endeavor, coupled with long development and construction phases and a complex regulatory process, investors are reluctant to invest in nuclear projects during the development phase, which can become “bet the company” decisions for the developer/owner. Additionally, nuclear projects have a history of going over budget/over schedule (as do other types of megaprojects), requiring additional backstops to support project completion.

The State of the US Nuclear Fleet Today

As we consider nuclear power projects, it is important to recognize the following:

The United States has the largest operating fleet in the world, with 94 reactors in operation (soon to be 95 when Palisades transitions to commercial operation).

With the exception of the two AP1000s at Vogtle in Georgia, the entire operating fleet is comprised of Gen II reactors.

The Gen II reactors were licensed for 40 years, and many will run for up to 80 years.

All 94 reactors were also built in regulated markets by regulated utilities when they were built.

Why Traditional Financial Models Undervalue Long-Life Reactors

What has changed? Now, many markets are deregulated, and the Gen III/III+ designs will be licensed for 60 years, which means that they will probably run for 100 years if properly maintained. A 100-year asset seems like it should be an attractive proposition, especially when it generates clean (emissions-free) baseload energy. However, financial modeling fails us. When calculating the present value of an energy generation asset, everything discounts to zero by the time that asset reaches 30 years in its operating life. That is what the math tells us. However, common sense would seem to recognize that a 70-year operating life must have some value. That is just the beginning of the story.

Immense financial demands mean that projects are often backed by complex funding arrangements, typically involving government support and/or regulated markets (outside the United States in part and the European Union in full). These arrangements ultimately pass down the financial risk to taxpayers and ratepayers. So, why should the taxpayers or ratepayers assume this burden?

France vs. Italy—A Case Study in Nuclear Energy Security

In 1986, Italy shuttered its nuclear energy program. France continued. From that point forward, the French people were paying the cheapest prices for electricity in Western Europe (remember, Europe was still divided; the Cold War was still a “thing”), and Italy was paying the highest prices. Italy was importing electricity. Italy was importing fuel to run its fossil plants. Does any of this matter in a project financial model? Nope. Does this matter in terms of impact on household income and on industrial output / economic competitiveness? Yup. Does this matter in terms of energy security? Yup.

So, how do we capture this value? Remember, this impact does not show up at the project level. As such, investors do not examine these impacts, as they do not benefit from them. Who benefits? The state, the region, the country. Who should care? Who can take this broader view, this longer-term view? The government(s).

Remember, too, with an expected service life of possibly 100 years for an AP1000, each plant can supply a substantial portion of electricity over multiple generations, reducing the need for numerous additional facilities, thereby allowing planners to focus on maintaining and upgrading existing infrastructure (instead of having to replace the facility multiple times). Once a facility is built, that is where it will stay. Thus, where the finite number of future fleets is built is a significant consideration—and a significant opportunity for the jurisdictions that host such projects.

In short, nuclear projects are important for public welfare and critical infrastructure with political implications, but they are costly and finite in number. This means that each potential plant should be fully scrutinized to maximize social utility. Yes, the project should be financially stable with predictable costs, but on the other hand, each plant should benefit the public to the greatest extent possible, and electricity production is far from the full extent of public welfare to be maximized.

How IEA, WNA, and OECD Approach Financial Modeling for NPPs

Traditional financial modeling has long served as the primary analytical tool for evaluating nuclear energy projects, both in the private sector and within government organizations. The International Energy Agency (IEA) emphasizes eight key criteria for evaluating the financing potential of nuclear projects, including factors such as upfront capital cost, construction schedule, operational efficiency, fuel costs, decommissioning expenses, and regulatory risk. Similarly, the World Nuclear Association (WNA) outlines the economic aspects of financing nuclear energy, highlighting the importance of predictable cost structures, financing mechanisms, and the potential for cost overruns. In addition, the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), in collaboration with the Nuclear Energy Agency (NEA), has developed models to assess the viability of future nuclear facilities, focusing on quantifying both predictable and unpredictable costs and identifying strategies to mitigate financial risk.

Across all these sources, a consistent theme emerges: power purchase agreements and government involvement mitigate project risk for investors, and the keys to measuring this mitigation (and with it, the net present value [NPV] of the entire project) are internal rate of return (IRR) and return on investment (ROI). Ultimately, these financial modeling frameworks provide a structured methodology for assessing whether nuclear projects are economically feasible and which financing structures will be most effective in managing both risk and return. Surprisingly, none of these sources reference the relationship between government investment and economic benefits as a decision point for assessing a potential plant; yet, this analysis should be towards the top of any government’s decision on whether or not to provide support to the private sector.

Economic Benefits Are Missing From Investment Decisions

“Why?”

Economic benefits include household income growth, job creation, growth in industrial and commercial sectors, increased tax revenue from those sectors and from the plant itself, decarbonization, reductions in consumer electricity prices, energy diversity, and enhanced energy security—all the things any taxpayer and altruistic government should be attempting to maximize to the fullest. Yet, project financial models do not have inputs for these impacts, as they are external to the project itself. Remember, too, that these impacts do not directly benefit the owner. Without fully incorporating these estimates, developers and, more importantly, policymakers are left with an incomplete picture of a potential project’s true value.

A Tale of Two States — Modeling Nuclear Investment Location

“So just get the best financial details and then decide where it goes based on the economic impacts, right?”

Not so simple. Balancing value and risk of megaprojects, like nuclear power projects, is at the core of any financing model. Financial models are based on projecting IRR and ROI. Financial models for nuclear reactors, however, must also attempt to project electricity prices over time, as the OECD and NEA point out, and electricity prices depend on a fleet’s location. Even so, we find most of the economic value of nuclear plants specifically comes not from direct plant operation or even the electricity production, but from the construction and operation of the plant as it interacts with the regional economy. In other words, the economic value of the plant is dependent on the fleet’s location.

Maximizing return while accounting for risk requires projecting probabilistic “expected values.” And because the financial and economic values of a plant are correlated, both should be accounted for when deciding on the “most viable” potential nuclear plant, which means measuring the true expected value of a potential nuclear fleet just got a lot more complicated.

For example, consider two hypothetical states: State A, a booming tech and commercial hub with high, stable wholesale electricity prices but a saturated labor market, and State B, a struggling industrial region with lower, more volatile electricity prices but high unemployment and a desperate need for a revitalized tax base. If analysts evaluate the proposed project using traditional financial metrics first, State A is the clear winner. The high, stable power prices guarantee strong, risk-adjusted revenues and a highly attractive IRR. When analysts only measure the economic impact after the fact to pad the project’s public relations, they will find those regional benefits are positive but less than if the project is built in State B. The project for State A is financially lucrative but economically stagnant. Conversely, if developers use an economic impact model first to choose the best location, State B wins by a landslide. The plant’s construction and operation would trigger a massive multiplier effect, revitalize the local tax base, and boost industrial competitiveness. However, when analysts run the financial metrics after the fact to determine if the project is “financially viable,” State B’s lower and volatile electricity prices might cause the project to fail standard investment hurdle rates. Now, consider evaluating both models simultaneously. An integrated approach reveals that the massive regional economic value generated in State B far outweighs the superior electricity revenues of State A. More importantly, it identifies the exact nature of the financial risk. Rather than rejecting State B outright based on traditional financial metrics, developers and policymakers can use this complete picture to design a financing structure that bridges the gap. By implementing stronger government guarantees or robust long-term Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs), they can mitigate the localized financial volatility and unlock State B’s immense, superior overall expected value.

Building an Integrated Economic Impact Model for Nuclear Fleets

Economic impact modeling is not a new concept. Plenty of thorough studies have been done on nuclear fleets already in operation, but only many years after the plant was constructed, not as a decision-making tool. Moreover, these analyses are generated with complex, time-consuming models and done independently of the fleet’s financial details. However, such analyses have not been adequately factored into the decision-making process for the development, construction, and financing of new reactors, especially in the context of Public-Private Partnership (PPP) approaches.

By combining financial spreadsheets with a simple network model, we can project the impact of a potential fleet of any number of small modular reactors (e.g., GEH’s BWRX-300s) and large reactors (e.g., Westinghouse’s AP1000s) in any state with any return on investment on that state’s household income, industrial output, commercial output, state tax revenue, and much more. This analysis engages both state governments and the public in the region, while still considering project costs and financing details. In turn, such analyses can serve as the foundation for PPP collaborations to structure viable projects, enabling governments to justify the “forward lean” that will be essential for project success.

A convenient current comparison is the four BWRX-300s that Ontario Power Generation is building in Darlington, Ontario. Analyzing the impact of four BWRXs in an economy similar to Ontario’s, our model projects the state’s total economic benefits to be $106.298 billion over an 80-year lifetime, including construction. If the Conference Board of Ontario assumed a 3 percent annual inflation rate and linearly scaled annual impacts to an 80-year lifetime, they would find a total impact of $109.510 billion based on their public estimates. Project costs are not overlooked either. The model estimates total overnight costs of $6.138 billion for the first unit and $18.825 billion for all four, similar to the $5.56 billion and $15.08 billion projected by Ontario’s government to construct the fleet.

More importantly, if a more optimal location for the same fleet exists, we could find it. That is, by combining financial details with economic impact models, a more accurate comparison of different potential sites is possible.

The Future of Nuclear Investment Modeling

As more companies, industries, governments, and world leaders look to nuclear energy as the solution to challenges faced around the globe, we intend to expand the model to encapsulate many more potential players—both domestically and internationally, across multiple jurisdictions, reactor technologies, and project types (both nuclear and non-nuclear). Modeling different economic impacts of different reactor combinations in different locations is critical to aligning developers’ financial decisions with more encompassing government intentions. While financial models are important, economic impact models take those values a necessary step further, encapsulating the full value of a nuclear energy project and ensuring the truly optimal decision about nuclear fleets is made.

Without modeling the economic impact of nuclear power projects, the full impact/value of the project is not assessed. The result is that decisions are being made on more incomplete information. However, it is important to recognize that the benefits analyzed in the foregoing discussion are not captured by the owners of the project; these are societal benefits that are lost if the project does not go forward. And here is the not-so-little secret: the benefits are massive.

Worldwide, government support (direct and/or indirect) is critical to the development and long-term viability of nuclear power plants. Yet government budgets are constrained, and many parties are competing for government attention and support. Doing the empirical analysis concerning the economic impact of a proposed nuclear power plant is a critical activity during the development phase of a project’s lifecycle because it makes the case for government support to enable the project. Further, if the project is structured with a long-term, creditworthy offtake structure, the government’s position can be refinanced, so that the project not only creates value for the taxpayers and ratepayers but also returns the money back to the participating government (which can then be redeployed for other projects and purposes).

In conclusion, when we think of nuclear energy as critical infrastructure, we have to go beyond financial models. Financial models are important to the analysis, but there are larger considerations at stake for national planning and development. When we think of something as “critical infrastructure,” it changes how we think of the project at a fundamental level.

The Bottom Line: If we ask you for 2 units of value to make a project happen, and we create 10 units of value over the life of the project, and none of that value goes into my pocket, and then we give you back those 2 units a few years after commercial operation, you take that deal every time.

About the Authors: Paul Murphy and Braedon Rudolph

Paul Murphy is the founder and managing director of Murphy Energy & Infrastructure Consulting, LLC, where he advises on legal, policy, and financing strategies for nuclear power projects worldwide. Recognized as an expert by the IAEA, NEA, and the US government, he has represented developers, investors, and contractors across the global nuclear industry and is an eight-time appointee to the US Secretary of Commerce’s Civilian Nuclear Trade Advisory Committee.

Braedon Rudolph is a 2nd Lieutenant in the US Marine Corps. He studied economics and physics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and has researched various complex systems including competitive equilibria in preference space, geometric arbitrage theory, and thick-tailed random matrices. In 2024, he founded Network Analysis Group, LLC, currently researching the economic impacts of potential nuclear energy sites around the world.

Note to the reader: As of the date hereof, the economic impact model developed by Rudolph & Murphy has now been applied to three reactor types and a fabrication facility across five US states and two foreign jurisdictions on behalf of both corporate and government entities.

text:
The likes of Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft are pouring billions into nuclear power to feed their data centres, reshaping the US energy landscape

Big Tech has fallen head over heels for the atom.

Over the past 18 months, Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft have each struck high-profile deals with nuclear operators and developers as they search for ways to power their ever-growing portfolios of data centres.

The AI boom has been the catalyst here. Data centres have always had a large appetite for power, but facilities dedicated to AI use between three to five times more energy than their more traditional counterparts, according to Hanwha.

The race to fill that deficit with a supply of round-the-clock, low-carbon energy has led Big Tech to nuclear power.

Why data centres need a different kind of power

Data centres are not ordinary consumers of electricity. They need it constantly, every hour of every day, with no tolerance for the dips and surges that come with wind and solar generation.

Battery storage technology hasn’t yet matured enough to deal with the intermittency of renewables at the scale Big Tech requires.

This leaves nuclear as one of the few sources of what the industry calls ‘baseload power’, meaning a steady, uninterrupted supply of energy that does not fluctuate with the weather.

It was this logic that drove nearly 200 companies, including Amazon, Google, Meta and the chemicals group Dow, to sign a pledge in 2025 backing the tripling of global nuclear capacity by 2050.

Speaking at the time, Sama Bilbao y Leon, Director General of the World Nuclear Association, said: “The unprecedented support announced today by some of the world's most influential companies to at least triple global nuclear capacity by 2050 sends a clear signal to accelerate policy, finance and regulatory changes that enable the rapid expansion of nuclear power.”

Meta's 6.6GW nuclear arsenal

Of the Big Tech firms, Meta has perhaps been most enthusiastic in its pursuit of nuclear capacity.

In January 2026 the company put pen to paper on a trio of 20-year power purchase agreements with Vistra, TerraPower and Oklo.

To date, Meta has committed to offtake 6.6GW of nuclear power by 2035, which is roughly equivalent to the average power demand of Singapore.

The Vistra agreement alone covers more than 2.1GW across three plants, Perry and Davis-Besse in Ohio and Beaver Valley in Pennsylvania.

After signing the deal, Jim Burke, President and CEO of Vistra, said: “This agreement is beneficial in many ways. It powers American innovation and AI technology, while allowing us to extend the operational life of these plants, boost the capacity of the nuclear reactors to support the grid, protect existing jobs while creating new ones and continue investing in the communities where our plants are located.”

The two other deals Meta signed earlier this year point toward a less proven but potentially more transformative future.

The firm’s partnership with TerraPower will focus on the construction of two Natrium reactors capable of generating up to 690MW, with the first expected online as early as 2032, while a further six units could add another 2.1GW by 2035.

Oklo, meanwhile, is developing a fast-reactor campus in Pike County, Ohio, that could deliver up to 1.2GW and come online in 2030, using what the company calls Aurora Powerhouse reactors capable of running on both fresh and repurposed nuclear fuel.

“Meta's funding commitment in support of early procurement and development activity is a major step in moving advanced nuclear forward,” said Jacob DeWitte, Oklo's Co-Founder and CEO.

Microsoft and the return of Three Mile Island

If Meta's story is about scale, Microsoft's is symbolic of the way nuclear’s reputation is bouncing back.

In 2024 the company signed a power purchase agreement with Constellation Energy to revive Three Mile Island's Unit 1, the reactor that sits beside the site of America's most serious nuclear accident.

Unit 2 suffered a partial meltdown in 1979 after a cooling malfunction, an incident rated Level 5 on the International Nuclear Event Scale.

Unit 1 continued operating until 2019, when it was shut for financial rather than safety reasons, and Constellation says the reactor is still in excellent shape.

The reactor is scheduled to come back online in 2027 and is projected to add around US$16bn to Pennsylvania's economy.

Bobby Hollis, who served as Vice President of Energy at Microsoft until May this year, said at the time: “As Microsoft continues its path to become a carbon negative company, this agreement brings a significant supply of new, reliable, carbon-free electricity back to the PJM power grid.”

Pennsylvania's Governor Josh Shapiro was similarly enthusiastic, describing a project that would safely reuse existing infrastructure.

“This restart will safely take advantage of existing infrastructure while creating thousands of energy jobs and strengthening Pennsylvania's legacy as a national energy leader,” he said.

Google's revival of a shuttered Iowa plant

Google has taken a similar approach in the Midwest, partnering with NextEra Energy to revive the Duane Arnold Energy Center near Cedar Rapids, Iowa, a 615MW plant that closed its doors in 2020.

The company has signed up to a 25-year power purchase agreement that will see it take the bulk of the plant's output when it resumes generation in early 2029.

The upsides for Google are clear. It is currently developing a US$576m data centre campus just a stone’s throw from the site, so renovation was practically a no-brainer.

The benefits for the wider community cannot be overstated, though. Reviving the power plant is expected to deliver more than US$9bn in benefits to Iowa and create at least 1,600 jobs during construction.

“AI is forcing an honest conversation about clean energy,” said Robert Little, gTech Sustainability Strategy Lead at Google, last year. “AI and cloud infrastructure need massive, reliable, clean power. Not just when the sun shines or the wind blows, but 24/7.”

The Duane Arnold deal forms part of a broader partnership between Google and NextEra to explore new nuclear plants across the US – their third gigawatt-scale collaboration to date.

“Nuclear is a big piece of the solution as we work toward powering Google's operations with clean energy every hour of every day,” explains Michael Terrell, Head of Advanced Energy at Google.

Amazon's spread bet on PPAs and small modular reactors

Amazon’s largest nuclear energy endeavour is in Pennsylvania, where it has a power purchase agreement running until 2042 with Talen Energy.

The 1.9GW PPA, signed in 2025 at a cost of around US$18bn, sees energy from the Susquehanna Steam Electric Station go directly to an AWS data centre campus located just across the road.

But it is not just large-scale nuclear projects that the company is investing in.

In Washington, Amazon’s money is helping to develop a small modular reactor beside Energy Northwest's Columbia Generating Station.

In Virginia, Amazon struck a separate agreement with Dominion Energy to develop a 300MW SMR near the North Anna nuclear plant.

What links all three of these initiatives is the company’s US$500m investment in X-energy, the reactor developer behind the Washington project. Amazon says its support of X-energy will help fund manufacturing capacity for more than 5GW of new nuclear projects.

"Nuclear is a safe source of carbon-free energy that can help power our operations and meet the growing demands of our customers, while helping us progress toward our Climate Pledge commitment to be net-zero carbon across our operations by 2040," states Matt Garman, CEO at AWS.

What is an SMR?

Small modular reactors, or SMRs, are an emerging technology in the world of nuclear energy.

As the name suggests, they are more compact than traditional nuclear power plants and can be built to order, which has led some commentators to dub them ‘flat-pack power stations’.

All this has the potential to cut the time and cost associated with the construction of nuclear plants, which can often take more than 10 years.

That said, there are only two SMRs currently operational today – the KLT-40S in Russia and the HTR-PM in China – though many are currently under development all around the world, including in the UK.

SGE, a Polish firm that recently submitted a proposal to build 14 SMRs in the UK, is one of the technology’s leading proponents.

The company’s CEO, Rafał Kasprów, says: "Standardisation, repetition, modularisation and a fleet deployment strategy are the most effective ways to deliver new nuclear projects successfully, reducing costs, construction risk and delivery times."

A simple equation

Big Tech’s growing admiration for nuclear energy is a matter of arithmetic.

Each of the aforementioned organisations has promised to cut its carbon footprint while simultaneously building the most energy hungry infrastructure in corporate history.

Simply put, that sum no longer adds up without a source of power that runs continuously and without emissions.

After the Fukushima disaster in 2011, global investments in nuclear energy fell off a cliff, with many countries even deciding to phase out nuclear altogether.

Just 15 years later, the energy source is having a true renaissance, pushed on by technological innovations like SMRs and microreactors.

Whether this new relationship between Big Tech and nuclear will last remains to be seen. For now, though, nuclear is well and truly a part of the sector’s future.

text:
The wait for a large gas turbine now runs longer than the time it takes to design, permit, and build the plant it will sit in. Order one today from any of the three largest manufacturers, and the delivery slot lands four or more years out—if a slot is available at all. The queue to connect a new plant to the grid runs about as long. For developers racing to power the data centers hyperscalers are building, the timeline no longer works, and it is pushing the U.S. generation build toward whatever can be constructed without waiting in either line.That dislocation is the backdrop to a quieter story about where capital is moving, and it surfaced in July when a familiar U.S. plant operator changed hands. IHI Power Services Corp., a company with roughly four decades of experience running American power plants, became Kyuden Energy Partners Corp. on completion of its acquisition by Kyuden International Corp., the overseas arm of a company fully owned by Japan's Kyushu Electric Power Co. The rebrand is the news of the day. The more instructive part is what a foreign utility chose to buy: not power plants, but the capability to run them.

A Brand-New World

Tony Dabbene, who led IHI Power Services through the transition and stays on as CEO, was blunt about the market. "We are seeing the most dynamic environment in decades," he told POWER, pointing to demand tied to the hyperscalers' data center buildout. Major gas turbine manufacturers, he said, are quoting lead times of four-plus years, with interconnection queues running about the same. The manufacturers' own disclosures bear that out: GE Vernova's gas turbine backlog and slot reservations reached 116 GW by mid-2026, and Siemens Energy has described itself as booked into the back half of the decade, treating 2029 delivery slots as near-term availability.What Dabbene described next was the market's response. Rather than wait for an interconnection that may not clear before mid-decade, developers are building behind the meter and on private grids that sidestep the queue entirely. To power them, they're reaching for whatever can be deployed the fastest: reciprocating engines, fuel cells, and battery storage paired with microgrids, engineered to achieve the high-availability targets that around-the-clock computing demands while managing the power-quality swings that come when those loads shift in an instant. "It is a brand-new world in the energy space," he said.This is where a multi-fuel operator has the edge. A company that already runs natural gas, hydro, biomass, wind, solar, and storage has done the work developers are now rushing toward—operating mixed generation and meeting high availability targets. The turbine shortage may be a headache for those building facilities, but it's an opportunity for reliable operators.
