text:
The most consequential number in current American energy planning is one that nobody in the room where it gets made believes.

I sell into data center buildouts, so I sit in that room. Someone asks how much power the site will need. No one really knows—the racks aren’t spec’d, the tenant isn’t signed, the whole thing hangs on a chip that ships in 18 months. They take the largest configuration anyone floats, add margin—200 MW, 500 MW, whatever the site could handle if everything broke its way.

COMMENTARY

Nobody is lying. What comes out of that room is a ceiling, and everyone understands it’s a ceiling. It’s the only responsible way to plan a project where being undersized costs you the tenant, and being oversized costs you a mildly embarrassing press release.

Then the number leaves the room and stops being a ceiling. It becomes an announcement, then an interconnection request, then five more in five more territories, because nobody knows which utility will get to them first and it would be negligent not to ask all of them. This publication has already documented where that leads. I’m not here to relitigate it.

I’m here about what it’s costing to believe it.

The Department of Energy since May 2025 has issued more than 40 emergency orders under Section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act. A handful of those have held at least 4.4 GW of coal-fired generation from retirement. In roughly 50 years, the department had never ordered a generating unit to keep producing past its retirement date. The orders run 90 days, are always renewed, and the justification is load growth.

Take Texas in late July. The Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) blew past a demand record that had stood since August 2023, with preliminary readings above 91 GW. The grid took it with more than 20 GW to spare, no emergency alert, no call to conserve. Real load, arriving, absorbed on a Wednesday evening.

Now look at the queue behind it. ERCOT is tracking more than 438 GW of large-load requests, nearly 90% from data centers—roughly five times the record that just got set. ERCOT has said plainly that its own forecast runs higher than it expects actual growth to be.

That’s the number doing the legal work. Not the 91. The 438.

I went looking at those coal plants ordered to remain open. Five produced 1.5 TWh in the first quarter of 2026, down 65% from the same quarter in 2025. I keep coming back to Centralia, Washington state’s last coal plant, 730 MW, set to close at the end of 2025 but now serving its third consecutive 90-day order. TransAlta’s chief executive said the unit likely would not be called on at all, because the U.S. Northwest is flush with hydro. The company has asked the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission for $19.9 million to cover the first order alone. Who pays is an open question because the Northwest has no regional transmission organization, and TransAlta has no retail customers. A plant nobody expects to run, kept warm by federal command, with the bill still an open docket.

Here is where a grid operator stops me, and fairly. The North American Electric Reliability Corp.’s latest long-term assessment puts a majority of regions at elevated risk in the coming years. Dispatchable plants are retiring faster than firm replacements are coming online. A plant running 15 days a year is still worth having on the 15th day. Keeping a boiler warm as insurance is certainly defensible.

I don’t dispute the insurance. I dispute the premium, and who set it. An insurance policy priced off a number the underwriter has publicly called too high is not insurance, just a subsidy with a reliability label on it. If the case for holding these plants open is genuine winter risk, make that case on winter risk, in the open, plant by plant, and let a regulator weigh it. Do not run it through emergency authority pointed at a queue that the queue’s own operator does not believe.

The frustrating part is that the alternative is not stuck on physics. I spend a lot of time around people building small reactors, and the engineering is not what is holding them up. The May 2025 executive orders set historically aggressive U.S. nuclear targets: 400 GW by 2050, 10 new large reactors under construction by 2030. The Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) finalized a new licensing framework in March; it proposed one for microreactors in May. This is the most ambition Washington has aimed at nuclear in a generation, and it is real.

But look at how the ambition moves. Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) in early 2025 applied to build the first U.S. utility-led commercial small modular reactor—a 300-MW unit at Clinch River. NRC staff recommended approval more than a year later, in June 2026. Now there’s a mandatory public hearing in Tennessee. Until commissioners sign, TVA cannot begin construction.

Consider that timeline. It took more than a year, and the most-watched advanced reactor application in the country, to reach a single evening meeting where someone decides whether a shovel is allowed in the ground. That is the asymmetry, and it has nothing to do with enthusiasm. A coal plant can be ordered to keep running in an afternoon. A reactor waits a year-and-a-half to reach the room where the meeting happens.

Coal got an order. Nuclear got a meeting.

I sell into this buildout, so weigh my incentive accordingly. The bigger that number, the better my year, and I have never once been in a position where correcting anybody would have made me money. What I can’t defend is applying federal emergency authority to a forecast the forecaster has disowned, aiming it at the oldest thing on the system, and calling the newest thing too slow while it waits for permission that we already know how to grant.

The load is coming. Some of it. Build for that part.

text:
(TestMiles) – Three of the five quickest 2026 vehicles below $50,000 are electric crossovers, while a V8 Mustang and GR Corolla keep gasoline in the race.

The old performance hierarchy has been scrambled

There was a time when a list of the quickest new vehicles for less than $50,000 would have been easy to picture before seeing a single name. Expect a low coupe, a rear-drive muscle car, perhaps a hot hatch and something with a turbocharger large enough to make the warranty department nervous.

The 2026 list looks very different. Rank the quickest qualifying vehicles by instrumented 0-to-60-mph time and the first three are electric crossovers. Not electric sports cars. Not six-figure technological showcases. Crossovers.

The Volvo EX30 Twin Motor Performance leads this group with a tested 3.3 second 0-60 mph. The Subaru Trailseeker and Toyota bZ Woodland tie behind it at 3.9 seconds. The first gasoline-powered entries are the Ford Mustang GT with a six-speed manual and Toyota GR Corolla with a six-speed manual, each came in at 4.2 seconds.

That makes the top five vehicles, with ties acknowledged, look like this:

Volvo EX30 Twin Motor Performance 3.3 seconds

Subaru Trailseeker 3.9 seconds

Toyota bZ Woodland 3.9 seconds

Ford Mustang GT 6MT 4.2 seconds

Toyota GR Corolla 6MT 4.2 seconds

Electric crossovers occupy the podium

The quickest vehicle in this group is also the smallest looking threat. Volvo’s 2026 EX30 Twin Motor Performance starts at $46,345, produces 422 horsepower and carries an EPA-estimated range of up to 253 miles. Volvo says it reaches 60 mph in 3.4 seconds. Independent testing has recorded 3.3.

That number would have sounded exotic-car quick not very long ago. It now belongs to a compact Volvo SUV whose design brief includes grocery runs, school traffic and fitting into urban parking spaces. The EX30 is not merely quick for an EV. At 3.3 seconds, it is simply quick.

Then come two vehicles that make the change in performance even more obvious. Subaru’s 2026 Trailseeker starts at $39,995 and uses two electric motors for a combined 375 horsepower. It has been tested at 3.9 seconds to 60 mph, making it the quickest Subaru yet. Subaru built the Trailseeker around all-wheel-drive utility, cargo space, ground clearance and outdoor use. Yet its straight-line acceleration is now in territory once reserved for dedicated performance machinery.

Toyota’s bZ Woodland is closely related in concept and hardware. It also produces 375 horsepower and has also recorded a 3.9-second run. Toyota starts the Woodland at $45,300 before its processing and handling fee. It offers up to 281 miles of EPA-estimated range on standard tires, 8.4 inches of ground clearance and up to 3,500 pounds of towing capacity.

None of those utility specifications sound like the ingredients for an affordable speed chart. That is precisely why the ranking matters.

Cheap speed has changed faster than car culture

Electric motors have an inherent advantage in the specific contest represented by a 0-60 time. They can deliver strong torque immediately, and dual-motor systems can use all-wheel drive to put that force to the pavement. Most EVs also do not need to work through a conventional multi-gear transmission during the launch.

The result is repeatable, low-drama acceleration that would have required a very different mechanical recipe a generation ago. A driver can be sitting in a quiet crossover one moment and moving at highway speed a few seconds later without a rising exhaust note or a string of gear changes.

That does not automatically make an EV the better performance car. Acceleration is one measurement. Steering feel, braking, mass, tire performance, thermal management and behavior after repeated hard use all matter. In testing, for example, the Trailseeker’s powertrain needs cooling after consecutive acceleration runs. That is useful context for anyone who mistakes a quick launch number for track endurance.

Still, the price-to-acceleration equation has plainly moved. Three of these five sub-$50,000 vehicles are battery electric, and all three occupy the fastest part of the list. The achievement is less about proving that electricity is superior to gasoline in every form of driving than showing how inexpensive serious acceleration has become when electric motors are involved.

The Mustang and Corolla refuse to leave quietly

The Ford Mustang GT is the vehicle most people would have expected to find here. Ford’s current 2026 build-and-price page lists the GT Fastback from $47,795. Its 5.0-liter V8 makes 480 horsepower in standard form and can be paired with a six-speed manual transmission. A manual Mustang GT has recorded a 4.2-second run to 60 mph.

The Mustang also demonstrates why a stopwatch cannot describe the whole experience. A V8 engine, clutch pedal, manual gearbox and rear-wheel-drive layout ask more from the driver and give more mechanical feedback in return. An EV can beat the Mustang away from a stoplight while completely missing the point of why somebody wanted a Mustang in the first place.

Then there is the Toyota.

Finding the word “Corolla” in a top-five affordable acceleration list still looks like a typographical error. It is not. The 2026 GR Corolla starts at $39,920 before Toyota’s processing and handling fee. Its turbocharged 1.6-liter three-cylinder engine produces 300 horsepower and 295 pound-feet of torque, sent through Toyota’s GR-FOUR all-wheel-drive system. With the six-speed manual, an instrumented 2026 test reached 60 mph in 4.2 seconds.

To be clear, this is not an ordinary Corolla with enthusiastic badges. The GR Corolla is a specialized performance hatchback developed by Toyota Gazoo Racing, with hardware, cooling, chassis changes and drivetrain engineering aimed at enthusiastic driving. But the name still matters. Corolla has spent decades representing durable, accessible transportation. Seeing it level with a V8 Mustang on this list is one of those useful reminders that the modern performance market no longer follows old stereotypes.

The automatic GR Corolla is slower to 60 in the same testing, so the six-speed manual is specifically the version that earns this place. That is another charming inversion of the current market: while electric cars make maximum acceleration easier, one of the gasoline cars fighting them does it with three pedals.

Acceleration is only one kind of performance

There is a temptation to turn a ranking like this into a referendum on electric vehicles. It is more useful as a snapshot of what buyers can now purchase.

For less than $50,000 at the starting-MSRP level, shoppers can get a Volvo that reaches 60 mph in 3.3 seconds, two practical electric utility vehicles that break four seconds, a traditional V8 muscle car with a manual transmission, or a 300-horsepower three-cylinder Toyota hatchback that can run beside that Mustang to 60.

That breadth would have been difficult to imagine when affordable performance meant choosing among variations of the same gasoline-powered formula.

It also creates a new buyer question. If a person wants the strongest launch for the dollar, EVs are increasingly difficult to beat. The motors respond instantly, all-wheel drive is easily integrated into dual-motor layouts, and the software can manage traction with extraordinary precision. Shoppers still need to consider charging access, range, insurance, tire cost and how they use the vehicle, but outright acceleration is no longer the expensive part of the equation.

If the goal is involvement, sound and a sense that the driver is participating in the process, the Mustang GT and GR Corolla make equally strong arguments from the opposite direction. Neither needs to win the first 60 mph to remain desirable.

The bigger change is that the old categories have collapsed. A Subaru aimed at campers, a Toyota built for muddy dogs, a small Swedish electric SUV, a V8 Mustang and a rally-inspired Corolla can now occupy the same performance conversation.

That is what the stopwatch is really telling us. Affordable speed did not disappear as the industry electrified. It spread into vehicles that nobody would once have thought to put on the same list.

title: Environmentalists want more time for public comment on the Roadless Rule rescission
description:
With less than 30 days left, conservation groups are requesting the government extend the public comment period for its proposal to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule.
According to the Center for Economic and Policy Institute, the two-year period of public comment was unprecedented.
The Bush Administration proposed scrapping the Roadless Rule in 2005, during which time there were two public comment periods, both more than 100 days.
Then, 146 members of Congress introduced legislation to reinstate the original Roadless Rule and repeal the Bush administration's substitute.
By the fall of 2006, a federal judge ordered the reinstatement of the Clinton-era Roadless Rule.
text:
With less than 30 days left, conservation groups are requesting the government extend the public comment period for its proposal to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule.

Earthjustice filed the request on behalf of several environmental groups, including the Wilderness Society, the Sierra Club, and others. The nonprofit says rescinding the landmark rule affects 45 million acres of national forest land — largely in the West — across 38 states.

Aaron Bloom, a senior attorney with Earthjustice, says there are no public hearings scheduled, except in Alaska. He says people should be able to weigh in on a decision of this magnitude.

"We are asking for public hearings throughout the country in accessible locations, so that the public that's impacted by this rule can show up and have their voices heard," he said.

Before the rule was enacted, Bloom points out, the federal government held hundreds of public hearings throughout the country. According to the Center for Economic and Policy Institute, the two-year period of public comment was unprecedented.

Currently, the public comment deadline is Sept. 21.

In its letter to the U.S. Forest Service and the U.S. Department of Agriculture, Earthjustice requests extending the public comment period to at least 120 days to increase the opportunities for the public to weigh in on the proposed rescission. The organization has not heard a response from the government. The departments also did not respond to a request for comment from the Mountain West News Bureau on Thursday.

"They have said nothing about that; when initially enacting the rule and adding additional protections, they held 600 public hearings across the country," Bloom said.

The Bush Administration proposed scrapping the Roadless Rule in 2005, during which time there were two public comment periods, both more than 100 days. In a timeline published online, Earthjustice also intervened then, saying the Bush administration's attempt to replace the Roadless Rule with a new state-centered version violated the Endangered Species Act and other provisions.

Then, 146 members of Congress introduced legislation to reinstate the original Roadless Rule and repeal the Bush administration's substitute. This was followed by a lawsuit filed by the attorneys general of California and New Mexico and the governor of Oregon, also challenging the new version.

More lawsuits followed throughout 2006. By the fall of 2006, a federal judge ordered the reinstatement of the Clinton-era Roadless Rule.

The Department of Agriculture, in citing its rationale for rescinding the rule during the Trump administration, said a "single, national blanket" approach "constrains responsible officials from exercising the timely, place-based discretion needed."

"In addition, evolving national priorities and changed conditions have required more active management approaches," the department went on to state.

Bloom believes public comment can make a difference, pointing to the rule being kept in place in 2005 after public outcry and public pushback helping to remove a provision to sell public land from the "One Big Beautiful Bill Act" in 2025.

"When the public rises up and speaks out and tells the administration, hands off our public lands, sometimes the administration will listen. We have to stand up for our public lands and make our voices heard," Bloom said.

The Roadless Rule applies to land in every state in the Mountain West except Colorado and Idaho, which have their own state-specific rules. People can submit their opinions online.

title: Indonesia doubles down on coal to power its aluminum expansion - ABC News
authors: ANTON L. DELGADO Associated Press, ABC News
description:
The Finland-registered nonprofit is tracking 32 prospective off-grid coal plants, built by private companies to exclusively power aluminum smelters.
“This captive coal boom all over Indonesia is essentially not tracked.
Building more captive coal for aluminum will worsen the toxic haze that often blankets Southeast Asian cities, like Jakarta, according to Muhammad Al Amin, with the Indonesian Forum for Environment.
“If companies want to expand captive coal to aluminum, I think it is very bad news and a very bad development,” he said.
“We have seen it, we have felt it — how communities suffer from the captive coal impact.” ___ Associated Press writer Edna Tarigan in Jakarta contributed to this report.
text:
BANGKOK -- Resource-rich Indonesia is expanding its production of aluminum as the Iran war disrupts supplies, relying on its abundant coal reserves to power new smelters that run contrary to efforts to curb carbon emissions that cause climate change.

Prices have risen due to fuel shortfalls and attacks on infrastructure that have slowed production in the Middle East of the lightweight, silverish metal used in everything from kitchen foil and power lines to smartphones and cars.

In working to raise its limited manufacturing capacity, Indonesia has a strong ally in China, which makes 60% of the world's aluminum but is keen to reduce pollution and emissions from smelters on its own shores. Chinese companies have invested in about three-quarters of the planned Indonesian projects.

Here's what to know about Indonesia's ambitious aluminum plans:

The Middle East usually makes about 9% of the world’s aluminum, but output from the region is expected to drop 44% this year from 2025, according to Fastmarkets, a commodities information agency.

Energy shortfalls drove Emirates Global Aluminium to back out of deals and Qatar Aluminium Ltd. to slash production, while Iranian strikes damaged Aluminium Bahrain's facilities.

A metric ton of aluminum traded for between $3,150 and $3,250 before the Iran war. But the conflict drove up that price to as high as $3,780 per metric ton in June. It’s now trading near $3,400 a metric ton.

The war has magnified the potential for other regions, like Southeast Asia, to replace Middle East production, said Andy Farida of Fastmarkets.

“When that supply is so unsure, end users look for alternatives,” he said. “The war has really accelerated this transformation and put Indonesia on the map.”

Aluminum is one of the most used metals in the world and its production is highly energy intensive. The process starts with the mining of bauxite ore, which is refined into alumina and then smelted into aluminum.

By the end of the decade, Indonesia wants to quadruple its alumina output to 32.5 million metric tons and ramp up aluminum production from around 1 million metric tons in 2025 to 14.5 million metric tons by 2030, according to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.

The Finland-registered nonprofit is tracking 32 prospective off-grid coal plants, built by private companies to exclusively power aluminum smelters. These are known as “captive coal” facilities.

There is limited public data on the emissions from these types of plants, according to Syahdiva Moezbar, with CREA in Jakarta. “This captive coal boom all over Indonesia is essentially not tracked. That is why it’s very concerning,” he said.

Such plans are contrary to Indonesia’s promises to cut its use of coal, the most heavily polluting major fossil fuel and a significant source of planet-warming emissions.

They also threaten to cause more damage at a time when the expansion of Indonesia's globally important nickel industry is sacrificing local environments for industrialization.

The aluminum industry accounts for about 2% of annual global greenhouse gas emissions, equaling about 1.1 billion tons of carbon dioxide equivalent each year, according to the World Economic Forum. That’s more than the total annual emissions of most countries.

If all Indonesia’s planned projects begin operating by 2030, CREA estimates that the country's own bauxite reserves will be depleted in less than 12 years.

China has invested between $5.5 billion and $6 billion in Indonesia's aluminum industry, according to CREA, which forecasts this to surge to $30 billion by 2030.

After Beijing set a domestic cap on aluminum production to curb overcapacity in 2017, Chinese companies expanded into other countries that have fewer restrictions, like Indonesia, according to Putra Adhiguna, with the Jakarta-based Energy Shift Institute.

Indonesia categorizes nickel and aluminum as “transition minerals” since they can be used in so-called clean technologies, such as electric vehicle batteries and solar panels.

That's left a loophole for companies to maintain that these nickel and aluminum investments, which are fueled by coal, are in keeping with climate change commitments, despite the fact that Chinese President Xi Jinping pledged to stop funding overseas coal plants in 2021.

It is unclear what final products Indonesia-origin metals, like aluminum and nickel, will end up in, said Binbin Mariana with the environmental advocacy group Market Forces.

“It is a huge loophole, an elephant can go through the loophole,” she said. “You say it’s a green product, but it is powered by coal... That’s definitely greenwashing.”

Aluminum smelters could run on cleaner energy like hydropower, but this would take longer and cost more.

Indonesia is prioritizing speed to capitalize on the window of opportunity that the Iran war has created, said Adhiguna, with the Energy Shift Institute. “The speed factor is really what is causing the havoc,” he said.

“This is really running against the grain, against the spirit, of the commitment to the climate movement," he said.

Building more captive coal for aluminum will worsen the toxic haze that often blankets Southeast Asian cities, like Jakarta, according to Muhammad Al Amin, with the Indonesian Forum for Environment.

The environmental advocacy nonprofit, also known as WALHI, has campaigned against increasing the use of coal on the Indonesian island of Sulawesi, which is a nickel production hub.

“If companies want to expand captive coal to aluminum, I think it is very bad news and a very bad development,” he said. “We have seen it, we have felt it — how communities suffer from the captive coal impact.”

___

Associated Press writer Edna Tarigan in Jakarta contributed to this report.

text:
This has brought total installations in the first half of 2026 to 30.8 GWh. Utility-scale energy storage capacity has nearly doubled from 88 GWh to 165 GWh in the first 18 months of the Trump administration, as grid operators, utilities and energy buyers turn to storage to strengthen reliability and meet rising electricity demand.

Demand for energy storage is outpacing expectations, prompting an 11.5 percent increase in the report’s forecast through 2030 to 683 GWh. The upward revision comes as the industry continues to set deployment records, with more than 10 percent of all energy storage capacity currently installed in the US coming online in Q2 alone.

“This record growth highlights that storage is a powerful reliability tool that strengthens our energy security, meets rising demand and puts downward pressure on electricity bills” said Tim Pawlenty, president and CEO of the Solar Energy Industries Association.

More than 74 percent of the energy storage capacity installed in Q2 was built in states won by President Donald Trump in 2024, led largely by Arizona, Texas, and Utah. Arizona led the country with 6.2 GWh of new storage installations in Q2, the strongest quarter for any one state on record. Arizona, which has the nation's fourth-largest solar market, is increasingly pairing its abundant solar resources with storage to capture more homegrown power, meet rising demand, and help keep electricity costs down.

“Energy storage is no longer just a California and Texas story anymore” added Shan Tomouk, BESS & Energy Lead at Benchmark Minerals. “We’re seeing strong pipeline growth in Arizona, Nevada, Oregon, Colorado and several other states.”

Battery energy storage supplied more electricity to the grid in the first eight months of 2026 than in all of 2025. During periods of extreme heat in states like Texas and California, storage has helped provide power when demand is highest, supporting grid reliability and helping protect consumers from price spikes. Texas and California installed 3.8 GWh and 3.6 GWh of storage, respectively, in Q2.

text:
A proposed development in Pecan Island is being pitched as an economic win for coastal Louisiana. But for many of the people who already live and work there, the more pressing question is what that growth could cost.

In Vermilion Parish, the debate also comes down to land, water, and whether a long-established coastal way of life can survive a major change.

Here's what to know

According to KLFY, state leaders see the Pecan Island proposal as a route to economic growth, while local farmers and fishers are concerned about what it could do to the coast.

That tension is especially sharp in a place like Pecan Island, where daily life is closely tied to the coast. For families who rely on farming and fishing, changes to land use or water access are not abstract concerns; they can affect jobs, food production, and whether younger generations will be able to stay in the community.

Local resident Craig Pitre's position shows that the response is not simply split into supporters and opponents. He moved to Pecan Island for the quiet and for more time to spend fishing and on the water. He recognized that development could change the lifestyle that drew him there, but he also understood that the project could be a source of growth for Vermilion Parish.

More background

When residents express worries about impacts to land and water, they are also raising concerns about the foundations of the local economy. Farming and fishing are not secondary issues in places like Pecan Island; they are central to how people make a living, preserve local culture, and remain rooted in the region.

What's being done?

Residents, along with people who fish and farm in the area, are openly questioning the proposal, asking what it would mean for the coast and for the industries that already sustain Vermilion Parish. If nothing else, they want a say in what happens.

"I really deeply care about our land, my community, my family," Brennon Sagrera, a local rice and crawfish farmer, told the outlet. "And like I said, my son's the 10th generation. I hope we can have 10 more there, but, I mean, I don't even know what it's going to look like by the time I'm an old man."

text:
India's transition to electric vehicles could support 7.2 million direct manufacturing jobs by 2040 if the country builds its own battery cells, according to a study released on September 1, 2026, in New Delhi by the International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT) and IIM Bangalore, launched at the 4th edition of the annual India Clean Transportation Summit (ICTS) 2026.

The study, titled "Employment implications of vehicle electrification under alternative fuel efficiency pathways in India," was produced by ICCT and the TCI-IIMB Supply Chain Sustainability Lab. It models three electrification pathways through 2040, ranging from currently notified fuel efficiency regulations to near-complete electrification across vehicle segments. Under the most ambitious pathway, EV-related economic output is projected to rise from $12.8 billion in 2024 to $620 billion by 2040, with annual EV production reaching 32 million vehicles.

Why Battery Localization Determines India's EV Job Gains

The study identifies battery cells as the highest-value component of an electric vehicle and finds that domestic cell manufacturing is the largest determinant of how much economic value India captures from the transition. Localized battery manufacturing could add nearly 2.9 million direct jobs over a pathway built on imported cells, alongside more than 17 million further jobs across supply chains.

The analysis also weighs jobs created in EV manufacturing against those lost or transferred from conventional engine, transmission and fuel-system production. It finds this balance turns positive only once domestic battery manufacturing crosses 25%; below that threshold, the transition displaces more manufacturing jobs than it creates across all three pathways.

India's Current Battery Capacity vs 2032 Localization Targets

India's domestic battery cell manufacturing capacity currently stands at approximately 1.4 GWh, meeting under 3% of projected 2032 battery demand across all scenarios. If the full announced pipeline of about 128 GWh is commissioned — comprising 50 GWh targeted under the Production Linked Incentive Scheme for Advanced Chemistry Cell Battery Storage and roughly 78 GWh of other announced automotive projects — India would exceed 30% localization by 2032 under every pathway.

What ICCT and Industry Researchers Are Saying

"Under the most ambitious scenario, India's EV transition could support over 7 million direct jobs in EV and battery manufacturing and more than 17 million indirect jobs by 2040," said Megha Kumar, Senior Researcher at ICCT and study co-author. "Achieving at least 30% battery localization by 2032 and 50% by 2040 will be critical to realizing this opportunity."

Aditya Gupta, Chief Operating Officer of the Supply Chain Management Centre at TCI-IIMB Supply Chain Sustainability Lab, said, "India can turn the transition to electric mobility into a major employment and industrial opportunity, but the gains will depend critically on how quickly we build domestic capabilities, particularly in battery manufacturing. The challenge is therefore not simply to create EV jobs, but to ensure that the workforce transitioning from the ICE ecosystem has the skills and opportunities to participate in this new economy."

Government's Electric Bus and Truck Financing Push

Speaking at the summit's opening plenary, Dr Hanif Qureshi, Additional Secretary at the Ministry of Heavy Industries, said the government is working on a financing mechanism to support 50,000 electric buses and 50,000 electric trucks over the next five years, noting that trucks make up barely 3% of the fleet, account for over 40% of emissions, and remain below 0.1% electrified.

Inside the India Clean Transportation Summit 2026

Rajesh Verma, Chairperson of the Commission for Air Quality Management, said the shift to clean air represents an economic opportunity that runs through domestic manufacturing of vehicles and batteries, in line with the Atmanirbhar Bharat and Viksit Bharat 2047 initiatives.

Amit Bhatt, India Managing Director at ICCT, said the summit arrives at a time when India is focused on energy security and self-reliance, with clean transport central to that goal.

The ICTS 2026 summit is themed "Driving an Atmanirbhar Bharat Through Clean Transport: Strengthening Energy Security, Manufacturing, and Sustainable Mobility," and is supported by the Ministry of Heavy Industries, the Commission for Air Quality Management, the Embassy of Denmark, the Raahgiri Foundation, EPIC India, and the Kerala State Electricity Board.

The site was chosen to complement ongoing economic development in the area, including recent investments from other industrial players and new transmission infrastructure from Entergy.

ONE Nuclear CEO Richard Taylor said: “Project Cayman, with its 2.88GW power capacity, demonstrates that ONE Nuclear is committed to supporting the future economic development of one of Louisiana’s most important industrial regions.

“The project will deliver the reliable energy needed to support new investment, create jobs, expand the local tax base and generate additional funding for community priorities and critical infrastructure.”

The project aims to deliver energy storage, dispatchable generation and technology infrastructure to strengthen regional grid reliability, especially as the region faces a surge in new industrial and technology-driven electricity demand.

Community engagement activities have already begun, with a series of public information meetings planned involving local parishes, government agencies and other stakeholders. These sessions are scheduled to run from September through December 2026.

The company described the LOI as a key step towards developing “reliable, scalable and technology-ready energy infrastructure” to address increased power needs for industry and data-driven businesses in Louisiana and beyond.

Taylor said: “ONE Nuclear is proud to invest in the region to support the rapidly growing energy needs created by other recently announced developments such as the SpaceX Starbase project and Hyundai’s $5.8bn steel mill.”

In June 2026, ONE Nuclear signed a LOI with Sunshine Partners US to consider joint development of power projects across five sites totalling about 18,275 acres in West Texas.

This group of properties, referred to as the “West Texas Platform”, covers five counties within the ERCOT West market.

text:
DHADING, Nepal (AP) — Workers shoveled thick mud from a flood-ravaged power station in central Nepal this week, trying to restore electricity to more than 20,000 people.

The floods that swept through Nepal and China, killing hundreds and leaving thousands missing, have also overrun hydropower facilities, knocking out about 10% of Nepal’s power capacity.

Once the immediate aftermath of the disaster is dealt with, the question will be how to restore power plants, roads, bridges, schools and health facilities without exposing them to the same vulnerabilities, disaster experts said.

“Authorities have to take a hard look in the mirror now and ask how they will be rebuilding in these places. They will also have to take a close look at other projects in Nepal that have not been built yet, whether they’ll be approved after this event,” said Jakob Steiner, a geoscientist at the University of Graz in Austria, who is currently based in Dhaka, Bangladesh.

Rebuilding for resilience, not just replacement

Hydropower projects that were operating or under construction were fully or partly destroyed across Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading, among the worst-hit districts.

Hundreds of workers in Nepal are unaccounted for from a dozen hydropower projects, according to the Independent Power Producers’ Association, Nepal. Many had taken shelter in the tunnels but are stuck, waiting to be rescued, according to officials.

“The tunnels are built to access hydropower infrastructure and to divert water,” Steiner said, describing the tunnels as big enough for trucks to pass through.

Apart from the hydropower projects, tens of kilometers (miles) of roads, multiple bridges and essential buildings like schools and hospitals have been destroyed.

Ramraj Narasimhan, a senior director with the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure, said rebuilding should focus on continuity of services rather than trying to make every structure indestructible.

“If it gets damaged, let it get damaged, but can we build in redundancy in the system?” he said.

That can mean choosing a better location for construction, alternate routes, backup power, improved early warning and financial tools such as insurance to speed recovery, Narasimhan said. Risk assessments should examine where a river bends, where slopes are unstable and where a single failure could cut off several communities.

Narasimhan’s organization estimates that $124 billion worth of Nepal’s infrastructure is exposed to climate-driven disasters, creating the potential for hundreds of millions of dollars in losses each year. A report by the coalition earlier this year found that Nepal’s average annual losses are nearly $760 million from various disasters, while the country’s national disaster funds is only a fraction of this amount.

Climate risks grow for Himalayan hydropower

Climate scientists said the Himalayan region — which is warming faster than many other parts of the world — is particularly at risk from increasing global warming as a result of human-caused climate change.

Climate experts said the flooding adds to evidence that infrastructure planning in the Himalayas should account for disasters that are increasing as the climate warms. Glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya are losing ice at an accelerating rate, while permafrost degradation, unstable slopes, glacial lakes and increasingly erratic rainfall are raising the risks of floods, landslides and debris flows, according to reports by Kathmandu-based climate research group International Center for Integrated Mountain Development.

The stakes are particularly high for Nepal because hydropower is both a foundation of its electricity grid and an important source of economic growth and export revenue. Much of the country’s potential is run-of-river hydropower, Narasimhan said, meaning facilities are closely tied to steep river corridors where land is limited and hazards can cascade quickly.

Steiner said smaller floods can sometimes be managed with diversions that keep debris and high flows away from expensive infrastructure and tunnels. But for events as large as the latest flood, he said, physical defenses may be overwhelmed. In those cases, early warning becomes the critical protection for people.

He said the flood was detected at the China-Nepal border after moving rapidly from its source, leaving little warning time upstream. But there was still time as the flood traveled downstream toward hydropower sites, raising questions about whether warnings could have reached workers sooner.

The disaster is also likely to intensify scrutiny of where future projects are approved. Himanshu Thakkar, coordinator of the South Asia Network on Dams, Rivers and People, said environmental, social and disaster-risk assessments need to reflect the specific landscape and past hazards of each valley, backed by land-use rules and stronger accountability.

Hydropower projects can themselves become “force multipliers” when large structures, debris and altered river channels add to downstream damage, Thakkar said. He argued that Nepal should also consider more decentralized solar power as part of a broader energy mix.

Thakkar said the question now is not only how fast Nepal can rebuild, but what it chooses to put back in the path of the next flood.

text:
Australia is becoming a more sophisticated battery-mineral exporter. But even that middle step, refining, is proving hard and largely foreign-owned. The country has world-class chemistry, produces a third of the world’s raw lithium, and the allied trust to be the West’s preferred supplier. What it lacks is the cell-manufacturing capability where value compounds and vulnerability concentrates—and, on current form, the political durability to fund it consistently across a single electoral cycle, let alone two.

Share

Australia’s Approach

Australia’s formal position is set out in the National Battery Strategy, released 23 May 2024 by the Department of Industry, Science and Resources. It identifies four priorities: stationary energy storage; upgrading battery minerals into active materials; batteries for heavy transport and equipment; and enabling technology for grid-connected batteries. The Strategy was accompanied by funding announcement of A$523.2 million for the Battery Breakthrough Initiative (production-linked incentives administered by the Australian Renewable Energy Agency (ARENA)) and A$20.3 million for Building Future Battery Capabilities (research and skills, including the Future Battery Industries CRC). Both those sit within the A$22.7 billion Future Made in Australia package, alongside a A$1.7 billion Innovation Fund and a A$7 billion Critical Minerals Production Tax Incentive (a 10% credit on processing/refining costs, 2027–28 to 2039–40).

But federal strategy and actual deployed funding, alongside industrial execution, has been lacking. In the May 2026 federal Budget, the government clawed back roughly A$1.3 billion of uncommitted clean-energy manufacturing funding, cutting the Battery Breakthrough Initiative from A$523.2 million to A$142.32 million and closing it to new applications. In the six months leading up to that budget, only A$4.2 million had actually reached recipients—A$2.3 million to PowerPlus Energy and A$2 million to Firebird Metals—with a further batch of applications still under assessment on budget night.

While the funding outlay has picked up following the Budget cut—with a much larger outlay to Sicona—the result is a program that raised expectations at A$523 million, spent almost nothing for its first year, was cut by more than two-thirds, and only then made its largest single commitment. That is hardly the settled, predictable funding environment manufacturers need to commit capital.

Queensland’s Labor government committed A$570 million to a Battery Industry Strategy in February 2024, including Queensland’s proposed Australian Battery Industrialisation Centre (ABIC), which proposed a dual-state and federal-funded commercialisation and scaling centre. After the LNP’s Crisafulli government won office in October 2024, all A$570 was redirected to other initiatives and the Strategy was scrapped entirely. Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie cited “uncertainty around the 2022 federal government commitment” as the reason; the effect was to abandon genuine state commitments to an industry critical to energy security.

Internationally, Australia’s domestic battery industry being shaped by overseas markets has also had another recent trigger: the US Inflation Reduction Act’s Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) rules, which restrict which supply chains qualify for US clean-energy tax credits. That has forced Australia to reposition itself as a Free Trade Agreement-compliant, non-FEOC processing partner for Western battery supply chains, rather than simply a passive mineral exporter—the logic behind both the Critical Minerals Production Tax Incentive and the October 2025 US–Australia critical minerals framework.

What Australia is Actually Investing In

The emerging picture is of a country hosting the bottom of the value chain and dabbling at the top. Australia has long been successful in extraction—it is the world’s largest lithium miner—and is investing in deployment, where the Capacity Investment Scheme (CIS), the federal government’s underwriting scheme for renewable generation and battery storage, is now driving a 40 GW national pipeline of—mostly imported—grid-scale batteries. What it has not built is the controlling, compounding middle: refining, active materials, and cell manufacture.

The genuinely Australian cell/materials ventures are small and often offshore. Energy Renaissance runs a pilot line at Tomago producing up to 4 MWh/month; its long-promised 5.3 GWh scale-up is not yet realised. Li-S Energy runs a 2 MWh lithium-sulphur pilot in Geelong and won A$7.86 million from ARENA in November 2025 to study a possible 1 GWh plant.

Sicona is the partial exception to the offshoring pattern. In late June 2026 it secured a A$45 million ARENA grant—the Battery Breakthrough Initiative’s largest single award from the reduced post-Budget pot—to build what ARENA and Sicona both describe as its first commercial-scale silicon-carbon anode facility. The facility will be located at BlueScope’s Port Kembla precinct and produce up to 230 tonnes per annum for customer qualification and commercial sales. That is a genuine, funded, sited step toward sovereign capability.

But that deal sits alongside, not in place of, Sicona’s larger ambition: a 6,500 tonne-per-annum plant in the US southeast (scaling to 26,500 tpa) to supply IRA-compliant material, first announced in 2024 and still referenced in Sicona’s own materials as of mid-2026, though without confirmed financing or a selected site. The picture is a dual-track strategy rather than a full offshoring or a full “reshoring”—Australia has, for now, the smaller but more concrete project; the larger, higher-volume commercial plant remains aimed at the US market.

Novonix, by contrast, makes its synthetic graphite anode entirely in Tennessee, with no announced Australian production facility. The two largest “gigafactory” plays—Recharge Industries (Geelong) and Magnis Energy (iM3NY, New York)—have respectively stalled and gone bankrupt. Australia funds research and pilots while commercial-scale activity happens elsewhere, or not at all.

Global Batteries at Scale: China’s Monopoly Game

China’s manufacturing and processing monopoly has created a decisive weight between countries that own the capabilities and those that don’t. Mazzucato’s observations serve only to underline how dominant China’s position is—her core distinction is between value creation and value extraction:

Value creation means generating new productive capacity—skills, IP, compounding capability, the ability to set terms for others; while,

Value extraction means capturing returns from value created elsewhere, without contributing to the conditions that make it possible.

China’s pre-established manufacturing base and scale—especially the abundance of energy required—enables them to consistently price-out competitors at a global level.

The Physical/Hardware Stack

The vertical dominance of China affects every level of any competitors trying to break into the industry, but there are two specific observations.

First, China’s monopoly over cathode and anode material production renders them a level of influence over the battery industry that is, for the foreseeable future, completely cornered at national scale, especially for nations that are pushing for specific clean energy or carbon neutrality timelines.

Second, on the Australian front, the Kwinana failure is influenced by both high production and energy costs, as well as the resulting lack of a market; established market dominance by China shuts off short-term profitable ambitions. Unless the Australian government works to find measures around that, that situation will continue to flounder. Both Sicona and Novonix are finding greater funding support overseas, on the back of previous Australian attempts—Magnis and Recharge—going bankrupt. The Albanese government, while pushing for net zero emissions by 2050, is also playing into China’s hands on a more strategic and fundamental level.

The Broader Technology Stack

In the broader technology stack, Australia, despite having more access to the raw resources required at the supply chain’s base, is falling behind Europe on regulation and standard setting.

Australia has smaller points of research and intellectual properties that can be developed, but without the manufacturing know-how at scale, costs will require outside support to carry a genuine domestic industry. And unless Australia drives involvement on standards internationally, will find obstacles that could scrap plans entirely as the market then potentially rejects the Australian product even if the industry is supported domestically.

The Geopolitical Dimension

Using the Farrell and Newman’s ‘weaponised Interdependence’ framework, nodes in the global ecosystem—subordinate nations—are at an asymmetric disadvantage to entities that have greater leverage over chokepoints of economic, intelligence or legislative balance. For batteries it comes down to, as expected, the United States and China.

The chokepoints are obvious for China: nearly 85% of cell production capacity by value; ~90%+ of graphite processing; ~99% of LFP cathode material; and the manufacturing equipment. CATL and BYD alone made 55.6% of the world’s EV batteries in 2025. For the US, they are more regulatory. The Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) rules that we mentioned earlier have already shaped the thinking of Australian companies and have increasingly rolling out restrictions since 2022. The US regulatory reach chases further up the supply chain than the US restrictions on solar panels—which pushed Chinese solar manufacturers to move assembly to Southeast Asian nations—and look to reach into the mining and refining areas of the supply chain.

While a lock-in, the FEOC rules also present a continuing opportunity for Australia; China’s battery industry has switched responses to find ways around the rule, such as licensing or geographic relocation into areas the United States isn’t looking to lock down, like Morocco. This has meant that despite the FEOC rules being presented as an attempt to reshore battery production and Trump’s tariffs, China still supplies around 60 per cent of all US lithium-ion imports.

That in turn means that Australia still has an opportunity for leverage in the US market; Australia has the rare earth metal reserves, a framework for critical minerals with the US, expanding relationships with South Korea and Japan, and further opportunities for allied trust in Europe.

But many of those are centred around critical mineral processing; of clear value, and a clear priority, but not necessarily supporting Australian battery cell manufacture itself.

Broader Risks

There are numerous, and ongoing, risks that Australia will have to bear with in the wider battery ecosystem. We’ll focus on three of the primary ones here.

Chemistry shift. The rapid rise of LFP and emerging sodium-ion chemistries for stationary storage reduces reliance on nickel and cobalt—two of the minerals underpinning Australia’s critical-minerals strategy. If global stationary storage shifts decisively toward sodium-ion (which uses none of Australia’s lithium and little of its nickel/cobalt), a portion of Australia’s mineral leverage in this specific application is bypassed, even as lithium demand for EVs continues to grow elsewhere.

Policy instability at both levels of government. The Battery Breakthrough Initiative’s clawback and Queensland’s withdrawal from their Battery Industry Strategy are not isolated events; they compound. When a state government cites uncertainty about a federal commitment as its reason for pulling out, and the federal government simultaneously cuts its own manufacturing fund, the signal to investors weighing where to locate a plant is that policy support is not durable across an electoral cycle, in either direction. In Queensland’s case, it published its Strategy and cancelled it within the same year.

IRA and EU subsidy competition. Novonix, a Brisbane company, builds its synthetic-graphite anode entirely in Tennessee, backed by a US$103 million IRA 48C tax credit and a US$754.8 million DOE loan—a straightforward offshoring case. Sicona is more mixed: it has now funded and sited a smaller commercial-scale plant in Australia (Port Kembla, 230 t/yr) but its larger-volume ambition (6,500–26,500 t/yr) remains aimed at the US southeast to supply “IRA-compliant” materials, and that larger plant is where most of its eventual production capacity would sit if built. Even in Sicona’s case, then, the United States retains the pull on scale; Australia’s own incentives, recently cut, cannot yet match the certainty or size of US production credits.

Trajectory and Policy Options

On current settings, Australia remains the world’s quarry for battery minerals, funds a thin and commercially fragile refining layer (majority Chinese-owned at its only scale project), and lets its research base be commercialised in the United States and Asia.

Increase the local-content requirements in the Capacity Investment Scheme (Immediate). CIS already underwrites a 40 GW pipeline of grid-scale batteries and states its intention to support “Australian supply chains and Australian manufacturers.” Attach a binding minimum local-content requirement (domestic precursor materials, locally integrated BMS software, or Australian-processed minerals) to future CIS tenders, rather than leaving it as an aspiration.

Protect and commercialise the IP pipeline (Immediate/Near-Term). Tie any residual Battery Breakthrough / Innovation Fund money to commercialisation-with-domestic-manufacture conditions, so Australian-originated patents (Sicona, Li-S, Deakin) are less easily off-shored.

Introduce a genuine production tax credit for active materials and cells (Near-Term). Model on IRA §45X, rather than one-off capital grants—the evidence (Novonix, Sicona) is that firms follow real production incentives, not announcements or strategy documents.

Extend friend-shoring to the cell layer (Near- and Mid-Term). Use mineral supply and current stability window as the bargaining chip in the US, Korean and Japanese partnerships, to negotiate co-investment in CAM and cell manufacturing on Australian soil rather than just mining and processing.

Conclusion

China holds the chokepoints and has begun to squeeze them; the United States and European Union are out-bidding Australia for the firms it incubated. The choice is not between “battery superpower” and “quarry.” It is between deliberately specialising upstream and securing that position through alliances, or committing real, durable production incentives—proof against a change of government at either level—to a few defensible cell niches. Drift, whether in direction or funding, delivers neither.

text:
(TestMiles) – The electric Genesis flagship pairs a pillarless entrance and lounge-like cabin with 657 hp, but its biggest tests are still ahead.

Genesis spent its first decade proving that a Korean luxury brand could compete with familiar German and Japanese names. The 2028 GV90 begins a more difficult assignment. This time, the company is presenting its first full-size flagship SUV as an alternative to the grandest vehicles from Range Rover, Bentley and Rolls-Royce.

That intention becomes clear before anyone sits down. The GV90 Neolun uses rear-hinged coach doors and hides the center pillar inside the door structure, creating an uninterrupted opening when both doors are wide. The standard GV90 keeps conventional doors and a more familiar three-row layout. Both are electric, both sit above the GV80, and both are expected in the United States in early 2027.

It would be easy to treat the unusual doors as the entire story. They photograph beautifully, and the visual association with Rolls-Royce requires no explanation. Yet the more consequential idea is that Genesis has developed a flagship around Korean hospitality instead of reproducing a British club room or a German technology showroom. The result combines real wood, leather, stone and available wool cashmere with conveniences intended to change how occupants use a parked vehicle.

The specifications are substantial. Two motors provide a combined maximum of 657 horsepower and 590 pound-feet of torque. The 123.5-kilowatt-hour battery is the largest installed in a Hyundai Motor Group electric vehicle. Genesis estimates about 310 miles for the seven-seat version, although that figure comes from the company’s internal testing and is not an EPA rating.

For all the confirmed hardware, several buying questions remain unanswered. Genesis has not announced a U.S. price, EPA-certified range, cargo volume or towing capacity. No independent crash-test result or road test can yet establish whether the flagship drives, charges and operates as serenely as its presentation suggests. The GV90 has made a dramatic entrance. Its next job is to prove that the spectacle works in ordinary ownership.

Coach doors are the headline, not the whole story

Genesis calls the Neolun’s opening the Neolun Arch Gate. The rear door first moves slightly outward and then rotates toward the back of the vehicle, allowing it to operate without waiting for the front door. When both sides are open, there is no fixed pillar dividing the entrance. The arrangement should make access easier for second-row passengers, older family members and parents helping children into seats.

Eliminating a fixed center pillar creates engineering obligations as well as visual drama. Genesis says it replaced the usual structure with dual high-strength steel beams in the doors, reinforced the passenger compartment with integrated steel tubes and structural foam, and created a concealed roll cage. The company describes part of that frame as 1.5 times thicker than conventional construction. Those are manufacturer claims awaiting independent validation, but they show how much work was required to turn a concept-car gesture into production hardware.

Once parked, the Neolun can become a face-to-face room. Its front seats rotate 180 degrees at the press of a button, giving passengers a place to talk or work while the vehicle is stationary. The available four-seat Executive Suite adds folding tables, a refrigerator, privacy blinds and a partition between the second row and cargo area.

The cabin’s cultural reference is more interesting than its equipment count. A real-wood second-row floor uses radiant heat inspired by ondol, the traditional Korean practice of warming a room from below. A six-zone glass roof can vary its transparency, while radiant panels warm armrests, side panels and door trim. These choices turn warmth, calm and privacy into part of the design language rather than treating luxury as a list of screens.

Why Genesis is reaching above the usual luxury class

The standard GV90 and the Neolun serve related but different customers. A six- or seven-seat conventional-door model is the practical flagship for families who need three rows. Neolun supplies the theatrical entrance, more elaborate materials and a rear-passenger emphasis. The limited First Edition sits at the top with the most exclusive finishes and the full four-seat treatment.

That separation matters because shoppers will encounter images of the open coach doors and Executive Suite long before they see a price sheet. Not every GV90 will contain every headline feature. Genesis will need unusually clear trim explanations so that the showroom vehicle does not feel less special than the launch photography.

Range Rover Electric is the closest conceptual rival because it combines a full-size SUV body, electric propulsion and an established luxury identity. Rolls-Royce provides the obvious door comparison, although its electric Spectre is a coupe and the Cullinan SUV still uses an internal-combustion engine. Bentley and Mercedes-Maybach also compete for buyers who regard the passenger experience as seriously as performance.

Genesis enters that group without a century of inherited status. Its advantage is freedom from old expectations. The body takes inspiration from the clean volume of Korean moon jars, and the interior is organized around the brand’s idea of treating a customer as an honored guest. Its disadvantage is that ultra-luxury buyers expect the retailer, software, service and personalization process to feel as considered as the vehicle. A beautiful cabin cannot compensate for a difficult charging stop or an unresolved electronic fault.

An electric flagship with serious hardware

The two-motor system sends power to all four wheels through electronic limited-slip differentials at the front and rear, a first for Hyundai Motor Group. Genesis says the arrangement can reduce slip on wet, snowy or uneven surfaces and manage power during faster cornering. It sounds promising for a vehicle this large, although no one outside the development team has yet established its real-world behavior.

Rear-wheel steering can turn the back wheels by as much as five degrees. At parking speeds, that should reduce the space required for a U-turn and help the 208.1-inch SUV behave more like a smaller vehicle. At higher speeds, the same system is intended to improve stability. A multi-chamber air suspension changes ride height and spring stiffness, while electronically controlled dampers use separate responses for sharp impacts and larger body movements.

Quietness is another part of the flagship brief. Genesis says every window uses acoustic glass more than five millimeters thick, including the windshield, roof and tailgate glass. Soundproofing material fills cavities in the main structure, and additional absorbers and seals target noise entering through the body. Electric propulsion removes engine sound, but that can expose tire, wind and suspension noise that a combustion engine once masked.

The 123.5-kWh battery supports a claimed 10-to-80-percent charge in 22 minutes when connected to a compatible 350-kW DC fast charger. That is a laboratory-style best case, not a promise for every stop. Charger capability, battery temperature, starting charge, weather and the vehicle’s charging curve all affect the result.

The estimated 310-mile range is similarly provisional. It applies to the seven-seat GV90 under Genesis internal testing, not an official U.S. certification cycle. The EPA label will allow shoppers to compare versions on the same basis and will add efficiency information that a single range number cannot provide. A very large battery can produce a useful distance while still consuming more energy per mile than a lighter electric SUV.

Safety engineering carries unusual responsibility

The wildest feature is above the passengers. Genesis describes the GV90’s roof airbag as a production world first. During a severe rollover, it is designed to deploy beneath the panoramic glass, reduce contact with the roof and help prevent an occupant from being ejected through the opening. It is one of 12 airbags in the vehicle.

The concept has a history. Hyundai Mobis showed a panoramic-roof airbag in 2017 after identifying ejection through sunroofs as a rollover concern. Putting the idea into a production flagship is a meaningful step, but a manufacturer’s description is not the same as a crash-test result. The GV90’s unusual door construction makes independent side-impact, rollover and roof-strength evaluations especially valuable.

Genesis also says seat-mounted airbags can deploy at different depths according to occupant posture, cushion airbags are intended to limit submarining beneath a belt, and third-row curtain coverage has been extended. An in-cabin monitoring system evaluates occupant type, belt use and sitting position so the restraint system can respond accordingly.

Battery protection receives similar attention. Individual cells are separated to slow heat propagation, the pack is designed to shed heat, and a cloud-connected management system looks for abnormalities before they become emergencies. Structural measures are intended to direct major components underneath the vehicle during a frontal collision rather than into the battery. Again, these are engineering descriptions that need to be judged alongside regulatory compliance, recall history and independent testing.

The missing numbers will decide the verdict

The technology inside the GV90 extends beyond the safety system. A 23.6-inch OLED display rises by 90 millimeters when parked and becomes a 24.6-inch entertainment screen. The driver uses a 25-inch head-up display instead of a conventional instrument cluster. Pleos Connect is based on Android Automotive, while Gleo AI is intended to answer conversational requests.

Remote Smart Parking Assist 3 can handle selected parking maneuvers from outside the SUV. Memory Reversing Assist records a path and can retrace it backward, a potentially helpful feature when the vehicle has entered a narrow driveway or alley. A 25-speaker Bang & Olufsen system supports Dolby Atmos and can imitate the acoustics of Boston Symphony Hall or Wembley Stadium. Fifteen air cells in each massage seat complete a list that makes some private aircraft appear under-equipped.

What is missing is more important than another surprise. Buyers need U.S. pricing for all three expressions, final standard and optional equipment, EPA range, energy efficiency, charging performance in cold and hot weather, usable cargo dimensions, payload and towing figures. They also need to know how the four-seat partition affects luggage carrying and whether the huge Neolun doors are convenient in a tight garage.

Genesis deserves credit for avoiding a timid flagship. The GV90 is visually restrained but conceptually bold, and it gives Korean ideas of hospitality a physical form. It may suit a family seeking a serene three-row EV, an executive who works from the rear seat or an established luxury owner ready to consider a younger badge.

The final judgment cannot be made from an opening ceremony. Luxury at this level is measured in the quality of every routine interaction, from the first door movement to the third winter charging stop. Genesis has shown that it understands occasion. Pricing, road behavior, safety results and ownership support will reveal whether it has also mastered confidence.

name: Congress
title: The Next Front for Reigning in Regulatory Preemption
authors: Christopher R.J. Pace, Sidney A. Shapiro, Minhua Li, Joseph Haydt, The Regulatory Review
description:
The next logical step to limit the administrative state is shown by recent Supreme Court concurrences.
I first wrote about it roughly 20 years ago in Supremacy Clause Limitations on Federal Regulatory Preemption.
Restricting such preemption would force Congress to make the tough calls on when state law needs to be blocked, rather than punting such calls to more insulated federal agencies.
The change would allow states to oppose such preemption by lobbying one body—Congress—rather than trying to monitor and influence countless federal agencies.
What advocates need to do now is press, and preserve, this issue—both in tort cases raising preemption issues and in court and administrative actions challenging federal regulations.
text:
The next logical step to limit the administrative state is shown by recent Supreme Court concurrences.

At the end of its most recent term, the U.S. Supreme Court decided two cases that signal what likely will be the next line of attack to limit the federal administrative state. In Monsanto Co. v. Durnell the Court held that a federal statute preempted state-law failure-to-warn claims involving Roundup weedkiller. In Trump v. Slaughter, the Court overruled Humphrey’s Executor v. United States and held that a statutory provision requiring the President to have cause to fire Commissioners of the Federal Trade Commission is unconstitutional. Neither outcome should have come as a surprise to Court scholars.

Less expected, but of potentially great significance, were the concurring opinions in Monsanto and Slaughter. Both, in their own way, prompt lawyers to challenge existing Supreme Court precedent about the force and effect of federal regulations on conflicting or inconsistent state law.

Most direct was Justice Clarence Thomas’s Monsanto concurrence. He explained that federal preemption, under which federal law supersedes conflicting state laws, arises from the U.S. Constitution’s Supremacy Clause, which only covers “this Constitution,” “laws of the United States which shall be made in pursuance thereof,” and “treaties.” Federal regulations are clearly not the Constitution or a treaty. And they are hard to characterize as the “laws” referenced in the Supremacy Clause because the U.S. Congress did not create them through the bicameral process and subject only to categorical veto, not line-item editing, by the President. And if such regulations are not “laws of the United States,” they alone cannot preempt state law.

Less direct, but similarly bold, was Justice Neil Gorsuch’s Slaughter concurrence. He endorsed the rejection of Humphrey’s Executor but explained how a consequence of doing so is to increase the President’s control over administrative agencies that exercise sweeping authority to regulate financial markets, businesses, employment, and more. Justice Gorsuch acknowledged that allowing so much “power to accumulate in the President’s hands invites real risks.” As a result, he admitted, the “Court has some work to do” to fix the problem of a too powerful, and newly centralized, administrative state. That work includes “restoring legislative … powers to where they belong: in Congress,” not the executive branch.

The Court in recent years has already taken some action to rein in the administrative state, including by limiting deference to government agencies’ interpretation of federal statutes, as in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, and requiring Congress to be clear in its delegation of “extraordinary” power to agencies, as in West Virginia v. EPA. Justices Thomas and Gorsuch appear to envision the next step to be judicial confirmation that federal agencies cannot displace the authority of sovereign state governments and the role of independent state law without clear direction from the more politically accountable legislative branch.

This is not a new or novel concept. I first wrote about it roughly 20 years ago in Supremacy Clause Limitations on Federal Regulatory Preemption. Restricting such preemption would force Congress to make the tough calls on when state law needs to be blocked, rather than punting such calls to more insulated federal agencies. The change would allow states to oppose such preemption by lobbying one body—Congress—rather than trying to monitor and influence countless federal agencies. And this change would reduce the burden on courts trying to resolve disputes over when state-by-state legal flexibility and variability must give way to a need for national uniformity—as decided by Congress subject to presidential veto, not by unelected administrators.

The state of the law today, as reflected in decisions such as Watters v. Wachovia Bank, allows federal regulations to preempt state law even without unmistakable Congress endorsement. But I believe that Chief Justice John G. Roberts, Jr.—who dissented in Watters—and at least Justices Thomas, Samuel A. Alito, Jr., Gorsuch, and Brett Kavanaugh are willing to revise and reform that doctrine and largely eliminate such autonomous preemption. Justice Amy Coney Barrett may also be so willing, though her views on the issue are less clear.

What advocates need to do now is press, and preserve, this issue—both in tort cases raising preemption issues and in court and administrative actions challenging federal regulations. They may face short-term defeats, but they will be vindicated in the longer term­­—and succeed in further curbing overreach by the federal bureaucracy.

title: Analysis-Texas' halt on powering data centers reflects US reckoning over 'ghost' demand
description:

The latter refers to companies such as Amazon, Alphabet's Google and ‌Microsoft, which operate massive data center networks.
Chicago-based Exelon cut its tally of high-probability data center demand by about 40% to 11 gigawatts, it said in an investor presentation on July 30, after the company began imposing stricter collateral requirements.
Electricity requests from proposed data centers have already increased costs in PJM Interconnection, the nation's largest grid covering 13 states, including Data Center ‌Alley in Virginia.
