title: I Bet Scout Will End Up Selling A Fully Gas-Powered Audi Before It Ever Sells A Fully-Electric Truck
description:
Gas prices are high, and with renewed trouble in Iran, may stay high for a while.
There was a plan to lower fuel prices through “Freedom Fuel” stations, which is maybe a good idea, though it wasn’t clear how this lower-cost fuel was being subsidized.
Maybe I’m wrong, but I think we’ll see a fully gas-powered Scout or Scout derivative on the market in significant numbers before we see a fully-BEV version.
Well, That’s One Way To Lower Fuel Prices A new gas station network promoted by the Trump White House seemingly popped up out of nowhere, offering lower fuel prices than competitors.
Gas prices have been a bit of a sore point for the Trump administration given that it spent a lot of time blaming the previous tenants for higher gas prices, only to have the exact same thing happen.
text:
I think the VW ID.Buzz might end up being the poster child for everything wrong with Volkswagen’s thinking over the last few years. A true grey-space idea with a strong design and a lot of, well, buzz, that was doomed by poor execution, extensive delays, and a wrong-headed commitment to a single power source. Is Scout next?

The Morning Dump today is going to focus on the space in between a good idea and the final product, which is where Scout seems interminably stuck. There’s now a report out there indicating that Audi might end up building a fully gas-powered version on the same Scout platform, and maybe Porsche, all of which might delay an EV version.

Nissan is going the opposite way, having realized a little too late that it needs a hybrid and therefore rushing the Rogue Hybrid to market. If you want to buy one, be warned, they aren’t going to have a lot of them. Is that a better or worse strategy? Nissan and Honda were going to merge, but that didn’t happen, and now the two finally have found something to do together.

Gas prices are high, and with renewed trouble in Iran, may stay high for a while. There was a plan to lower fuel prices through “Freedom Fuel” stations, which is maybe a good idea, though it wasn’t clear how this lower-cost fuel was being subsidized. It sounds like one way this occurred was by not paying for the fuel. Genius!

Honestly, Maybe Just Never Build The BEV Scout

Here’s a crazy thought: Don’t build the fully-electric Scout. Maybe build it eventually, one day, when solid state batteries are a thing. Just don’t do it now. I don’t think that many people will buy it and Scout’s parent company, Volkswagen, has more important things to do.

If you haven’t been following the Scout saga, we’re coming up on five years of talking about the trucks without ever driving the trucks. I don’t even want to type out all the back-and-forth in paragraph form, so I’m just going to make a brief bullet-pointed list I can copy and paste into the future articles surely coming on this topic:

May 2022: Volkswagen announces it’s bringing back Scout as an EV truck brand.

October 2024: Volkswagen finally shows two vehicles, the Terra (a truck) and the Traveler (an SUV). They look incredible, honestly, and Scout confirms that they’ll offer both a BEV and a hybrid EREV. The company also says it will use a direct sales model.

January 2025: Scout’s CEO admits that more people were pre-ordering the EREV option than the pure-BEV model.

February 2025: It starts to dawn on people that these trucks wouldn’t be available until 2027 at the earliest (probably 2028), which they announced, but does bring up the question of how to maintain momentum.

October 2025: VW, the parent company, is running short on cash, so the pure BEV-model is reportedly going to be delayed.

November 2025: With tariffs in full swing, other VW Group companies start to wonder when they’re going to get a Scout, and if they can use the new Scout production facility. At the top of this list? Audi, which wants a Defender-fighter.

January 2026: This has been an issue from the start, but the lawsuits start ramping up as car dealers get super mad that VW is finally building a product they think they can sell and… not allowing them to sell it.

April 2026: VW CEO Oliver Blume tells Manager Magazin that the company is open to partnering on the Scout platform.

A lot of other things happened, so just take that as a quick gloss to catch you up with today’s news. As has been widely reported, VW of America is getting a new boss in the form of current Audi sales head Marco Schubert. An article about those changes from Automotive News contains this little tidbit about rumors of a pure combustion version:

A combustion engine version would potentially delay the Scout program further and raise questions about the economics of a vehicle program designed for a market undergoing a rapid powertrain transition.

Scout’s first models are currently expected to enter production at its new factory in Blythewood, South Carolina. The range-extender SUV is targeted for 2028, while the pickup could follow around 2030.

VW Group is investing roughly €3 billion in the plant. Using the facility for Audi vehicles as well could improve utilization and strengthen the business case for the investment.

Large Audi SUVs such as the Q7 and Q9 could potentially be built there, alongside Porsche derivatives including the Cayenne and a larger SUV expected to follow.

[Ed Note: Only one word comes to mind when I hear about the possibility of an ICE vehicle being built on the Scout’s platform: compromise. -DT].

When Scout was first considered, people were going insane for electric cars in theory, and automakers were rushing to get them to market. The reality has changed, so it does raise the question of whether or not the Scout brand makes sense at all. Will Americans embrace EREVs? Obviously, many of us here think it could be a good idea, but no one really knows.

Audi and Porsche are stuck because they don’t build any vehicles in the United States yet, at the same time, desperately need to be profitable in the US while somehow sidestepping tariffs. It’s a shitshow, and VW’s new Scout facility in South Carolina just makes sense. Also, almost no traditional OEM is making great margins on electric cars, whereas plenty of traditional OEMs are cashing them checks with large SUVs and trucks.

At this rate, what’s even the argument for making an all-electric truck? Lucid founder Peter Rawlinson, an expert in these things, has said it’s basically impossible to make a good, affordable, and profitable large EV truck given current technological constraints.

Having learned the hard lesson of constantly delaying a product in order to stick to a powertrain and concept with the ID.Buzz, perhaps VW can learn another lesson and just delay the BEV forever. Holistically, it’s better for the company as a whole for it to start building big Audi and Porsche SUVs in South Carolina than it probably is to make a pure-BEV Scout that’ll almost certainly lose money.

So, this is my bet. Maybe I’m wrong, but I think we’ll see a fully gas-powered Scout or Scout derivative on the market in significant numbers before we see a fully-BEV version.

Nissan Is Speeding Up The Rogue Hybrid Rollout

It’s rare that a company gets a car to market faster (see above), which makes Nissan’s move to rush the 2027 Nissan Rogue ePower hybrid all the more surprising. The company has been in a rough spot lately and lacks the resources of, say, a Toyota to make such a quick change.

At the same time, the Rogue is by far the most important product to Nissan and a hybrid option is sorely needed. How is it pulling this off? Again, from Automotive News:

The 2027 Rogue Hybrid, which Nissan initially will import from Japan, won’t transform the nameplate overnight. Each of the brand’s 1,050 U.S. dealerships will receive one or two in November. Supply is expected to increase to about 6,000 units by March as the hybrid lineup expands with two additional trims.

“If Nissan keeps the supply scarce, and the demand is strong, we’ll make money on them,” said Scott Smith, chairman of the Nissan National Dealer Advisory Board.

Localization of production will drive higher volumes and improved profitability. Assembly of the next-generation gasoline Rogue is scheduled to begin at Nissan’s plant in Smyrna, Tenn., in summer 2027. Domestic production of the hybrid is planned by early 2028 and could expand the plant to three shifts, from two today. Nissan also is evaluating whether to produce e-Power hybrid components at its engine plant in nearby Decherd, Tenn.

That explains it. These early hybrids are imported and, probably, not going to be as profitable as the locally-built versions. With Nissan losing market share to hybrids from most other competitive automakers (CR-V and RAV4, especially), maybe better to have something than nothing.

Nissan And Honda Will Develop A Software-Defined Vehicle Platform Together

Nissan and Honda nearly merged in 2024 before the whole thing blew up, though I’m feeling a little more hopeful about Nissan’s prospects with its new CEO (the old CEO is pictured above). Something was bound to come out of the companies buddying up and, now, we know what it is.

From a Nissan press release:

Nissan Motor Co., Ltd. and Honda Motor Co., Ltd. have entered into a joint development agreement to standardize multiple electronic control units (ECUs)* that form the core of next-generation software-defined vehicles (SDVs), along with the in-vehicle operating system and key parts of the middleware, and vehicle control software that run on these ECUs.

The E/E architecture incorporating the jointly developed ECUs and software is planned for application in both companies’ next-generation SDVs from fiscal year 2029 onward.

As part of their strategic partnership, Nissan and Honda continue to explore opportunities for collaboration across a range of areas to accelerate progress toward carbon neutrality and help realize a future with zero traffic fatalities involving their vehicles. In particular, the software domain centered on SDVs, which is key to vehicle intelligence and electrification, has been identified as an important area of collaboration, given the rapid pace of technological innovation and the need to strengthen competitiveness through improved R&D speed and investment efficiency.

Recognizing the need to strengthen competitiveness through faster development cycles and more efficient investment, the two companies have conducted extensive studies on potential collaboration in the software domain. As a result of these discussions, Nissan and Honda have agreed to jointly develop and standardize the core ECUs and software that underpin next-generation SDVs.

Cool. Or just merge, already.

Well, That’s One Way To Lower Fuel Prices

A new gas station network promoted by the Trump White House seemingly popped up out of nowhere, offering lower fuel prices than competitors. Gas prices have been a bit of a sore point for the Trump administration given that it spent a lot of time blaming the previous tenants for higher gas prices, only to have the exact same thing happen. Obviously, a seemingly never-ending conflict with Iran doesn’t help.

What no one could really answer is how the gas stations were offering cheaper prices. According to this report from The New York Times, there’s maybe a hint in a new lawsuit:

The lawsuit was filed by the Georgia-based Mansfield Energy against KRSM, a company based in New Jersey, and its president, Syed Kazmi. From May 21 to July 7, KRSM picked up 1.1 million gallons of fuel worth nearly $4 million from a fuel supply terminal in Pennsylvania, the suit claims.

Then, KRSM sold that fuel to gas stations that were part of the Freedom Fuel Network, which was able to sell gas at lower prices than its competitors did, the lawsuit claims.

“KRSM was able to sell such fuel for such low prices and garner such publicity because it never paid plaintiff for such fuel,” the lawsuit says.

For its part, KRSM says this is all just confusion, but has, according to the lawsuit, continued to not pay for the fuel it sold. If that ain’t a metaphor for life in 2026 I don’t know what is.

What I’m Listening To While Writing TMD

Andrew WK–yes, that bloody nose party hard guy–has quietly come out with an instrumental jazz record called Temptation To Exist. I am pleased to inform you that it’s very good. Here’s “Manhattan Beach,” one of the standouts from the album.

Remember when we relaunched our video player and it was kind of a disaster? Sorry about that. We’re going to try again today. Please let us know if something goes funky.

August 28, 2026 [Storage Terminals Magazine]- Blue Point One, a joint venture between CF Industries Holdings, Inc., JERA Co., Inc. (JERA) and Mitsui & Co., Ltd. (Mitsui), has broken ground on a new low-carbon ammonia production facility in Modeste, Louisiana.

The project represents a $3.7 billion investment by the three joint venture partners and is expected to produce approximately 1.4 million metric tons of ammonia annually when it begins operations in 2029. Upon completion, the facility is expected to rank among the world’s largest ammonia production plants.

CF Industries, which holds a 40 percent stake in the joint venture, is partnering with JERA, which owns 35 percent, and Mitsui, which holds the remaining 25 percent. The facility is being developed at CF Industries’ Blue Point Complex, which has additional space for potential future expansion.

The groundbreaking ceremony was attended by US Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins, US Deputy Secretary of Agriculture Stephen Vaden, Assistant Secretary of the Army for Civil Works Adam Telle, US Representative Julia Letlow, as well as Louisiana state and local government officials.

Large-scale low-carbon ammonia production

Blue Point One is being designed with an average annual production capacity of 1.4 million metric tonnes and is expected to use autothermal reforming (ATR) technology. The process produces hydrogen for combination with nitrogen in the ammonia manufacturing process.

The project is also designed to capture and permanently sequester approximately 98 percent of the carbon dioxide generated during production. According to the project partners, this is intended to give the facility a substantially lower environmental footprint than conventional large-scale ammonia production facilities.

Carbon dioxide generated at the plant is expected to be transported and permanently sequestered through a joint venture between 1PointFive, a subsidiary of Occidental, and Enbridge.

The facility is intended to serve both established agricultural markets and emerging applications for ammonia in the energy sector. The project is also expected to support domestic fertiliser supplies while creating additional capacity for US ammonia production and exports.

Investment and employment

In addition to the $3.7 billion investment by the Blue Point One partners, CF Industries plans to invest a further $550 million over four years in shared infrastructure at the site. The infrastructure is intended to support future expansion of ammonia production and fertiliser manufacturing capabilities.

Linde is investing more than $400 million in a new on-site air separation unit, which will supply the oxygen and nitrogen required by the Blue Point One facility.

The project is expected to create more than 100 permanent manufacturing positions once operational. During construction, an estimated 3,900 jobs are expected to be supported over a four-year period.

The development is also being positioned as an important investment in Louisiana’s industrial and manufacturing base, with local officials highlighting its potential contribution to employment and regional economic activity.

CF Industries President and Chief Executive Officer Chris Bohn said the project brings together US energy resources, engineering capabilities and international partnerships. He also pointed to the facility’s potential to strengthen domestic nitrogen supplies for American agriculture, expand export capacity and create employment in Louisiana.

Louisiana Economic Development Secretary Susan Bourgeois said the project builds on the state’s established industrial capabilities while supporting domestic fertiliser production and the manufacture and export of products considered important to the US economy and national security.

Strengthening the low-carbon ammonia supply chain

For JERA and Mitsui, the project represents an opportunity to establish infrastructure for a lower-carbon ammonia supply chain connecting the United States with international markets.

Irtiza Sayyed, JERA global energy solutions chief executive officer and JERA senior managing executive officer and chief operating officer of the Low Carbon Fuels Business, described the groundbreaking as an important milestone toward establishing a reliable low-carbon ammonia value chain. He said the project reflects the importance of partnerships and practical infrastructure in scaling lower-carbon energy solutions.

Mitsui President and Chief Executive Officer Kenichi Hori said the development would build on the company’s long-standing relationship with Louisiana while contributing to a low-carbon ammonia supply chain serving the United States, Japan and other markets.

The project also has significance for the surrounding communities. Ascension Parish president Clint Cointment highlighted CF Industries’ long-standing involvement in local community initiatives and said the new investment could create jobs, strengthen the regional economy and support the development of next-generation industrial activity.

Donaldsonville Mayor Leroy L. Sullivan likewise pointed to CF Industries’ nearly six decades of activity in the community, noting the potential for the Blue Point One investment to generate employment and broader economic benefits for Donaldsonville, Modeste and surrounding areas.

With construction now underway, Blue Point One is targeting commercial operations in 2029. If completed as planned, the facility will add significant low-carbon ammonia production capacity in the United States while linking agricultural, industrial and emerging energy markets to a new carbon management infrastructure network.

text:
Cooling from air conditioning saves lives — more than 5,000 a year in the United States alone — but it also heats up the planet and taxes our electrical grid, scientists say.

As the world warms, heat waves strike nearly every continent and United Nations officials estimate that about half a million people die a year from heat, air conditioning is needed and being used more than ever. A study in Nature Health reported Monday that air conditioning saved nearly 58,000 lives between 2010 and 2020 in the U.S. Air conditioning use is skyrocketing around the world, with electricity demand from cooling expected to triple, according to the International Energy Agency and the United Nations Environment Programme.

It’s also more of a problem than ever. Because most of the electricity for cooling comes from the burning of fossil fuels, the U.N. projects the amount of heat-trapping gas spewed into the atmosphere from air conditioning use to rise from 4.5 billion to 7.2 billion tons in the next 25 years or so. That 7.2 billion tons is almost as much as the carbon pollution from the United States and Europe now.

“Everyone knows air conditioning works, but air conditioning from a climate change perspective is not an ideal,” said Kai Chen, an epidemiology professor at the Yale School of Public Health who was the senior author on the new study. “It leads to more carbon emissions … then it accelerates the climate warming problem.”

Because of a global energy crunch triggered by the war in Iran, eight countries — Bangladesh, Cambodia, Jordan, Malaysia, the Philippines, the Seychelles, Singapore and Sri Lanka — have limited how cool air conditioning can be in offices or even mandated one day a week for public offices to switch it off, according to the IEA. In 2025 the Indian government proposed limits on how cool air conditioners can go.

Experts from 75 countries and 250 cities are trying to walk the tightrope of creating more cooling to reduce deaths from the rising heat, but without worsening climate change. The Global Cooling Pledge will meet in September in Singapore.

Air conditioning is rescuing more people on hotter days

One measurement experts use to tally accumulated heat as related to potential air conditioning use is something called “cooling degree days,” a calculation of how much energy is needed to cool buildings when it’s hot outside. The number of cooling degree days in the United States has increased by 28% since 1990, with 2024 setting a record, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. Through May, 2026 has been on pace to beat 2024 for the most cooling degree days, EIA data shows.

In Europe, the number of cooling degree days has more than doubled since 1990, and air conditioning use there has jumped up by 44%. Meanwhile, usage has tripled in India and more than doubled in Southeast Asia, the IEA reported.

In the new study, Chen and his team went through 30 million U.S. death records over an 11-year time span, used county-by-county calculations for levels when heat becomes dangerous and calculated how many lives air conditioning saved during extreme heat. The most lives saved were in Arizona, Florida, Texas, Louisiana and southern parts of Nevada, Alabama and Mississippi. More than a dozen northern states, from Washington to Maine, had fewer than 10 lives a year saved, according to the study.

Chen said the study concluded that “the essential role” of air conditioning saved on average 5,267 lives a year. But it also found that has to be balanced with “overuse.” He pointed to offices — like his — which are cooled so much that many workers wear sweaters even in the summer. More than half the cases researchers looked at could be considered overuse, he said.

Many places use 75 degrees (24 degrees Celsius) as a reasonable limit for air conditioning, Chen said.

He also said the study found that using more air conditioning than needed doesn’t save more lives, but it does worsen climate change.

Fairness, smog and urban waste heat

Air conditioning in cities adds extra warmth to the urban heat island effect, as anyone who walks by air conditioning units knows because that’s where waste heat is expelled outdoors, Chen said. And the added power use increases traditional soot and smog air pollution.

It’s also an issue of fairness since many of the world’s most vulnerable populations don’t have access to or can’t afford air conditioning, according to both Chen and U.N. officials.

Lily Riahi, head of the cooling buildings and energy unit at UNEP, said that in this year’s heat waves, “many families had to choose between paying for medicines or running their air conditioner.”

“In a warming world, thermal comfort should not be a luxury,” UNEP chief heat officer Eleni Myrivili said. “It’s becoming a prerequisite for health, dignity and increasingly survival.”

Solutions include using nature and AC

Riahi said the goal is not less cooling but rather “smarter and more equitable cooling,” and she pointed to Singapore as an example for effective solutions.

“Singapore is a country I think has really tackled cooling from a very comprehensive perspective, looking at individual adaptation measures, early warning systems, passive measures in the city in terms of urban greenery, which saves them, I think, $35 million in energy costs per year,” Riahi said. Officials there also require new and old buildings to have more efficient cooling and ventilation systems.

Singapore has lowered temperatures in some places by 14 degrees (8 degrees Celsius), Riahi said.

But sometimes it can get so hot and humid in places that even green solutions aren’t enough and air conditioning will be needed, Riahi said.

Until it’s too hot and humid, fans and a low level of air conditioning work, Chen said.

name: American Energy
title: Gary Dalton: Data centers should pay their way, and Wisconsin should set the pace
description:
Microsoft’s data center campus in Mount Pleasant sits on ground assembled for Foxconn.
Foxconn was subsidy-led: Wisconsin committed billions in refundable tax credits for the promise of jobs and additional investment.
This is the general story for data center investment in our state.
Data centers get blamed for Wisconsin’s electric rates, but our rates were already higher than most of our neighbors before a single data center broke ground.
The contracts should be written so Wisconsin is financially indifferent to whatever happens with the data centers.
text:
The column below reflects the views of the author, and these opinions are neither endorsed nor supported by WisOpinion.com.

Microsoft’s data center campus in Mount Pleasant sits on ground assembled for Foxconn. The two projects share the footprint yet differ. Foxconn was subsidy-led: Wisconsin committed billions in refundable tax credits for the promise of jobs and additional investment. The state’s $2.85 billion tax-credit commitment was scaled back to $80 million once it was clear those jobs were not coming. Microsoft purchased the footprint and deployed its own capital. Its own incentive package is modest by comparison, capped at $5 million a year. Its first building is already operational.

This is the general story for data center investment in our state. These companies have invested billions of dollars. Under the Very Large Customer (VLC) tariff, approved by the Public Service Commission (PSC) in April, they are also required to pay the full cost of the power infrastructure built to serve them. Transparency will confirm whether that holds. In a pending request, We Energies has proposed that data centers cover over 80 percent of the cost of generation and storage projects entering rates in 2027 and 2028.

Data centers get blamed for Wisconsin’s electric rates, but our rates were already higher than most of our neighbors before a single data center broke ground.

A regulated utility recovers its fixed costs, such as poles, wires, plants, and storm hardening, over the power it sells. Wisconsin’s electricity sales were essentially flat for two decades. Every dollar of improvement or repair landed on the same base of customers. The result was nine We Energies rate increases since 2013, with two more now proposed.

VLCs change the math. Those costs can now be spread over a larger and growing base of energy users. The alternative isn’t lower prices. Wisconsin already imports roughly 12 percent of its electricity and buys it on a regional market where capacity recently cost $424.30 per megawatt-day, up from $5 in 2021.

Consider. If Wisconsin is hostile to hyperscale load, the load goes elsewhere. With that hyperscaler goes the capital, grid modernization, tax base, negotiating leverage, and the larger base that would have spread cost. Instead, Wisconsin keeps the aging fleet, which it eventually pays to replace anyway, alone.

Transparency and enforceability make rules-based regulation and accounting work, and business should insist on both. The terms should be specific. Cost-allocation percentages that survive an audit. A commission-ordered rider adjusting a large customer’s bill when its actual draw stops matching the forecast. A minimum payment floor on plants built specifically for one customer, so a company’s disappointing result doesn’t become everyone else’s bill. A requirement that the largest customers cut back during the few dozen peak hours a year that drive costs. The contracts should be written so Wisconsin is financially indifferent to whatever happens with the data centers.

Will transparency and enforceability slow us down? Indiana approved a $3.3 billion gas plant conversion in eight and a half months, Louisiana 2,262 megawatts in about ten months, Georgia 1,400 megawatts in five and a half months, all inside Wisconsin’s own statutory clock. Accountability and speed are not a trade.

VLCs care most about speed to power. Wisconsin’s certificate authority over the transmission needed to serve new load therefore gives the Commission a lever over the pace of additional development. The Commission should use that authority intentionally, sequencing new certificates against capacity confirmed built or firmly scheduled. That governs certificates not yet filed. It is not a case against building fast.

Some runway between a load commitment and the generation built to serve it is useful. It’s what pulls new capacity forward. Overextend it, though, and the gap gets filled with more imports.

Treat the VLCs as partners and the larger opportunity is grid, skills, and clean firm capacity that outlast any single tenant.

Two PSC dockets are open for comment: 5-UR-112 through September 18, and 5-ES-113 through September 28. Docket 5-UR-112 is the We Energies rate case, where the cost-allocation terms actually get set. Docket 5-ES-113 is the PSC’s draft Strategic Energy Assessment. Businesses file in these dockets routinely.

Author’s disclosure: I own WEC Energy Group stock, about three percent of my holdings.

PowerFlex, a provider of intelligent energy management, EV charging, solar and storage systems, has acquired The Mobility House North America to bring together the company’s fleet charging and energy management capabilities.

The combined business will offer customers a broader suite of software, energy, and infrastructure solutions while advancing the companies’ plans to enable cleaner, more flexible electricity grids through intelligent charging and bidirectional energy technologies.

PowerFlex delivers charging solutions for large-scale commercial fleets, including last-mile delivery, municipal and utility fleets, while The Mobility House brings expertise in electrifying transit agencies and school bus fleets, as well as capabilities in bidirectional charging and vehicle-to-grid integration. The Mobility House launched a new vehicle-to-grid integration platform for utilities earlier this year.

The companies aim to expand the solutions available to customers across a wider range of fleet applications, integrate their software platforms over time to create a unified customer experience, and enhance product capabilities with expanded AI-driven features.

The Mobility House’s experience in bidirectional charging will help accelerate the development and deployment of vehicle-to-grid and vehicle-to-building capabilities, the companies said. Their customers will also gain access to PowerFlex’s project development and engineering capabilities, public charging features and integrated energy management platform.

PowerFlex’s experience in commercial solar and energy storage will offer new opportunities for heavy-duty fleet operators seeking to optimize energy costs and sustainability outcomes. The PowerFlex X energy management platform monitors, controls and co-optimizes onsite assets like EV chargers, solar, energy storage and microgrids, reducing overall energy costs through algorithms that maximize distributed energy resources.

As part of the share exchange transaction, The Mobility House will become a minority shareholder in the combined business.

“The Mobility House North America has built a genuinely differentiated platform in the fleet segment including vehicle-to-grid capability that is already operating in utility programs, and customer relationships earned over 10 years,” said Raphael Declercq, CEO of PowerFlex. “Paired with PowerFlex’s energy management platform and commercial scale, we can now serve the full spectrum of North American electrification needs from a single, integrated company.”

California Attorney General Rob Bonta and the California Energy Commission filed a lawsuit Friday against the Trump administration and the developer of Golden State Wind over the “buy back” agreement the two parties reached for an offshore wind lease off the state’s central coast.

Golden State Wind’s lease area in Morro Bay, OCS-P 0564, had an estimated 2 GW of installation capacity. The Canada Pension Funds Investment Board and Ocean Winds, a joint venture owned by Engie and EDP Renewables, submitted the $150.3 million winning bid for that lease. In April the developers reached an agreement with the Trump administration to receive $120 million in exchange for the lease being cancelled.

The Trump administration has made similar deals with several offshore wind developers, starting with a March deal with TotalEnergies, a French multinational energy and petroleum company. Under that deal, TotalEnergies agreed to “relinquish” two offshore wind leases off the coasts of North Carolina and New York with a combined capacity of 4.2 GW in exchange for $928 million.

“This ‘TotalEnergies model’ of buyout operates with the cynical logic of an extortion racket,” said California’s lawsuit filing. “The Trump administration first abuses its authority to make the offshore wind energy leases worth significantly less than what the developer paid at auction; then, offering the original bid amount in exchange for lease cancellation works as the proverbial unrefusable offer given these companies’ fiduciary responsibilities to their investors.”

The lawsuit also criticized the deals the Trump administration has struck with these developers for the lease proceeds to be reinvested into other forms of energy generation — for instance, TotalEnergies agreed to invest the $928 million into U.S. oil, natural gas, and liqueified natural gas production.

The administration also reached an agreement with Invenergy to cancel its 1.5-GW-capacity Morro Bay lease. The lawsuit said that in anticipation of the wind projects under development off its coast, California invested over $100 million to support them, “including creating a statewide offshore wind strategic plan and developing its ports and transmission facilities to support offshore wind.”

Keep up with the story. Subscribe to the Utility Dive free daily newsletter

“California expected that these investments would yield economic growth, new jobs, significant progress toward its clean energy and climate policy goals, and a powerful clean energy source to diversify its grid,” the lawsuit said. “[The Bureau of Ocean Energy Management] has proceeded with no regard for California’s significant reliance interests in Lease OCS-P 0564, including millions of dollars invested with the support of Congress, the Department of the Interior, and California voters to develop the State’s offshore wind industry.”

Several other parties have criticized the Trump administration’s method of buying back leases. In a June Sierra Club release, Senior Advisor Nancy Pyne called the agreements “shady backroom deals.” Liz Klein, former director of the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management, said in April that the deals are creating a concerning precedent.

text:
There’s a growing consensus that public EV charging may just turn out to be a profitable business after all, and operators are squarely focused on utilization rates. How do we design charging sites to maximize customer utilization?

EVSE manufacturer Kempower has released a new white paper that presents an analysis of real-world data from the company’s public EV charging sites in North America.

The white paper examines how charging site design can influence utilization, energy delivered and long-term site economics. Data from Kempower’s EV charging management software, ChargEye, indicates that the number of charging plugs has about three times more impact on site utilization than the total installed charging power.

The analysis also found that, on average, the charging sites using a distributed architecture achieved 83% higher utilization than sites that used fixed-power charging dispensers. Kempower’s distributed charging architecture dynamically shares available power between multiple charging points based on real-time vehicle demand.

“Public charging is increasingly becoming an infrastructure utilization challenge, not simply a power deployment challenge,” said Jed Routh, Vice President, Markets & Products North America. “Our ChargEye data shows that giving more vehicles access to charging and dynamically distributing available power can help operators get more from their charging infrastructure.”

text:
This article originally appeared on Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, non-partisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment. Sign up for their newsletter here.

PHILADELPHIA—A simmering debate over the future of Philadelphia’s Bellwether District has been reenergized by a Planning Commission presentation last month that identified the industrial zone as one of only two sites in the city capable of hosting a large data center.

Neither the commission nor the site’s owner, HRP Group, report any such proposals to date.

HRP acquired the 1,300-acre tract after a catastrophic 2019 fire forced the previous owner of a massive refinery on the site, once the oldest and largest on the East Coast, to stop operations and into bankruptcy. HRP then worked with the Environmental Protection Agency and the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) to remediate the portion of contamination it inherited responsibility for as it planned to transform the land for the Bellwether District.

The process continued an ongoing clean-up that Sunoco, a previous owner of the refinery, had been required to pursue since 2003, but is only set to remediate the site enough for nonresidential use. Far more remediation would have been necessary to make it suitable for parks or housing, as some advocates hoped. A ban on those environmentally sensitive uses was renewed during the sale to HRP, limiting its long-term versatility.

Thus far, HRP has landed two marquee tenants, a beverage manufacturer and a nuclear-medicine business, and built the first two of a dozen envisioned warehouses in what will become a massive industrial park. Critics worry about the potential for heavy truck traffic to a site that inundated nearby Black neighborhoods with refining pollution for more than a century.

In 2024, HRP announced that it had negotiated a $10 million community benefits commitment with grassroots groups, the week after the Philadelphia City Council unanimously approved a 10-year extension of potential tax breaks for tenants of the site under the state’s Keystone Opportunity Zone program.

HRP has not commented on the likelihood of a data center on the site. In December, Amelia Chasse Alcivar, HRP’s executive vice president of corporate affairs, told technical.ly that the developer wasn’t building data centers speculatively, before confirming a lessee’s demand, and won’t discuss specific tenants. Still, she said the firm was “certainly entertaining those conversations.”

Philadelphia’s I-3 zoning of the district allows for “intensive, high-impact uses,” and matches that of a far smaller data center in north Center City, the Planning Commission said. An April briefing revealed that Exelon presented a proposal to PJM, the regional grid operator, for a large new substation to distribute electricity for a hypothetical data center at Bellwether.

Bruce Bohri, a spokesperson for the Planning Commission, said that the agency identified the two compatible sites because they are over 40 acres, zoned for industrial use and vacant. “We in no way intended to advertise these sites to developers or the public,” he wrote.

Shawmar Pitts, managing co-director of Philly Thrive, an environmental justice coalition influential in the effort to end refining operations, said his organization was not confident that the Bellwether District will remain data center-free. “I’ve been around long enough to see what’s happening without the smoking gun,” he said.

Philly Thrive made waves when it didn’t sign HRP’s community benefits commitment. Pitts said the group wanted a more robust environmental clean-up of the site and a prohibition on harmful construction to be included.

“They did what corporations do. They just wanted to step right over us,” Pitts said. While Philly Thrive was part of a negotiating process parallel to that of the main Community Advisory Panel, the commitment was enacted without Philly Thrive’s endorsement.

Donna Henry, executive director of the Southwest Community Development Corporation, said that while she’d be very concerned about the impact of a data center on the property, she has not heard of a proposal through her membership on Bellwether’s Community Advisory Panel.

Both Henry and Marilyn Howarth, an occupational and environmental medicine physician at the University of Pennsylvania who has long studied the land’s contamination, said a data center proposal would attract massive public backlash. Howarth said Philadelphia’s strict air management regulations would be a significant obstacle for any data center.

These kinds of urban roadblocks, along with the cost of real estate, are part of why data centers are being built in more rural areas. On Aug. 18, Gov. Josh Shapiro signed an executive order enacting stricter guardrails for the development of data centers in Pennsylvania, shifting from his earlier support amid growing attention to the facilities’ impacts on water demand, energy prices and noise pollution.

Other Options for the Site

Data center or not, Michael Miller, a partner at Philadelphia-based urban planning and design firm OLIN and an author of a report describing an alternative vision for the property, stressed the importance of the land within the city’s urban fabric.

“Will it be integrated with the city? Will there be public access? […] Are we just investing in a lot of road infrastructure for trucks serving distribution centers?” Miller said. He voiced the need for versatility in long-term planning and cautioned against the creation of single-use districts.

In a statement provided for this article, Alcivar highlighted the LEED status of recent construction in the Bellwether District, as well as its solar-ready roofs, EV-equipped infrastructure and plans to plant 10,000 new trees on the grounds. She said the campus would be elevated above the 100-year floodplain and have sustainable stormwater management, as well as improved connection to nearby public space and green transportation modes.

Miller, as well as environmental engineering professors Mira Olson of Drexel University and Peter DeCarlo of Johns Hopkins University, who worked on the city’s Refinery Advisory Group while at Drexel, all said the site was complicated in ways that made a stronger clean-up process harder, both financially and legally.

Pennsylvania Act 2, known formally as the “Land Recycling Program,” was designed in part to allow polluters and landowners to take on long, often-complicated and always-expensive environmental remediation work on private property to relieve liability. The program, administered by DEP, will govern the clean-up of the refinery site to nonresidential standards and even looser, site-specific direct-contact standards for lead in the soil.

“The Act 2 process allows for the DEP and the EPA and the city to get together and decide, ‘Well, which of the environmental regulations should we be using? Should we be loosening them?’” said Howarth, the Penn physician. “I think that is not serving the interests of Philadelphians well.”

Robyn Briggs, a spokesperson for DEP, said Act 2 allows remediation to be funded by “capable parties,” like owner HRP and former owner and polluter Sunoco, instead of taxpayers. “DEP thoroughly reviews all Act 2 submissions, including cleanup plans for proposed remedies, to ensure site remediation will be protective of human health and the environment, consistent with regulatory requirements,” she wrote in a statement.

Many who had long pushed for a change at the site are glad that HRP’s plans are bringing an end to refining operations, especially given the financially superior bid of a company hoping to relaunch refining that emerged during bankruptcy proceedings. The acquisition by a nonrefining developer “inherently improved the surrounding environment on the day of acquisition,” said Alcivar. The refinery once produced 16 percent of Philadelphia’s carbon footprint.

But others saw such a momentous transition away from refining as an opportunity to pursue an even bolder future, like building a park, housing or new mixed-use areas. The fact that new owners, plans and environmental remediation will only equip the land for nonresidential use is a disappointment to Miller, Howarth, DeCarlo, Pitts and others.

“I would have liked to have seen it at least remediated to a better level than was required for zoned industrial use,” DeCarlo said. Pitts emphasized Philly Thrive’s push for a more robust clean-up and the report that Miller worked on advocated for a lot of recreational access.

After 130 years of damaging production, however, doing so would take an enormous amount of resources, and the land’s future was being decided largely through its sale in bankruptcy court, where attention to anything but efficiency is limited.

Furthermore, a 2012 deed restriction enacted by Sunoco, with DEP’s approval, mandated that the property only be used for energy and chemical production while prohibiting more sensitive construction like schools, homes and parks. Therefore, there was little short-term justification for DEP to require a clean-up adequate for those uses. ”The Act 2 cleanup standard, residential or nonresidential, must align with the planned and actual land use,” Briggs wrote, citing the deed restriction.

But the energy and chemical production requirement was lifted in 2020 to make way for the sale to HRP and its non-refining vision. The ban on more environmentally sensitive uses, however, remained in a new consent order and agreement.

Howarth therefore sees the agreement as unfair to the city and its residents: “It was a terrible injustice to the people of Philadelphia that an agreement was made without their knowledge and consideration and input to give up 1,300 acres in the middle of Philadelphia,” she said, highlighting the region’s struggle for housing and green space.

A Tension Point

Activists and experts have long called into question HRP and Sunoco’s plans to address lead in the soil. Without fully removing the contaminant from the soil or all contaminated soil from the site, HRP plans largely to cap dirty soil with asphalt, which DEP anticipates will be a permissible remedy, while disposing of some soil offsite.

Olson, the engineering professor, and Miller, the urban planner, both said that capping contaminated soil can be an acceptable remediation approach for industrial use, given the expense and risks of removal. Still, it raises some concerns. “There are always cracks where water can get in, and then mobilize the pollutants to travel offsite or to other points of exposure,” said Olson.

Any areas not capped, however, will be remediated by Sunoco to a site-specific direct-contact standard of 2,240 parts per million, far higher than even the nonresidential use statewide health standard of 1,000 ppm. DEP felt the value “was protective of human health for nonresidential land use” on the site.

Russell Zerbo, an advocate with Philadelphia-based Clean Air Council, disagreed, as did Olson and Howarth. “In fact, the science on lead safety is going in the other direction,” Howarth said.

“The science says that there’s no safe amount of lead,” added Zerbo.

Sunoco’s affiliate in charge of remediation did not respond to a request for comment for this article.

The Time for Cleanup “Would Be Now”

Some experts and community leaders spoke about the Bellwether District as a happy, potentially temporary, compromise between oil refining and more utopian visions: It identified a company willing to finalize the clean-up of the land so that it could then reap the profits of developing it. If things changed many years from now, experts said it would still be possible to clean the land up to a higher environmental standard.

But generating the money and will would be harder in the future than in 2019, when the future of the site was up in the air and responsible parties were easy to identify. “If the city ever hopes that this may be anything other than industrial, the time to require it to be cleaned up would be now,” Howarth said. She blames the standards of Sunoco’s ongoing Act 2 clean-up and the lack of democratic input on the deed restriction for limiting the long-term versatility of the land.

“Everybody had great ideas for the land after the fire. They fell on deaf ears when the DEP and the EPA were the ones under Act 2 deciding what the clean-up level would be,” Howarth said. “Once that decision to clean up only to an industrial standard was made, all of those other options were off the table.”

text:
September begins a budget push in Congress

September looks busy for Congress, which faces a looming budget deadline. The House of Representatives returns today, while the Senate will remain in recess until Sept. 14. Unless Congress takes action, most federal funding will run out on Sept. 30 when the fiscal year ends. That leaves few days in the legislative calendar ahead of that deadline, with midterm election campaigning beckoning.

In August, the Senate passed a stopgap budget bill extending government funding into December. However, it came with riders unlike the House’s earlier-passed “clean” funding bill, which those lawmakers must now decide whether to accept. The House has so far passed only three of its full appropriations bills for next year’s budget, while the Senate hasn’t passed any.

House hearings will resume this week, including ones on advanced nuclear reactors and patent fees. The Energy and Commerce Committee will meet Tuesday to consider several AI- and quantum-related bills as well as an update to satellite and spectrum licensing rules. However, the key science policy fight will be over the provision in the Senate stopgap funding bill that temporarily blocks a proposed Office of Management and Budget rule on federal grantmaking. The proposed rule has sparked concern not only because it would give political appointees final say over grants, but also power to terminate active ones at will. Some parts of the rule drew opposition from Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins (R-ME), and more recently among Republicans in the House, such as Rep. Nick LaLota (R-NY), who reportedly circulated an August letter to OMB calling for the rule’s withdrawal. Democrats have widely opposed the rule.

Science agencies, national labs, among targets of Chinese hacking group

The Department of Justice announced last week that it had taken steps to dismantle a Chinese state-sponsored hacking group that targeted multiple federal agencies, including NASA, the Department of Energy, the National Institutes of Health, and three unnamed national labs. Federal authorities seized domains supporting two of the group’s hacking platforms on Aug. 26, making them inoperable.

According to court documents, the hacking group, known as QTFY, attempted to gain access to NASA networks in 2019 using a virtual private network vulnerability but was unsuccessful. It is unclear how many of the group’s other hacking attempts were successful, though the three national labs are among entities described as “victims” of the group. FYI has reached out to DOE for comment.

“Today’s announcement demonstrates the Justice Department’s steadfast commitment to going on the offensive against cyber threats to the national security,” Assistant Attorney General for National Security John Eisenberg said in a press release. “These court-authorized seizures deny PRC-linked hackers access to tools they use to mount online attacks against our nation’s critical infrastructure.”

NSF announces $290M in quantum research alongside new Treasury readiness initiative

Last week, the federal government announced new efforts to advance quantum research and prepare for the technology’s potential security risks. The National Science Foundation is committing $290 million to support eight Quantum Leap Challenge Institutes, which will focus on quantum sensing, communications, and computing.

That funding establishes three new research centers and extends five existing ones, bringing together 36 universities and federal laboratories with more than 30 corporate partners. They will work over the next five years on technical challenges that include fault tolerance and quantum error correction, while developing the field’s next generation of scientific talent.

Also last week, the Treasury Department announced a new Quantum-Readiness Task Force, a public-private collaboration designed to help financial organizations and government agencies transition toward post-quantum cryptographic standards. The department said the task force will help deliver the goals of an executive order focused on quantum cryptography that President Trump signed earlier this summer.

Quantum information science is identified as a priority in the White House’s recently published National Security Science and Technology Strategy, which says the field is important to maintaining US economic and technological leadership.

title: NEVI Funds and Flying Cars: Florida's EV Charging Plan Under Fire
description:
NEVI Program Background The National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure Program (NEVI) was a $5 billion allocation within the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law to spur private investment in public electric vehicle infrastructure along the nation’s highway system.
After FWHA resumed the NEVI program, Congress stepped in during its budget process and rescinded some of the states’ NEVI funds that had not yet been spent.
Florida Department of Transportation New Secret NEVI Plan On July 29, the Miami Herald published an updated Florida NEVI plan, obtained through a Freedom of Information Act request, that had not previously been known.
SACE does not support FDOT’s proposed plan to use NEVI funds for eVTOL charging and calls on FHWA to deny the state’s request.
NEVI funds are clearly intended for one thing: charging electric cars and trucks that drive on roads.
text:
NEVI Program Background

The National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure Program (NEVI) was a $5 billion allocation within the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law to spur private investment in public electric vehicle infrastructure along the nation’s highway system. Funding was distributed to states based on population size. Florida was allocated $198 million.

In February 2025, the program was unlawfully frozen by the Trump administration. A lawsuit brought by 17 States and several non-profit organizations, including SACE, resulted in a complete victory for the plaintiffs. In August 2025, the court required the US Department of Transportation’s Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) to resume funding and ensure that States can move forward with building NEVI-funded charging infrastructure.

After FWHA resumed the NEVI program, Congress stepped in during its budget process and rescinded some of the states’ NEVI funds that had not yet been spent. Florida, which hadn’t spent any of its money, lost $44.6 million due to the rescission, reducing the amount of NEVI funds the state now has to put toward charging infrastructure to $153.4 million.

NEVI Updated Program Guidance

As part of NEVI program requirements, each State’s Department of Transportation is required to submit an annual plan to the Federal Highway Administration for approval. Florida has been publishing publicly accessible annual plans as recently as January 2025, but has yet to spend any of its NEVI funds.

Following the federal court order that unfroze NEVI funds, the FHWA released new NEVI guidance that, among other things, gave states more flexibility in building out their fast-charging networks. FHWA directed states to submit updated NEVI plans that aligned with the new guidelines. Florida never did, or so we thought.

Florida Department of Transportation New Secret NEVI Plan

On July 29, the Miami Herald published an updated Florida NEVI plan, obtained through a Freedom of Information Act request, that had not previously been known. The updated plan reallocates the State’s now $153.4 million in NEVI funds from building charging infrastructure for on-road EVs to building charging infrastructure for electric vertical take–off and landing (eVTOL) aircraft. Imagine a giant, passenger-carrying drone that acts like a flying taxi; that’s an eVTOL.

According to the September 2025 plan, State officials said the private market has already done enough to build EV charging stations across the state and declared that “FDOT will not waste taxpayer dollars and spend it on everyday passenger vehicles. Instead, FDOT’s proposal… takes an innovative and strategic approach to offer the greatest benefits to Floridians by supporting a new emerging mode of transportation.” That new emerging mode of transportation is flying cars.

Electrify On-Road Transportation And Use Program Dollars As Designated

To be clear, SACE supports clean energy innovation and the electrification of all forms of transportation, including aviation. But the intent of NEVI funding is clear, as articulated on FWHA’s website: to provide funding to States to strategically deploy EV charging infrastructure and to establish an interconnected network to facilitate data collection, access, and reliability.

SACE does not support Florida’s new NEVI plan because it veers sharply from what the NEVI program was designed to do: to increase charging infrastructure for on-road electric vehicles. An eVTOL is classified as an aircraft, not a motor vehicle. The NEVI standards and requirements, as laid out in law, clearly define what EVs and EV charging stations are. Nowhere do the standards and requirements mention infrastructure for flying cars.

Additionally, SACE takes issue with the Florida Department of Transportation’s claim that the shift from EV charging infrastructure to eVTOL is justified because the charging needs of Florida residents and businesses have been met; we don’t believe they have.

Florida’s Charging Needs Are Unmet

Florida touts the nation’s second-highest adoption rate for EVs with over 618,000 in cumulative sales. This past quarter, EVs in Florida reached 9.4% market share, meaning nearly 1 in every 10 cars sold in Florida is electric, well above the national average of 7.4%. Conversely, the state ranks 16th in the nation per capita in access to charging infrastructure. That lopsided equation makes it a burden for some EV drivers and fleet operators to access available chargers.

FHWA’s updated NEVI guidance allows states to use the funds to tackle a host of EV charging challenges. So even if, as FDOT claims and FWHA accepts, the state’s highways are fully built out with fast charging for passenger cars, there is more work to be done.

For instance, roughly one-third of Floridians live in multi-unit housing (MUD), where many are renters and most lack access to home charging. This is a problem because 80% of EV charging happens at home, where residential electricity rates are cheaper, and plugging in is easy. Hence, the inability to access home charging undercuts EVs’ affordability and convenience.

EV drivers who can’t charge at home rely on public fast charging, which can cost up to 6 times as much as paying for electricity at residential rates and adds hassle to owning an EV rather than ease. The private sector is struggling to meet the MUD charging need, which is limiting Floridians’ access to more affordable transportation. NEVI funds could help solve this problem.

Additionally, Florida has the second-highest adoption rate of medium- and heavy-duty vehicles, such as delivery vans, box trucks, and tractor-trailers, in the country. Electric versions of these vehicles typically require higher-capacity charging stations and need greater spacing at charging sites to accommodate the larger vehicles and trailers.

Florida is woefully lacking in fast-charging sites that can accommodate medium- and heavy-duty vehicles along its major freight corridors, creating a roadblock for Florida businesses that want to electrify their fleets and save money. NEVI funds could also help solve this problem.

Public Funding Should Benefit the Public

Florida’s “secret NEVI plan” not only calls for using funds to charge flying cars but also for installing the charging infrastructure at places like private airports, golf courses, and condominium rooftops, which are clearly not places the public can access. But then flying cars aren’t something the public can afford, either.

SACE does not support FDOT’s proposed plan to use NEVI funds for eVTOL charging and calls on FHWA to deny the state’s request. NEVI funds are clearly intended for one thing: charging electric cars and trucks that drive on roads.

text:
Canada has released what is essentially the final update before the first import window for Chinese-built electric vehicles (EVs) closes, and despite another increase in August, thousands of available quota spots are set to go unused.

According to the latest Global Affairs Canada report, updated August 28, 15,603 of the available 24,500-vehicle quota has now been utilized, leaving 8,897 spots remaining. That means about 64% of the quota has been used with the first six-month window ending August 31.

The previous update, released August 21, showed 15,063 vehicles imported, meaning the total increased by just 540 vehicles over the past week.

All of those additional vehicles were recorded in August, bringing the month’s total from 4,950 to 5,490 vehicles. That puts August within striking distance of July, which remains the busiest month of the first window with 5,982 imports.

Imports Ramp Up in Final Months

It is interesting to note how the program has ramped up since it launched in March. The first two months saw zero imports, which is understandable as it would take time for automakers like Tesla to reorganize supply and logistics to export from China again after a two-year hiatus. The month of May saw the first surge, while things quietened down again in June.

However, July and August have seen even larger surges. Had imports reached similar levels in previous months, the first import-quota window would have been fully utilized.

Nearly 9,000 spots will carry over

But since that didn’t happen, there is virtually no chance the full quota will be utilized with only days remaining in the first window. There would need to be another 8,897 vehicles imported in just 3 days to reach the 24,500 limit.

Those unused spots won’t disappear, however. They will carry over into the second six-month import period beginning September 1, potentially providing considerably more capacity as additional automakers prepare to bring Chinese-built vehicles to Canada.

Based on the August 28 utilization figure of 15,603 vehicles, as many as 33,397 spots could therefore be available on September 1 if no additional imports are recorded before the first window closes.

Second import window could look very different

The second six-month window could end up looking considerably different from the first. Until now, Tesla has likely accounted for the overwhelming majority of imports under the quota. Lotus has imported the Eletre, and Lincoln the Nautilus Hybrid, but those have only amounted to a few hundred vehicles.

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – In case you missed it, the Washington Examiner recently reported that Congressman Brett Guthrie (KY-02), Chairman of the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, announced that the Committee will examine legislation to ensure communities are not being charged for the water used by data centers.

In Case You Missed It:

“The House Committee on Energy and Commerce will weigh in on legislation to address water use by data centers as public backlash against artificial intelligence facilities grows.

“The committee plans to hold a hearing on Thursday, Sept. 3, to discuss a draft of the Water Cost Accountability Act, which is aimed at ensuring communities do not bear costs from data center water consumption or infrastructure, a committee spokesperson told the Washington Examiner.

“While data centers consume a fraction of the water of many other industries and have proven that new technologies are actually reducing new water consumption, nonetheless, Americans should have confidence that data center developers are acting responsibly with local water supplies,” Chairman Brett Guthrie (R-KY) said in a statement.

“The Water Cost Accountability Act is an important step toward safeguarding our nation’s drinking water and determining whether there are new costs associated with additional water demand,” Guthrie added.

“The draft bill would allow states receiving grants from State Revolving Loan Funds to prohibit public water systems from charging customers additional costs for data centers connecting to the public water system or for expanding their infrastructure. Those costs would instead have to be recovered from the data center’s owner or operator.

“It would also require the Environmental Protection Agency to provide a report to Congress on the sources of water used by “qualified data centers,” which are defined as data centers whose intake exceeds 200,000 gallons per day on average.

“Members of the public have increasingly expressed concern about the strain data centers place on local resources such as water and electricity. In April, a Gallup poll found that 50% of people opposed to data center construction cited the impact on resources, including water, energy, farmland, and forests.

“Data centers consume water directly for cooling their computer servers and indirectly for electric power. The amount of water used by a data center depends on several factors, including the facility size, cooling technology, local climate, and data center type.

“U.S. data centers in 2014 directly consumed 21 billion liters of water. By 2023, total water use had grown to 66 billion liters, according to a 2024 Berkeley Lab report. The report found that hyperscale data centers are expected to consume between 60 billion and 124 billion liters of water by 2028.

“The data center water bill is similar to the bipartisan Ratepayer Protection Act, which was unanimously voted out of committee in July and aims to ensure that households do not bear the cost of energy consumed by data centers.”

text:
Although it’s part of an industry famous for changing slowly, New Mexico’s largest utility has moved quickly to update its electricity supply to cleaner alternatives.

The Public Service Company of New Mexico, or PNM, said it delivered 80% carbon-free electricity in 2025 after investing in solar energy, batteries, and wind. During the daytime, the sun powers fans, air conditioners, and more across the state. In the evening, solar energy stored in batteries keeps the lights on, while the wind turns turbines that meet other electricity needs. (For details, see part one of this story.)

This remarkable transformation to a climate-friendly system has unfolded in just five years. As recently as 2021, power plants fueled by climate-warming coal and gas generated nearly 80% of PNM’s total electricity.

“We know it’s the right thing,” said Laurie Williams, PNM’s senior vice president of integrated planning and transmission development.

‍

An ambitious policy

Much of this progress stems from a state law passed in 2019 called the Energy Transition Act. It contains a series of renewable energy mandates, beginning with a statewide standard of 50% renewable energy by 2030.

Investor-owned utilities like PMN must generate 80% of their electricity from renewable sources by 2040 and achieve 100% zero-carbon electricity by 2045.

PNM is ahead of schedule. The company said that it will meet the zero-carbon requirement by 2040, five years before the deadline.

Williams explained that the transformation of the company’s energy supply is not solely motivated by complying with state laws.

“I would say it’s been more driven by the culture,” she said.

Over her 34 years with the company, “We’ve understood more and more about climate and the impacts on climate of traditional fossil fuels,” she said. “We’ve got to be part of solving the problem,” she added. “So I think there’s been a shift in mindset.”

PNM formerly owned the majority of a large coal power plant called the San Juan Generating Station. This plant closed in 2022, and PNM opted to replace all of its capacity from the coal power plant with renewables.

‍

‘A chance to diversify the economy here’

The Energy Transition Act sets aside money to help workers who lost their jobs due to the closure of the coal plant and nearby coal mine as well as for the development of new renewable energy in the same county as the former coal plant.

Advocates criticized the program for a three-year delay in distributing the money, but funding did get allocated and spent. The state government reported that 2,800 workers have been retrained so far, well above the target of 2,000 workers.

“There’s not a lot of opportunity in New Mexico. It’s an area that, you know, we struggle,” Williams said.

She pointed out that the state’s economy is largely dependent on oil and gas. But New Mexico’s vast renewable energy resources offer new pathways to prosperity.

“It feels like there is a chance to diversify the economy here in a way that could be really meaningful for the citizens and for the future of the state,” she said.

Many Native Americans worked at the San Juan coal plant and mine. The Energy Transition Act established a fund specifically to help Native American communities with the energy transition. Every tribe that lives near a fossil fuel power plant that closes gets automatic membership on a committee that helps decide how and where funds should be allocated.

Money has been spent on sustainable agriculture, food sovereignty, irrigation, new solar projects, worker retraining, and direct payments to displaced workers.

‍

Small-scale solar

Utilities aren’t the only ones on a building spree. Small-scale solar installations in New Mexico more than doubled from 2020 through 2025, and PMN reports that over 13,000 of its customers have solar panels.

Those who can’t or don’t want to put solar panels on their homes can purchase small shares of large solar farms. Sixteen community solar projects operate in the state, and 31 more are planned for a total of 200 megawatts of shared solar power coming online.

The Biden-era Inflation Reduction Act granted New Mexico $156 million to help build solar power for low-income communities, but the Trump administration clawed the money back.

‍

Not just clean, but also cheap

As New Mexico’s grid gets cleaner, the state is also avoiding the price hikes that have become common around the country.

Nationwide, residential electricity prices have spiked by 32% in the last five years (May 2021 through May 2026). In New Mexico, prices have increased by just 7% during that same time frame.

The state’s electricity prices remain below average, with residential electricity at $0.14 per kilowatt-hour in May 2026 compared to the national average of $0.18 per kWh, and household electricity bills in New Mexico are among the lowest in the country.

‍

One last piece of the puzzle: interconnection

When more renewables are added to a grid, more pieces need to be connected. In many locations, new renewables projects face a multiyear waiting time to be plugged into the grid, which slows the transition to cleaner energy sources.

“The moral of the renewables story is transmission,” Williams said. “You must have significant levels of interconnection to all of your neighboring entities.”

New Mexico developed policies to bring renewables online quickly, reliably, and cheaply, including quick turnaround times for reviewing and approving applications for new projects, low fees for interconnecting, and transparency in data sharing and reporting to the public.

New Mexico was the only state to earn an “A” grade for interconnection policies in a recent report by the Interstate Renewable Energy Council and Vote Solar.

Williams explained some of the myriad engineering challenges that go into converting a traditional fossil-fueled electricity system into the grid of the future.

“This really is the biggest math problem on the planet to solve, kind of a generational challenge, but really, really fun and really interesting, but not at all straightforward,” she said.

A lot goes on behind the scenes every time an air conditioner kicks into gear. But at least in some places, the web of decisions, policies, and infrastructure is producing a more climate-friendly way to keep lights, fans, and air conditioners running, even in the heat of summer. And that’s pretty cool.

‍

This article was originally published by Yale Climate Connections.

Clemson University’s Department of Forestry and Environmental Conservation (FEC) moved into a cutting-edge new home at the beginning of the 2026 Fall semester.
