text:
Clemson University’s Department of Forestry and Environmental Conservation (FEC) moved into a cutting-edge new home at the beginning of the 2026 Fall semester. The new FEC building, located at the intersection of Perimeter and Cherry Roads, offers 82,436 square feet of sparkling new classrooms, research labs and office space that will make it the envy of forestry and agricultural programs the world over.

Staff members in the College of Agriculture, Forestry and Life Sciences (CAFLS) collaborated with the design team at Moseley Architects to create a structure that is not only functional, efficient and visually appealing, but that also showcases high-performance, sustainable construction that stores carbon, supports rural economies and demonstrates the next generation in wood construction using locally sourced lumber.

The four-story building consists of three wings that embrace a carefully landscaped courtyard facing a woodland. Students can move easily from indoor to outdoor classrooms, turning the dense urban forest of the University’s main campus into a living-learning tool.

Mass timber

The structure was built with mass timber-framed construction, a product researched and developed by Clemson’s Wood Utilization and Design (WU+D) Institute, a leader in the development of sustainable building materials. Mass timber is made by binding smaller pieces of lumber together to form large structural elements such as beams, columns, and panels, and is an environmentally sustainable alternative to steel and concrete. There are three common types of mass timber: cross-laminated timber (CLT), glue-laminated timber (glulam) and nail or dowel-laminated timber (NLT/DLT).

Clemson’s two other mass-timber buildings on its main campus, the Andy Quattlebaum Outdoor Education Center and the Samuel J. Cadden Chapel, have become popular University landmarks.

The FEC building’s glulam beams were made by SmartLam, whose chief executive officer is Clemson alumnus Derek Ratchford ’94. The CLT wood came as a gift from Norfolk Southern Railway, the same company behind the bright red caboose that is a fixture in the South Carolina Botanical Garden.

Passers-by could watch the massive, layered beams forming the skeleton of the FEC building as it rose from a former parking lot; construction began in April 2024. Wood products were displayed during construction to serve as a learning tool for the Department of Forestry.

Pat Layton, strategic advisor to the WU+D Institute, explained that construction of a new building became essential because the FEC department’s former home, Lehotsky Hall, was not only deteriorating but also was one of the highest energy users on campus.

“Energy conservation was a key cost item to getting it built,” she says. “It started with a renovation, but that turned out to be more expensive than building new, so, like the IPTAY headquarters, we had to start from scratch.”

Polka dots and earth tones

Students in FEC programs are prepared to be leaders in sustainable forestry, wildlife and fisheries conservation, and ecology through excellence in instruction, scientific inquiry, and outreach to the citizens of South Carolina, the nation and the world. It partners with industry, state and federal agencies, and non-governmental organizations to protect and advance the region’s most valuable assets: its forests, wetlands, and aquatic ecosystems.

“The building was designed with faculty, staff and students in mind, along with the idea that field materials, which often are dirty and wet, enter the building in the basement and move upstairs after processing for research and development,” explained Layton.

Extra care was taken to blend the interior with the natural world. The University’s traditional brick-and-metal panel palette was woven into the exterior, while visible public spaces feature wood in the structure, flooring, walls and ceiling.

Visitors pass through the main entrance doors into a two-story atrium with floor-to-ceiling windows and a grand staircase of oak and steel leading to the second level. A close look reveals opaque dots covering the large windows that wrap around the building, specially designed to prevent birds from flying into them.

Walls painted in gentle blues, greens and earth tones enclose the hallways, offices and classrooms that fill the building’s expansive interior, complemented by exposed white oak plank flooring and custom shelving made from timber sourced from the University campus. The more one looks, the more one sees the small details, like the images of fish that decorate lobby chairs, and the big ones, like the fact that 95 percent of the offices and classrooms have window views.

During an informal tour of the third floor, FEC administration coordinator Sandy Priddy pointed out the view of Tillman Hall through the large windows in a meeting space specially designed as a seminar room for graduate defenses.

“We have 100 graduate students at any given time, so there’s always proposal defenses and final defenses, and now there’s a big, beautiful room for that!” said Priddy, pointing out that the space also comes with an attached patio that shares the Tillman Hall view. “It’s perfect because, once they finish, they can go outside and celebrate.”

Sustainability and flexibility

In line with Clemson’s sustainability ethos, the mass timber structure offers significant environmental advantages, such as reduced embodied carbon compared to traditional building materials like steel and concrete. From the start, the design team leveraged the building’s location on a former parking lot to minimize land impact, enhance tree canopy coverage, and reduce urban heat island effects. The use of southern yellow pine from local sustainable forests showcases Clemson’s dedication to regional ecological practices and industries.

The interior is designed to be just a flexible as the exterior, with functional spaces and covered outdoor areas continuing the easy movement from indoors to outdoors. Project rooms distributed throughout the building can host small group discussions one day and serve as laboratories the next. A trio of classrooms in the south wing has walls that can retract to create a 3,000-square-foot space for large gatherings.

The project is pursuing two Green Globe building certifications from the Green Building Initiative to maximize efficiency and promote sustainability.

“This building will be more than wood, bricks and mortar,” says Greg Yarrow, CAFLS associate vice president for strategic initiatives. “It will be a hub of innovation, research and education. It will help us lead into a sustainable future, where students and faculty alike come together to tackle the most pressing forestry, natural resources and environmental issues of our time.”

Dean of CAFLS Matt Holt concurred with Yarrow, adding that the new building’s thoughtful design perfectly reflects the spirit of the University’s land-grant mission, which is the living core of CAFLS and the FEC department.

“We wanted a home for FEC that represented the character of the department and the future its graduates are helping to shape,” Holt says. “This building does that through its materials, its flexibility and its strong connection to the campus landscape.”

text:
A recently opened health hub in Central Australia has become the highest-rated Green Star building in the Northern Territory after receiving a 6-Star Green Star Design and As Built certification.

Awarded by the Green Building Council of Australia, Central Australian Aboriginal Congress' new Mparntwe Health Hub — which only opened this year — becomes the first building in Central Australia to achieve both Design and As Built certifications.

The rating considers energy and water efficiency, building materials, construction waste, transport, climate resilience and the health and comfort of people using the building.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Senator Malarndirri McCarthy (@malarndirri)

"Our job is to improve the health of Aboriginal people in Central Australia, and we recognise that the environment people live in is fundamental to health," said Congress Chief Executive Ebony Abbott-McCormack.

"The healthcare industry is resource intensive, so when we had the opportunity to build the Health Hub, we wanted to make sure we were doing everything we reasonably could to reduce its environmental impact and better care for country."

Sustainability measures at the Health Hub — designed by Susan Dugdale and Associates and constructed by AS Build — include increased natural light and fresh air, improved acoustics and temperature control, low-toxicity materials, recycled and recyclable products and reduced construction waste.

Located centrally in Mparntwe / Alice Springs, it also encourages walking and cycling to reduce unnecessary travel.

Ms Dugdale said it was rewarding to work on a project where "sustainability was treated as a core part of the project from the beginning".

"Congress set the bar high, not just on environmental performance, but also for the health and wellbeing of the people who use the building," she said. "The 6-Star rating reflects that ambition and shows the kind of result you get when an organisation is truly invested to its community and place."

Whilst the project initially targeted a 5-Star rating, Ms Abbott-McCormack said achieving the 6-Star design — the highest level — is a "fantastic result," as is "continuing the process to As Built certification".

"It shows we didn't just design a sustainable building — we actually delivered it," she said.

"It also shows that being remote doesn't mean lowering the bar. World-leading sustainable buildings can be delivered right here in Central Australia."

Congress' broader sustainability strategy isn't just confined to the Health Hub. Solar has been installed across eight Congress buildings, with a ninth installation planned, while the organisation has reduced its vehicle fleet by 16 vehicles and introduced 15 electric vehicles.

As a result, more than 9,000 litres of fuel are saved each year, Congress argues. These sustainability measures deliver ongoing cost savings which are being redirected towards improving the health of Aboriginal people in Central Australia — the core mission of Congress.

Molo Remains the Core Asset The Molo Graphite Mine in Madagascar forms the foundation of NextSource's investment case.

text:
NextSource Materials Inc. (TSX:NEXT) advanced 9.26% in the session shown, generating renewed bullish momentum as investors reassessed the company's potential role in the emerging ex-China graphite and battery-materials Supply chain.

The Investment thesis centers on the Molo Graphite Mine in Madagascar, complemented by NextSource's longer-term strategy to develop Downstream battery anode material capabilities closer to major battery markets.

This creates a potentially differentiated model. Rather than remaining exclusively a graphite miner, NextSource aims to participate across a larger portion of the battery-materials value chain.

The latest share-price strength suggests improving market confidence, although investors still need to weigh production execution, expansion financing, downstream development and graphite-market conditions.

Investment Overview

NextSource Materials is developing an integrated graphite supply strategy built around its Molo operation.

Graphite is a critical component of lithium-ion batteries, where it is predominantly used in battery anodes.

The company therefore sits within several overlapping investment themes:

Electric vehicles → Battery Manufacturing → Anode Demand → Graphite consumption → Supply-chain diversification

NextSource's opportunity is particularly relevant because global graphite processing remains highly concentrated.

Western governments and battery manufacturers are increasingly interested in diversifying critical-mineral supply chains.

If NextSource can establish reliable production and downstream processing outside the dominant existing supply network, its strategic relevance could increase materially.

Why NextSource Materials Stock Is Rising

The 9.26% advance indicates strengthening short-term investor sentiment.

Molo Provides an Operating Foundation

Unlike many graphite companies that remain entirely dependent on future mine construction, NextSource has already moved Molo into its initial production phase.

That provides an important platform from which management can pursue larger-scale expansion.

Expansion Could Transform Production Scale

The company's growth strategy involves increasing Molo's production capacity substantially beyond its initial configuration.

Successfully executing that expansion could materially improve the company's commercial profile.

Battery Anode Strategy Adds Downstream Upside

NextSource intends to move beyond natural graphite concentrate by developing facilities capable of producing higher-value battery anode material.

This could potentially increase margins while strengthening relationships with battery customers.

Molo Remains the Core Asset

The Molo Graphite Mine in Madagascar forms the foundation of NextSource's investment case.

The project contains high-quality flake graphite capable of serving multiple markets.

Natural flake graphite can be used across industrial applications, while appropriately processed material can ultimately enter battery supply chains.

The quality and size distribution of graphite are important because different end markets require different product specifications.

NextSource's ability to produce material suitable for premium applications could therefore influence realized pricing and margins.

Production Ramp-Up Is Critical

Reaching initial production is only one stage in building a successful mine.

The next challenge is demonstrating consistent operations.

Investors should focus on whether Molo can achieve:

Stable plant throughput.

Consistent graphite recoveries.

Reliable product quality.

Predictable operating costs.

Regular customer shipments.

Operational consistency is particularly important for battery-material customers, which typically require rigorous qualification and supply reliability.

A mine that produces intermittently may struggle to secure premium long-term customers regardless of resource quality.

Expansion Represents a Major Re-Rating Opportunity

NextSource's planned expansion at Molo represents one of the largest potential catalysts for the investment thesis.

Higher production could significantly increase Revenue potential and improve operating leverage.

However, expansion also introduces financing and construction risk.

Management must ensure that additional capacity is aligned with realistic customer demand.

The preferred progression is:

Customer qualification → Offtake visibility → Expansion financing → Construction → Production growth

Building capacity before securing sufficient demand could weaken returns.

Conversely, aligning expansion with committed customers could substantially de-risk the strategy.

Battery Anode Material Could Move NextSource Up the Value Chain

Mining graphite concentrate captures only part of the potential Economics associated with battery materials.

Before graphite can be used in Lithium-Ion Battery anodes, it requires additional processing.

This can include purification, shaping and coating.

NextSource's downstream strategy seeks exposure to these higher-value processing stages.

If successful, the company could potentially capture more economic value per unit of graphite while becoming more deeply integrated into battery manufacturers' supply chains.

This is strategically important because governments increasingly want not only critical-mineral mines but also domestic or allied processing capacity.

Supply-Chain Diversification Is a Powerful Catalyst

Graphite supply and processing are geographically concentrated.

This has created concern among governments and manufacturers seeking secure battery-material supplies.

Trade restrictions or geopolitical tensions could make diversified sources increasingly valuable.

NextSource's broader opportunity therefore extends beyond Commodity pricing.

Customers may assign strategic value to:

Geographic diversification.

Traceable supply.

Reliable long-term production.

ESG standards.

Non-dominant-market processing.

Successfully demonstrating these attributes could strengthen the company's competitive position.

Automotive Qualification Can Take Time

Battery supply chains have demanding qualification processes.

Automakers and battery manufacturers cannot simply substitute one graphite supplier for another without extensive testing.

Material must meet strict requirements involving purity, particle characteristics, performance and consistency.

This creates a long commercialization cycle.

However, once qualification is achieved, customer relationships can potentially become durable because manufacturers are reluctant to repeatedly change critical battery inputs.

For NextSource, successful qualification could therefore become an important competitive moat.

Graphite Pricing Remains a Challenge

The bullish structural demand outlook does not eliminate near-term commodity risk.

Graphite markets have experienced pricing pressure as supply growth has sometimes exceeded immediate demand.

Low-cost incumbent producers can also create intense competition.

This means NextSource cannot rely solely on expectations of rising graphite prices.

The company needs competitive operating costs and differentiated products capable of attracting customers even during weaker pricing environments.

Downstream battery-material exposure could help reduce dependence on raw concentrate prices, but it also adds operational complexity.

Madagascar Creates Both Opportunity and Risk

Molo's location provides access to a substantial graphite resource, but jurisdictional considerations remain important.

Mining companies operating internationally must manage regulatory relationships, infrastructure, logistics, taxation and community engagement.

Political or regulatory changes could affect project economics.

Shipping graphite from Madagascar to global customers also requires reliable logistics.

title: No Ban, No Problem: Ninth Circuit Upholds EPA's PBT Exemption Rule | ArentFox Schiff
description:
The Rule at Issue Under the TSCA, manufacturers of new chemical substances generally must file a PMN with EPA before manufacture.
In the 2024 rule, EPA added provisions specifying when PBTs may qualify for statutory low-volume or low-exposure exemptions.
UAW’s Comment-Response Claim: The court found EPA was not required to substantively respond because the comment did not address an issue presented in the proposed rule.
Conclusion The Ninth Circuit’s decision confirms that EPA’s case-by-case approach to evaluating PBT exemption requests will remain in place for the foreseeable future.
Companies developing or manufacturing PBT substances should build their exemption strategies around robust exposure-control documentation, monitor EPA’s evolving approach, and consider whether the exemption pathway offers meaningful timing advantages over the full PMN process.
text:
The Rule at Issue

Under the TSCA, manufacturers of new chemical substances generally must file a PMN with EPA before manufacture. Although the statute gives EPA 90 days to complete PMN reviews, in practice, the process often takes much longer. TSCA also gives EPA discretion to exempt manufacturers from all or part of the PMN process under certain scenarios if the proposed use will not present an unreasonable risk.

In the 2024 rule, EPA added provisions specifying when PBTs may qualify for statutory low-volume or low-exposure exemptions. Rather than categorically barring PBTs, EPA adopted a case-by-case review framework.

Who Challenged the Rule

Alaska Community Action on Toxics and Environmental Defense Fund argued EPA lacked authority and should have categorically barred exemptions. , and that the exemption provision was arbitrary and capricious.

The International Union, United Automobile, Aerospace and Agricultural Implement Workers of America (UAW) argued EPA failed to adequately respond to a rulemaking comment concerning TSCA Section 2604(e) consent orders.

Why the Court Rejected the Challenges

Environmental Petitioners’ Statutory Authority Claim: Applying the independent-review framework required by Loper Bright, the court concluded that TSCA gives EPA discretion to evaluate exemption requests on a case-by-case basis.

Arbitrary and Capricious Claim: The court held that EPA reasonably considered both a categorical ban and a case-by-case approach.

UAW’s Comment-Response Claim: The court found EPA was not required to substantively respond because the comment did not address an issue presented in the proposed rule.

A Note on the Decision: The court issued the ruling as an unpublished memorandum disposition, meaning it is not precedential under Ninth Circuit Rule 36-3. Even so, it provides useful insight into how at least one appellate panel views EPA’s authority under TSCA’s exemption provisions.

Practical Notes

EPA will continue reviewing PBT exemption requests on a case-by-case basis.

Applicants for exemptions for PBTs should expect that most applications will be denied. Applicants should anticipate rigorous scrutiny and be prepared to demonstrate that their proposed uses minimize or eliminate meaningful exposure pathways.

The exemption pathway may provide a more efficient regulatory pathway than full PMN review in appropriate circumstances. Companies should therefore monitor EPA’s evolving track record on granting or denying exemptions.

Illustrative scenarios: A sealed closed-loop semiconductor process may be viable. A consumer-facing furniture application likely would not because EPA would likely conclude the proposed use presents potentially unreasonable exposures.

The decision illustrates that agencies can still prevail after Loper Bright where US Congress has granted meaningful discretion to the implementing agency.

Conclusion

The Ninth Circuit’s decision confirms that EPA’s case-by-case approach to evaluating PBT exemption requests will remain in place for the foreseeable future. Companies developing or manufacturing PBT substances should build their exemption strategies around robust exposure-control documentation, monitor EPA’s evolving approach, and consider whether the exemption pathway offers meaningful timing advantages over the full PMN process. If you have questions or concerns about how this decision may affect your operations or TSCA compliance strategy, please contact a member of the group.

text:
Maximum budget per category and number of expected awards are listed in Section 1.3.1, Funding Amounts, of the RFP. For example, in the Solar for Savings RFP, a total of $6.5 million is budgeted towards residential-serving community solar projects, where one or more awards will be awarded in that category. Though there are no minimum grant amounts for grant awards for the Solar for Savings: MI Solar for All pilot projects, Solar for Savings proposals that aggregate single-family residential rooftop solar projects are preferred.

Projects applying under the residential-serving community solar area must share 50 percent or more of the benefits generated by the solar array with eligible low-income households within the same utility service territory as the solar array. Please see U.S. EPA Solar for All Terms and Conditions, which have to be met by all Solar for Savings grant awardees. Residential-serving community solar projects must provide benefits that are additive, either providing new benefits to eligible low-income households or expanding existing services to serve additional new-income households. These benefits do not have to be provided on an electricity bill and can be provided in innovative fashions that best serve your community. A project that proposes to have MI Solar for All help fund installations of residential-serving community solar but does not intend to share 50 percent or more of the benefits from the solar array with eligible low-income households does not meet U.S. EPA Solar for All Terms and Conditions.

Front-of-the-meter community solar projects are eligible and can be administered in partnership with a utility or otherwise. For a list of electric utility providers, contact information, and service territories, please visit the Michigan Public Service Commission’s (MPSC) website. Front-of-the-meter residential-serving community solar projects within MI Solar for All do not necessarily have to provide benefits on an electric bill and could provide participating low-income households benefits in innovative fashions as long as they meet U.S. EPA Solar for All Program Terms and Conditions.

For guidance on how a program serves a household, please see the U.S. EPA Frequent Questions about Solar for All. It share examples of recent guidance from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development for how benefits may be shared indirectly from solar photovoltaic systems in situations where households do not have individual electricity meters. Please note that for-profit entities may partner with entities eligible to apply for Solar for Savings funding, like nonprofits and governmental entities. For a more specific illustration of how an investor-owned utility might approach this situation, please contact EGLE-MISFA@Michigan.gov.

Please visit MPSC's generator interconnection webpage for more information. Each utility has its own interconnection procedures. The MPSC website provides links to this information for investor-owned utilities and member-regulated co-operative utilities, as well as hosting capacity maps for Consumers Energy and DTE Electric. Multifamily dwellings with multiple meters could submit projects under the residential rooftop solar or residential-serving community solar areas of the Solar for Savings funding opportunity.

If submitted as a residential rooftop solar project, the multifamily solar project would have to provide direct electric bill reductions to each participating low-income household. This could occur from installing solar arrays to service each household (one solar array for each low-income household meter in the multifamily dwelling). This approach is commonly seen in Michigan. If the utility allows its interconnection, it is also technologically possible to install one large solar array for a multifamily dwelling, where the power is divided and shared amongst different residents within the building.

If submitted as a residential-serving community solar project, the multifamily dwelling could install solar to serve dwelling units and common spaces. The project must meet U.S. EPA Solar for All Terms and Conditions for residential-serving community solar (e.g., 50 percent or more of the solar array benefits are shared with eligible low-income households in the same utility service territory, 5 Megawatts of alternating current (MWac) or smaller, etc.). The benefits from the community solar array could be shared in innovative methods, as long as the participant benefit requirements for the U.S. EPA Solar for All Program are met.

Applicants and their subrecipients may identify indirect charges as part of the proposed budgets. If a Negotiated Indirect Cost Rate Agreement (NICRA) is available, that may be used. If funds are awarded, a copy of the NICRA will need to be submitted to EGLE. If an applicant does not have a NICRA, a de minimis rate of 5 percent of direct costs may be used instead. U.S. EPA Solar for All Terms and Conditions advise the following for indirect costs: an indirect rate can be applied to total direct salaries and wages, applicable fringe benefits, materials and supplies, services, travel, and up to the first $50,000 of each subaward (regardless of the period of performance of the subawards under the award). Indirect costs excludes equipment, capital expenditures, charges for patient care, rental costs, tuition remission, scholarships and fellowships, Participant Support Costs, and the portion of each subaward in excess of $50,000.

text:
California Attorney General Rob Bonta and the California Energy Commission have filed a lawsuit against the Trump Administration and Golden State Wind LLC challenging the buyout of Golden State Wind’s offshore wind energy lease.

California said the U.S. Department of the Interior reallocated $120 million in federal taxpayer funds to pay Golden State Wind to abandon its offshore wind energy lease in federal waters off California’s Central Coast.

The state added that the agreement requires Golden State Wind to invest an equal amount in out-of-state fossil-fuel projects and is asking the court to strike down the deal.

Golden State Wind paid the U.S. $120 million in 2022 to purchase an offshore wind lease in the Morro Bay Wind Energy Area for a 2GW offshore wind farm, with additional commitments of more than $30 million for workforce training, supply chain development and benefits to local communities.

DOI announced on April 27, 2026, that it would terminate the lease under an agreement with Golden State Wind, with the federal government to reimburse the company $120 million from the Judgment Fund.

The California Energy Commission served an investigative subpoena on Golden State Wind in May seeking documents and information related to the buyout, while the California Department of Justice and CEC sent a Notice of Intent to Sue in June.

California has invested more than $100 million in ports, transmission systems and industries to support offshore wind generation, while its offshore wind strategic plan calls for 25GW of capacity by 2045.

The state said cancelled offshore wind projects threaten more than 174,750 jobs, infrastructure investment and long-term economic development.

California argues the deal violates federal laws including the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act and the Judgment Fund Act.

“The Trump Administration’s backroom buyout with Golden State Wind to stop offshore wind development in favor of gas and oil drilling is, unfortunately, a classic playbook for them to line the pockets of their Big Oil donors,” said Attorney General Bonta.

“Let’s be clear: California will continue to aggressively fight back against the Trump administration’s outrageous abuse of taxpayer dollars to abandon offshore wind investments that could have delivered union-paying jobs and reliable clean energy to Californians.”

“Offshore wind presents an opportunity for our state to scale up an innovative new clean energy industry that reduces pollution while providing new jobs and investment for the people of our state,” said David Hochschild, Chair, California Energy Commission.

“We will not let the Trump administration’s reckless actions turn back the clock. California’s clean energy future is worth fighting for. See you in court.”

From backup power to grid asset The deal arrives as the energy storage industry undergoes fundamental repositioning.
text:
NeoVolta Inc. and South Korean battery giant SK On have announced a five-year strategic collaboration valued at approximately $1.09 billion that will supply 18 gigawatt-hours of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cells for energy storage systems manufactured in Georgia, marking one of the largest domestic battery supply agreements since the passage of the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” (OBBBA).

The deal, announced August 31 by both companies, establishes a two-phase partnership: an initial signed agreement for SK On to supply 9 GWh of U.S.-manufactured LFP cells to NeoVolta Power from 2027 through 2031, plus a framework for an additional 9 GWh arrangement under which NeoVolta Power will manufacture battery packs for purchase by SK On over the same period.

"This collaboration represents an important milestone in NeoVolta's expansion into large-scale energy storage and the continued buildout of our U.S. manufacturing platform," stated Ardes Johnson, Chief Executive Officer of NeoVolta, in the company's announcement.

Strategic timing: From residential roots to utility scale

The announcement represents a dramatic acceleration of a strategy Johnson outlined to Battery Technology just three months ago. In a May 2026 interview with Battery Technology, the CEO emphasized that NeoVolta's domestic manufacturing roadmap "predates the OBBBA," explaining that the company had "long planned to establish US-based manufacturing across the full storage spectrum — from residential systems through the often underserved commercial and industrial 'middle market,' and into utility-scale storage."

That vision is now materializing at commercial scale. The SK On partnership will supply pouch-type LFP cells produced at SK On's Georgia factory to NeoVolta Power's Pendergrass, Georgia facility, which manufactures battery energy storage systems (BESS) for commercial, industrial, and utility-scale applications. According to the company's announcement, the collaboration is expected to accelerate NeoVolta Power's expansion to a two-line manufacturing platform targeting up to 8 GWh of annual BESS production capacity by 2028.

The deal validates Johnson's earlier assertion about building ecosystems, not just products. "What truly shortens deployment timelines is building the ecosystem around it," he told Battery Technology in May. "That means working with developers, community choice aggregators, utilities, and program operators that need reliable technology partners and a consistent supply of systems to scale their programs."

SK On and ESS as EV hedge

For SK On, the NeoVolta partnership represents a strategic hedge against weakening electric vehicle demand. According to Reuters, "the agreement comes as SK On expands into the energy storage system business to offset weaker demand for electric vehicles."

"This partnership strengthens SK On's position in the US BESS market and brings together SK On's U.S.-made LFP battery technology with NeoVolta Power's growing energy storage manufacturing capabilities," stated Daejin Choi, Head of ESS Business at SK On, in the joint announcement.

SK On had set a target of securing more than 20 GWh of global energy storage system orders this year and is in talks with several U.S. customers over additional supply contracts totaling more than 10 GWh, according to Reuters. Competitors including LG Energy Solution and Samsung SDI are also repurposing EV battery production lines for energy storage as U.S. EV subsidies phase out.

LFP chemistry as insulation from commodity volatility

NeoVolta's commitment to lithium iron phosphate chemistry—rather than nickel-manganese-cobalt formulations—provides strategic insulation from raw material price volatility, a consideration Johnson emphasized in our May interview.

"Our use of lithium iron phosphate chemistry helps avoid exposure to nickel and cobalt volatility, while our US assembly platform improves logistics, quality control, and alignment with domestic content incentives," Johnson explained. He added that the company is "preparing for where policy and market requirements are headed," noting that "as domestic content thresholds and FEOC [Foreign Entity of Concern] requirements increase over time, we anticipate the industry moving further upstream."

The all-domestic supply chain—SK On's Georgia-manufactured cells paired with NeoVolta Power's Georgia-based pack assembly—positions the collaboration to meet evolving domestic content requirements under OBBBA. As the release notes, "by pairing US-manufactured LFP cells with US-based BESS manufacturing, [NeoVolta] believes its platform is positioned to serve customers seeking reliable and domestic content BESS solutions."

From backup power to grid asset

The deal arrives as the energy storage industry undergoes fundamental repositioning. As Johnson told Battery Technology in May, "the industry conversation is shifting from simply pairing solar with storage to recognizing that storage itself is the primary grid asset, with solar as an optional generation source layered on top."

This philosophical shift—from viewing batteries as backup devices to treating them as dispatchable, revenue-generating grid infrastructure—underpins the commercial logic of multi-gigawatt-hour supply agreements. The target markets reflect this evolution: according to the press release, the partnership targets "utility, commercial, industrial, AI data-center markets." The inclusion of AI data centers is particularly notable, reflecting explosive growth in power-intensive computing infrastructure.

Production timeline and industry implications

NeoVolta Power's initial Pendergrass production line "remains on track to advance through commissioning and production-ramp activities," with cell deliveries and pack production scheduled to begin in 2027 and continue through 2031.

The NeoVolta-SK On collaboration represents one of the clearest examples to date of how OBBBA and related domestic content incentives are reshaping battery supply chains. Rather than importing finished products from Asia, the partnership establishes an end-to-end domestic value chain: Korean battery technology transferred to U.S. manufacturing, paired with U.S.-based system integration.

This model—foreign technology expertise combined with domestic production—may become a template for other international battery manufacturers seeking to serve the U.S. market while meeting increasingly stringent domestic content requirements.

For NeoVolta, the deal validates the strategic bet Johnson described in May: that focusing on "efficient product design with a growing domestic manufacturing footprint" would position the company as policy shifts toward domestic sourcing.

"We're not only planning for what the supply chain needs today," Johnson told Battery Technology. "We're preparing for where policy and market requirements are headed."

With 18 GWh of committed collaboration and a manufacturing platform designed to scale to 8 GWh of annual capacity, NeoVolta and SK On are now positioned to help define what that future looks like.

text:
Advanced microgrid technology automatically keeps the lights on when outages occur

EDITOR’S NOTE: For photos of the Trenton microgrid, please click here.

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. – Duke Energy Florida has launched its second large-scale battery facility, capable of providing backup power to the local community to prevent outages. The site is located in Trenton, located 30 miles west of Gainesville in Gilchrist County.

How it works

The 11-megawatt Trenton lithium battery facility was first placed into operation in 2022 to store energy, balance demand and defer traditional power grid improvements. This summer, Duke Energy Florida upgraded the facility so that approximately 1,500 customers in the surrounding area can receive backup power for up to four hours, reducing long-duration outages and further supporting overall reliability, grid operations and critical services.

When the battery detects an outage, it automatically disconnects from the electric grid to supply backup power to neighboring customers. The concept is referred to as “islanding” or a microgrid. The facility functions like a large-scale generator for the community, providing backup power in much the same way a standard generator supports a single home or business.

The company’s first Florida microgrid was located in the Alachua County town of Micanopy. Duke Energy Florida currently owns, operates and maintains a total of six battery facilities throughout the state, which store power for use during high demand periods.

Powering homes and businesses in any type of weather

This microgrid technology is one of many investments Duke Energy Florida has made to help create a stronger, more resilient electric grid on behalf of its two million customers.

Over the last five years, the company has upgraded 60% of wooden transmission poles to stronger materials. Approximately 50% of the distribution system is underground, protected from the elements and making the lines easier to get to if outages do occur. Over 82% of customers are also served by self-healing technology, which automatically detects outages and re-routes power to the lines, preventing millions of minutes of outages every year.

Our view

“We are continually making smart grid investments to improve reliability for our customers, while keeping costs as low as possible,” said Melissa Seixas, Duke Energy Florida state president. “This second microgrid in Trenton lets us supply backup power directly to the local community, helping to keep our customers powered when they need it most.”

Duke Energy Florida

Duke Energy Florida, a subsidiary of Duke Energy, owns 12,500 megawatts of energy capacity, supplying electricity to 2 million residential, commercial and industrial customers across a 13,000-square-mile service area in Florida.

Duke Energy

Duke Energy (NYSE: DUK), a Fortune 150 company headquartered in Charlotte, N.C., is one of America’s largest energy holding companies. The company’s electric utilities serve 8.7 million customers in North Carolina, South Carolina, Florida, Indiana, Ohio and Kentucky, and collectively own 55,700 megawatts of energy capacity. Its natural gas utilities serve 1.6 million customers in North Carolina, South Carolina, Ohio and Kentucky.

Duke Energy is executing an energy modernization strategy, keeping customer value at the forefront as it invests in electric grid upgrades and efficient generation resources to strengthen the system and serve growing energy needs.

Achieving Carbon Neutrality in Core Operations–A First for the Industry

At the launch event,CATL officially confirmed that it had achieved carbon neutrality across its core operations by the end of 2025–becoming the world’s first battery maker to reach this milestone while shipping at a terawatt-hour(TWh)scale.

To date,all 20 of CATL’s battery plants have secured ISO 14068-1 zero-carbon factory certification.Nineteen of these are located in China,while the remaining one is in Thuringia,Germany.Across all certified facilities,100%of the electricity used in core operational processes comes from zero-carbon sources.

Robin Zeng,Chairman and CEO of CATL,noted during the event that corporate decarbonization has evolved from a mere social responsibility into a central growth driver.As global carbon-neutrality efforts accelerate,zero-carbon batteries will soon cease to be a competitive differentiator and become a baseline requirement for market participation.

Robin Zeng(Chairman and CEO of CATL)

Green Smart Manufacturing:Efficiency and Data Transparency Go Hand in Hand

Jiang Li,Vice President,Board Secretary and Head of Corporate Sustainable Development Management Committee of CATL,stressed that carbon neutrality cannot be built on estimates–it demands reliable data,clearly defined boundaries,and systematic execution.To meet this need,CATL developed its own carbon-data traceability and management platform–CATL Carbon Chain Management System,enabling precise monitoring,full-chain traceability,and dynamic control over emissions across all manufacturing sites and along the upstream and downstream supply chain.

This granular approach to carbon data is woven into every stage of production.During its visit to Z-Base,EnergyTrend observed a production line nearly one kilometre long operating at a pace of“one battery cell per second.”To uphold quality at such scale,CATL has integrated AI-powered visual inspection into the cell-production process,swiftly detecting even the smallest surface defects and ensuring that only flawless cells reach customers.

Notably,in the facility’s advanced-technology display area,CATL showcased a sodium-ion battery capable of stable power supply at-40°C.This breakthrough in extreme-temperature performance directly addresses the long-standing challenge of winter instability in energy-storage plants situated in high-latitude regions,while also enhancing the reliability and safety of electric mobility solutions in cold climates–thereby expanding the potential applications of zero-carbon battery technology.

CATL Headquarters(Ningde,Fujian)

Driving Decarbonisation Across the Entire Value Chain

Having met its operational emissions target,CATL now faces the larger challenge of achieving carbon neutrality across its entire value chain.At the conference,the company unveiled its roadmap to full-value-chain carbon neutrality by 2035,alongside a new set of Green Procurement Guidelines.Bryan Huang,Head of Procurement Center at CATL,stated that CATL will continue to intensify efforts in material innovation,green material production,and low-carbon logistics to drive down emissions at every link in the value chain.

From 2027 onwards,submitting verified carbon-footprint data will become a mandatory condition for new supplier onboarding.At the same time,CATL has launched its Zero-Carbon Supply Chain Empowerment Initiative,initially partnering with 30 core suppliers on deep-joint decarbonisation projects.Suppliers that demonstrate outstanding low-carbon performance will receive preferential treatment,including priority order placement and long-term strategic cooperation agreements.

Leveraging its enormous purchasing power,CATL is effectively transmitting low-carbon standards upstream to global mining and battery-material suppliers,thereby accelerating the green transformation of the entire industrial chain.On the international front,its Thuringia plant in Germany has maintained zero-carbon factory certification for two consecutive years,providing a concrete example of how overseas production can be successfully localised and decarbonised.

Beyond Passenger Cars:The Rapid Expansion into All Scenarios

The technological spill-over from batteries is also breaking down traditional sector boundaries.At the conclusion of the site visit,EnergyTrend took a ride on the“East Lake Star”sightseeing vessel,which is powered by CATL batteries.The 27-metre commercial boat,equipped with a 293 kWh battery pack and a designed cruising speed of 15 km/h,demonstrated impressive zero-emission operation and exceptionally low noise levels.

East Lake Star(Ningde,Fujian)

The New Industry Benchmark

Taken together,ultra-high manufacturing yields and fully traceable,end-to-end carbon footprints have become the new baseline for the global new-energy industry.As carbon-management requirements become ever more embedded in international trade rules,companies across the entire supply chain–both upstream and downstream–must integrate efficient manufacturing with transparent,verifiable data if they are to maintain their competitive edge throughout the coming decade of global energy transition.

text:
The prevailing public narrative is that U.S. electricity demand is soaring and gas is the only option to meet that growth. The data tells a much different story.

In its August short-term energy outlook, the Energy Information Administration (EIA) projects that total electric power sector generation will climb 4.6% from the beginning of 2026 through the end of 2027. Strong growth, certainly, and a break from the past decade, but not unprecedented.

What is most interesting in EIA’s data is the composition of the new generation. The agency projects that wind and solar will supply 93.7% of the projected increase through 2027—186.4 million megawatt-hours (MWh) of the forecasted 198.8 million MWh rise. Adding expected hydropower generation pushes the renewable share to 98.5%, or 195.9 million MWh. By contrast, EIA expects coal and gas generation to climb just 1.3 million MWh through 2027, supplying less than 1% of the projected national increase in electricity output.

Importantly, the projected increase in utility-scale wind and solar generation is a national trend. As the graphic shows, EIA expects output from the two renewable resources to climb significantly in almost every major U.S. power market.

Figure 1- EIA projects strong growth in solar, wind generation through 2027

IEEFA has written extensively about the renewable (and dispatchable battery storage) transition underway in the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), which operates the market serving about 90% of the state’s electricity demand. Texas has the highest power demand of any individual state in the country, by far. Not only is that transition continuing as the state rushes to meet the burgeoning electricity needs of new data centers and other industrial sources, but the buildout of large-scale solar and wind will be the largest of any power market in the country. Through 2027, EIA projects total ERCOT generation will increase 42.4 million MWh— all of which will be supplied by wind and solar.

The ability of renewables and dispatchable battery storage to meet rapidly rising demand was on full display in ERCOT in July. The system smashed its previous generation record July 22, hitting a peak of 91,089 megawatts (MW) at 6 p.m. local time. This was 3,692 MW above the July 21 mark and 5,508 MW above the system’s previous peak record of 85,508 MW set Aug. 10, 2023. The market barely noticed. At the peak hour, real-time ERCOT prices averaged just $29.11/MWh. In contrast, in 2023 prices climbed to $4,477.12/MWh during the peak hour, and were well over $1,000/MWh for most of the afternoon and early evening.

The reason for the significant price differential is straightforward: Solar and battery storage have changed the ERCOT market, making it both more flexible and reliable while keeping prices in check. Solar generation topped out at 12,993 MW in 2023 and hit 10,435 MW at the peak hour, just over 12% of total demand. On July 22, solar generation climbed to a high of 33,634 MW early in the day and was at 28,712 MW during the peak hour, providing 31.5% of total demand. This solar generation reduced the need for more costly gas and coal, which were both lower at the peak hour in 2026 than in 2023, even though demand was much higher.

Then, as solar generation began to decline, batteries flooded into the market. For more than an hour beginning at 7:45 p.m. July 22, batteries injected more than 10,000 MW into the ERCOT system, providing between 10% and 14% of total demand, negating the need for expensive gas peakers or additional coal generation.

Texas is clearly one of the energy transition leaders, but it is no longer alone. EIA expects wind and solar to grow faster than gas and coal generation in nine of the 11 U.S. power markets through 2027. In those nine areas, EIA projects that wind and solar generation will rise by 161 million MWh while gas and coal output will fall 63 million MWh.

Table 1- EIA projects sharp growth in wind and solar output, flat gas and coal generation

Source: EIA STEO data, IEEFA calculations

The outlier in the ongoing U.S. transition is PJM, the nation’s largest power market, serving all or parts of 13 Midwestern and mid-Atlantic states and the District of Columbia. Its long-troubled process for connecting new generation has led to the delay and/or cancellation of thousands of megawatts of planned solar and wind projects. System rules have also discouraged the construction of battery storage capacity, further undercutting renewables. As a result, while EIA expects wind and solar output to climb in PJM through 2027, almost three-quarters of the region’s generation growth will come from gas and coal.

Perhaps most telling, some 44% of PJM’s projected increase in generation through 2027 is expected to come from the region’s aging coal-fired power plants. These facilities have faced serious economic problems in the past decade, with many being unable to compete profitably and seeing their output decline as a result.

The Keystone and Conemaugh plants in Pennsylvania, essentially twin facilities with two 850-MW units each that came online between 1967 and 1971, are emblematic of these market issues.

Generation at these plants has fallen sharply over the past decade, dropping from an annual capacity factor of roughly 80% in the late 2010s to the 20%-30% level over the past three years. However, the continuing uncertainty around the region’s new project queue and PJM’s sky-high capacity payments, driven by projections of sharply higher regional electricity demand, have given all of PJM’s coal plants a temporary reprieve.

Figure 2 – Electricity generation falls at two large PJM coal plants

Source: S&P

PJM’s operating power plants benefit handsomely from the system’s sharply higher capacity payments, at consumers’ expense. All told, customers across PJM will pay almost $50 billion over the next three years due to the recent surge in capacity costs. In theory, these higher prices will encourage the construction of new generation, ultimately lowering costs. However, whether the theory becomes a reality will not be known for years; meanwhile, existing generators profit while customer costs rise.

The economic impact of PJM’s reliance on gas and aging coal plants also was evident in the early July heatwave that pushed regional demand to a new record. On July 2, PJM demand climbed to 168,158 MW, beating the system’s previous peak (set back in 2006) of 165,563 MW. In contrast to the relatively ho-hum price reaction in ERCOT discussed above, PJM prices soared. GridStatus data show that real-time prices during the peak hour on July 2 (from 5 p.m. – 6 p.m.) climbed to almost $2,000/MWh, and were over $200/MWh from 11:10 a.m. until 9:30 p.m.

More solar generation, which provides extremely reliable, low-cost power during summer peaks (again, see the example of Texas) would likely have dampened the region’s high prices on July 2. In addition, battery storage—of which PJM has virtually none—almost certainly would have lowered the region’s peak prices, as has occurred frequently in both ERCOT and CAISO, which are both smaller regional markets that have embraced battery storage. ERCOT currently has 21,864 MW of installed battery storage capacity, with roughly another 16,000 MW expected online by the end of 2027. Installed battery storage in CAISO totaled 17,125 MW as of Aug. 1, with more under construction.

Regulators, politicians, and market participants in PJM need to take a hard look at the measures being implemented in other regions. The data shows that renewables work, particularly when coupled with dispatchable battery storage. They are reliable, readily deployable, and keep prices stable.

text:
One of East Coast’s largest data centers accused of ‘violating federal laws’

The largest planned AI data center in New Jersey is being accused of violating federal law after a Floodlight visual investigation found the site running dozens of unpermitted gas-powered generators.

Thermal drone footage the organization captured in mid-August showed the partly completed DataOne facility in Vineland was operating at least 45 of the site’s 62 generators at the time.

DataOne has stirred controversy since breaking ground in 2025 due to persistent noise complaints, unpermitted construction and a contentious zoning process. It’s located about 40 miles outside Philadelphia and slated to provide AI computing power to Microsoft as part of a $17-billion deal with Nebius, a Dutch AI infrastructure giant.

Located roughly a mile from two schools, the tractor-trailer-size generators emit substantial amounts of health-harming air pollution linked to asthma, heart attacks and even premature death.

None of the 62 generators have permits.

Federal and state law requires DataOne “to have a final permit before bringing those generators onsite, and certainly before firing them up,” former EPA air enforcement chief Bruce Buckheit told Floodlight.

Buckheit, who served under multiple Republican administrations, believes DataOne’s activities do “violate federal law” and that the company should immediately stop operating the generators and pay a fine for “their illegal emissions.”

A New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection spokesperson confirmed that the agency “has issued no permits, nor are any permit applications under review for power generators at the DataOne facility in Vineland.”

The spokesperson said the agency noticed the generators during a site inspection on July 29 and has yet to make “a full compliance determination.” They declined to answer follow-up questions.

Buckheit said “that one might be seeing administrative enforcement action [soon].”

DataOne did not respond to questions regarding its unpermitted generators but said the company “remains committed to meeting all applicable environmental and permitting requirements.”

Nebius did not respond to requests for comment by publication. Microsoft declined to comment. The Environmental Protection Agency told Floodlight, after being presented with its findings, that New Jersey’s regulators are responsible for air permitting over DataOne.

DataOne is the first data center in New Jersey seeking to build its own power plant.

The controversial tactic was pioneered by Elon Musk’s data centers along the Tennessee and Mississippi border and has since gone mainstream: Nationwide, as of April, nearly 60 data centers are planning to build their own gas plants, according to research by energy analytics firm Cleanview.

The “bring your own power” strategy has resulted in yearslong backlogs for gas-powered turbines, with facilities increasingly turning to even less conventional energy sources, such as modified jet engines and portable generators.

In Vineland, DataOne originally submitted a permit application for more than 30 Bergen gas-burning engines, which are commonly used to propel cruise ships. NJDEP, however, found multiple deficiencies in DataOne’s air permit application for the engines, according to public records reviewed by Floodlight.

DataOne withdrew the application in May and instead now plans to rely on an array of Bloom fuel cells capable of producing 300 megawatts. Though powered by gas, fuel cells use a combustion-free electrochemical process to generate electricity and result in far less health-harming air pollution than Bergen engines.

However, the fuel cells still produce large amounts of carbon dioxide, and a Bloom official testified at a planning board meeting that if completed, they could emit more than 2 billion pounds of the climate-warming gas every year.

Until the fuel cells are operational, however, the facility is relying on the unpermitted gas generators, the first of which appear to have been turned on in October, according to maintenance logs.

It’s unclear how long the equipment has been operational, but thermal drone footage captured by a data intelligence company appears to show 25 of the unpermitted gas generators operating in late June.

Local residents have complained of a pervasive humming noise coming from the data center for months, sparking a lawsuit in New Jersey state court over noise pollution that many suspect is linked to the generators. Andrew and Stevi Groetsch live less than a mile from the site and say the noise has awoken them in the middle of the night and often disturbs bedtime stories with their kids.

“It’s just constant. It never goes away,” Andrew Groetsch said. The couple has complained about the noise since November and hope NJDEP, the county and the EPA will “at least get that part of it shut down and put a closer eye” on the rest of the project.

“If you don’t follow one rule, what makes us have any reason to believe that you would then follow others?” Stevi Groetsch asked. “It’s so upsetting.”

If the DEP decides to issue an enforcement action over the unpermitted generators, it wouldn’t be the first time New Jersey officials have cited DataOne for violations.

A lawsuit brought by local residents alleges that the Cumberland County Department of Public Health cited DataOne for violating noise ordinances for nighttime sound levels at the site in March. Earlier this month, the City of Vineland issued two stop work orders, including for moving the fuel cells onsite without permission — the same fuel cells meant to eventually replace the unpermitted generators.

“It seems that this industry, in particular, values speed to market more than almost anything else,” Buckheit said. He suspects the company won’t stop operating the generators until they are issued a stop work order because they “seem to believe that it’s better to ask for forgiveness than for permission.”

This article was produced in partnership between Floodlight and The Guardian.

title: As US grid reliability risks mount, distributed BESS offer solutions - Energy-Storage.News
description:
Elsewhere, microgrids can provide reliable electricity to areas without grid access or with only weak links to utility distribution networks.
WestLight receives funding for Northern California microgrid California Community Choice Aggregator (CCA) WestLight Energy has received final funding to build a microgrid in Northern California’s Pescadero community.
According to WestLight, these grant funds will be combined with contributions of US$10 million from WestLight Energy and US$3 million from the County of San Mateo.
This marks Otter Tail Power’s first BESS project.
That project, combining .5MW of solar PV generation with 21MWh of BESS across two microgrid sites, also utilises a BESS solution from Eos.
text:
Advances in BESS capacity have made it viable for residential and commercial properties to install on-site solar generation systems that capture energy during production periods and store it for later use. These buildings can remain connected to the grid, drawing conventional power when costs are low whilst switching to stored renewable energy during peak demand.

The consequences of grid vulnerability were starkly illustrated in August, when Gary, Indiana experienced approximately 14 days of power outages affecting tens of thousands of residents. Whilst the widespread outages were initially caused by wind storms, citizens of Gary have filed a class action lawsuit against utility NIPSCO alleging it failed to trim vegetation near power lines.

Data from the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission (IURC) shows that NIPSCO charges the state’s highest electricity rates at US$233.62-per-1,000kWh. IURC records further indicate that NIPSCO maintains the poorest reliability performance of all utilities operating in Indiana, despite these premium rates.

Elsewhere, microgrids can provide reliable electricity to areas without grid access or with only weak links to utility distribution networks. This also enables local communities to deploy renewables and be protected from disruptions that cause blackouts or disconnection from the main grid.

Crucially, in some parts of the US, such as rural California, which suffer intensifying and longer wildfire seasons, microgrids can reduce the need to build out grid infrastructure, which can cause wildfires if wires come down during storms or are inadequately maintained. California has already seen a buildout of state-supported microgrids by its three investor-owned utilities (IOU).

Last week, the state’s governor, Gavin Newsom and the state’s Senate and Assembly came to an agreement on Senate Bill 492 (SB 294), which sets out the wildfire liabilities of IOUs Pacific Gas & Electric (PG&E), Southern California Edison and San Diego Gas & Electric (SDG&E).

Against this backdrop of reliability concerns and rising electricity costs, three recent projects demonstrate how rural and distributed BESS deployments are addressing energy resilience across diverse American communities.

WestLight receives funding for Northern California microgrid

California Community Choice Aggregator (CCA) WestLight Energy has received final funding to build a microgrid in Northern California’s Pescadero community.

Announced 27 August, WestLight will receive a US$3.5 million grant from utility Pacific Gas & Electric’s (PG&E’s) Microgrid Incentive Programme (MIP), a California Public Utility Commission (CPUC)-directed programme that all three California investor-owned utilities (IOUs) administer.

In addition to the US$3.5 million MIP grant, PG&E is providing up to US$4 million to pay for interconnection and microgrid studies and required PG&E grid upgrades to enable the microgrid to safely island.

According to WestLight, these grant funds will be combined with contributions of US$10 million from WestLight Energy and US$3 million from the County of San Mateo.

The project is a collaborative effort led by WestLight and supported by entrepreneur Irma Rodriguez Mitton of Arriba South Coast as the community liaison, the Sustainability Department and Office of Emergency Services from the County of San Mateo, and the Clean Coalition as a technical partner.

WestLight stated that the 700-person rural farming community of Pescadero has experienced recurring power outages that disrupt residents, businesses, schools and essential services.

Mitton, founder and Executive Director of the community-based nonprofit Arriba Southcoast, worked with community members to identify a solution to the town’s frequent outages. After identifying the MIP as a potential funding source, Mitton sought a partner with the necessary technical expertise, ultimately collaborating with WestLight Energy, which assembled the additional partners, funding and technical capabilities needed for the project.

Construction is anticipated to begin in mid-2029, with service expected to begin in mid-2031.

Once completed, the 1.5MW solar and 8MWh BESS microgrid is expected to serve nearly all of Pescadero, providing three days of backup power in average winter conditions and seven days in average summer conditions.

The MIP rules were approved in 2023, stating that an individual project can get up to US$15 million, with IOUs sharing the total based on their relative size and needs: Southern California Edison (SCE) got the biggest share, at US$83.3 million, PG&E US$79.2 million and San Diego Gas & Electric (SDG&E) share was US$17.5 million.

In March 2025, PG&E announced its intent to award up to US$43 million in grant funding for nine community-driven microgrids in the state.

Richardson Electronics to deploy 18 BESS units across remote Alaskan communities

US power electronics manufacturer Richardson Electronics has announced it will deliver 18 customised BESS for deployment across seven remote communities in Alaska.

The multi-million-dollar programme will provide a combined energy storage capacity of 7MWh, with project completion expected by the end of 2027.

Richardson claimed that each system is being engineered to meet the unique energy requirements of its respective community, with a focus on performance, reliability and operation in demanding environmental conditions.

As remote communities in Alaska work to strengthen energy resilience and improve the reliability of their power infrastructure, renewable energy and energy storage technologies are becoming increasingly important. Richardson Electronics has developed customised energy storage solutions designed to operate reliably in Alaska’s challenging climate and extreme temperatures.

Richardson further stated that the project demonstrates its ability to combine its engineering, manufacturing and systems integration expertise with complementary technologies from its partners to address complex power management applications.

In 2024, utility Golden Valley Electric Association (GVEA) announced it would receive US$206 million from the US Department of Agriculture’s Empowering Rural America (New ERA) programme to help develop three projects, including a 46MW/92MWh BESS in Fairbanks, Alaska.

Shortly after, utility Chugach Electric Association successfully commissioned a 40MW/80MWh BESS in Anchorage, Alaska.

University of Minnesota Morris installs 1MW/6MWh Eos BESS

The University of Minnesota (UMN) Morris is advancing an energy storage project with the installation of a 1MW/6MWh non-lithium battery on its campus.

The project brings together UMN Morris, utility Otter Tail Power Company and Open Access Technology International (OATI) in a partnership “to demonstrate non-flammable zinc-based long-duration energy storage (LDES) in a real-world utility and campus setting.”

OATI will install zinc hybrid cathode battery and storage system maker Eos’ Z3 BESS solution.

OATI stated that Eos’ aqueous zinc chemistry, which can operate across a wide range of temperatures, is suited to Minnesota’s extreme seasonal conditions. forms the basis of the Z3 system, engineered for safe, durable operation and supporting frequent charge and discharge cycles with minimal degradation over time.

Under the partnership, Otter Tail Power will operate the Z3 system, connected directly to the utility’s electrical system. The installation became part of Otter Tail Power’s infrastructure following approval by the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission (MPUC) in March 2026. This marks Otter Tail Power’s first BESS project.

While Otter Tail Power will use the Z3 BESS to support grid reliability, the university will have dedicated research periods throughout the project’s anticipated 20-year lifespan to study the battery’s performance under different operating scenarios.

OATI’s GridMind software will manage and optimise the battery’s operation, including when it charges and discharges based on grid conditions and utility needs.

The system is expected to be commissioned on the university’s campus in 2027, with Burns & McDonnell providing engineering support for its installation.

The system has been intentionally sited along a highly travelled campus walkway, where students, visitors and community members will be able to see the technology firsthand. The BESS will join a diverse portfolio of energy technologies already operating on campus, including lithium-ion battery storage, wind turbines, solar arrays and an agrivoltaics installation.

Funding was provided by the Minnesota Environment and Natural Resources Trust Fund, as recommended by the Legislative-Citizen Commission on Minnesota Resources (LCCMR).

UMN Morris claimed that its campus generates more than 60% of its daily electricity needs from on-site renewable resources, including wind power from its two wind turbines and solar energy from campus solar arrays.

In June, OATI announced it had partnered with the Paskenta Band of Nomlaki Indians to integrate advanced microgrid controls into a two-part solar and BESS project in Northern California.

That project, combining .5MW of solar PV generation with 21MWh of BESS across two microgrid sites, also utilises a BESS solution from Eos.

text:
Electric cooperatives across the country are breaking ground on projects under the Wildfire Assessment and Resilience for Networks consortium, a Department of Energy-funded effort to combat wildfire threats and protect consumers’ access to electricity.

More than 30 participating co-ops gave project updates during NRECA Research’s second annual WARN consortium meeting in Washington, D.C. The meeting also included presentations by wildfire mitigation technology providers and NRECA staff supporting the WARN project.

NRECA Research manages the overall project for the benefit of the consortium and the association’s wider membership, with Holy Cross Energy serving as the lead co-op.

“You have a group of cooperatives doing what we do best—coming together and collaborating and bringing multiple parties to an effort that individually would have been burdensome and difficult for any cooperative to tackle on its own,” NRECA Chief Operating Officer Jeffrey Connor said at the Aug. 26-27 gathering.

The co-op WARN projects, funded partly by the DOE’s Grid Resilience and Innovation Partnership grant program, will improve system reliability and resilience and help mitigate the risk of utility-ignited fires.

The initiative will also help co-ops assess the value of wildfire-related resilience upgrades, including protecting grid assets, property and other resources—information that can guide investments in mitigation nationwide.

“The work that you do through these grants and through this program is going to create an example that others can follow,” Connor said. “That is part of the responsibility that NRECA has with you, to make sure that the learnings and the successes that you have and the challenges that you overcome are known to other electric cooperatives as they go out and tackle these same issues.”

The WARN consortium is made up of 35 co-ops that banded together to apply for funding through GRIP, a $10.5 billion NRECA-backed program created through the bipartisan infrastructure law of 2021. NRECA has worked to protect the program ever since. Altogether, WARN will provide more than $140 million in wildfire mitigation funding to co-ops across 17 Western and Midwest states.

“The work you’re leading is reshaping how America prepares for wildfires, how cooperatives protect the communities they serve, and how our nation strengthens the grid under conditions that are evolving faster than ever,” Vicki Tran, deputy assistant secretary of the DOE’s Office of Electricity, told co-ops at the event.

The expertise built through the WARN consortium “will be shared throughout the entire NRECA cooperative network nationwide,” she said.

As of Aug. 26, seven co-ops have been cleared to start construction on WARN projects:

Holy Cross Energy (Glenwood Springs, Colorado): Replacing overhead power lines in Garfield County with underground infrastructure. Construction began earlier this year, with 13 miles of new underground lines expected to be energized in 2029.

Springer Electric Cooperative (Springer, New Mexico): Installing fire-resistant mesh wraps on 371 poles across the Kiowa National Grasslands in Colfax and Harding Counties, New Mexico. The co-op is aiming to complete the project this September.

Beartooth Electric Cooperative (Red Lodge, Montana): Undergrounding 5.1 miles of power line in its East Rosebud Corridor in 2026-2027. Construction on the second phase of the project to underground lines around the East Rosebud Lake community will take place in 2027-2029.

Capital Electric Cooperative (Bismarck, North Dakota): Converting an 11-mile, three-phase power line to underground conductors. Construction began in April and finished at the end of July.

Consumers Power Inc. (Philomath, Oregon): Undergrounding circuits and upgrading meter bases in the remote Santiam Canyon, where devastating wildfires in 2020 destroyed much of CPI’s system. CPI anticipates breaking ground in the coming weeks, with completion targeted for September 2027.

Cotton Electric Cooperative (Walters, Oklahoma): Performing a range of upgrades including vegetation management, copper conductor replacement, pole inspection and replacement, and recloser modernization. Project completion is targeted for 2028.

Highline Electric Association (Holyoke, Colorado): Installing 28 reclosers at various points on the co-op’s distribution line and within distribution substations to automatically detect faults and stop and restart power flows based on wildfire risk. Project completion is targeted for 2027 or 2028 at the latest.

Other WARN consortium members are making progress on their projects and may get the greenlight soon to start construction, said Lauren Khair, senior director of energy research and resilience for NRECA’s Business and Technology Strategies group.

“In the next few months, many of the WARN consortium members will be ready to proceed to construction and put these critical investments to work in their communities,” Khair said.

She also flagged existing DOE money available for consortium members to cover their investments in advanced wildfire mitigation technologies, including drones, cameras and sensors to help increase their overall system reliability and situational awareness.

“This is a great time for us to reflect on the process so far and the progress that we’ve made but also the great things that are awaiting us,” Holy Cross President and CEO Bryan Hannegan said.

Hannegan is the principal investigator for the WARN project and works in coordination with NRECA Research on the initiative.

The value of the WARN project “goes far beyond a successful construction project,” said Greg Owen, manager of engineering services for Capital Electric in North Dakota. “We learned about the hazards surrounding wildfires, how to be aware of wildfire risks in both real-time alerts and long-range planning.

“By better understanding how and where wildfires are likely to occur, we can plan system improvements to align our reliability goals with hazard mitigation outcomes,” he said.

Consumers Power in Oregon “is grateful for the opportunity to work with NRECA and the WARN consortium,” project manager Austin Jackson said. “The [cooperation], shared expertise and grant funding will allow us to finish undergrounding electric services in the Santiam Canyon. This work will strengthen the system and help reduce wildfire risk for a community recovering from devastating fires in 2020.”
